p.seg: 1.1 "Esteeming Scholars First"
When entering a state, if one does not cherish its scholars,
then the state will perish.
Upon encountering the worthy, if one does not urgently attend to them,
they will neglect their ruler.
Without the worthy, there is no urgency;
without scholars, there is none to deliberate on state affairs.
To neglect the worthy and forget scholars,
yet still be able to preserve one's state,
has never been possible.
In the past, Duke Wén fled and later rectified the world;
Duke Huán left his state and dominated the feudal lords;
King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè suffered humiliation from the King of Wú,
yet still became a revered ruler of the central states.
These three were able to achieve fame and success under heaven,
all because they endured great humiliation in their own states.
The highest ideal is to never fail;
the next best is to fail yet still achieve success.
This is called employing the people.
I have heard it said:
"It is not that I lack a peaceful dwelling,
but that I lack a peaceful heart.
It is not that I lack sufficient wealth,
but that I lack a contented heart."
Thus, the noble man takes on difficulties himself and eases them for others,
while the multitude eases themselves and imposes difficulties on others.
The noble man advances without compromising his aspirations,
and inwardly examines his feelings.
Even if mixed among common people,
he ultimately harbors no resentment,
for he has self-confidence.
Therefore, by undertaking what is difficult,
one is sure to attain what is desired;
it is unheard of to pursue only desires
and avoid what is detested.
Thus, oppressive ministers harm the ruler;
flattering subordinates harm their superiors.
The ruler must have ministers who oppose him;
the superior must have subordinates who argue frankly.
Those who debate differing views should be persistent,
and those who offer loyal admonitions should be outspoken.
Only then can the state be preserved long.
If ministers value their ranks and remain silent,
close ministers become mute,
distant ministers become reticent,
resentment accumulates in the people's hearts,
flattery and sycophancy surround the ruler,
and good counsel is blocked,
then the state is endangered.
Did Jié and Zhòu not have scholars under heaven?
They were killed and lost the world.
Hence it is said:
"Presenting state treasures
is not as good as recommending the worthy and advancing scholars."
Suppose there are five awls,
and this one is the sharpest;
the sharpest is sure to be blunted first.
Suppose there are five knives,
and this one is the ground one;
the ground one is sure to wear out first.
Thus, sweet wells are exhausted first;
tall trees are felled first;
divine tortoises are scorched first;
sacred snakes are exposed first.
Therefore, Bǐ Gān's death
was due to his uprightness;
Mèng Bēn's killing
was due to his courage;
Xī Shī's drowning
was due to her beauty;
Wǔ Qǐ's dismemberment
was due to his achievements.
Thus, such people
rarely do not die because of their strengths.
Hence it is said, "Extreme prominence is hard to maintain."
Therefore, even a worthy ruler
does not love ministers without merit;
even a kind father
does not love useless sons.
Thus, one who cannot fulfill the duties of a position
is not the right person for it;
one who does not deserve a rank but receives its emolument
is not the true master of that emolument.
A good bow is hard to draw,
yet it can reach high and penetrate deep;
a good horse is hard to ride,
yet it can bear heavy loads and travel far;
a talented person is hard to command,
yet he can make the ruler respected.
Thus, rivers do not dislike small streams filling them,
so they can become great.
The sage
does not refuse any task,
does not oppose any thing,
thus he can become a vessel for the world.
Therefore, the water of rivers
does not come from a single source;
a robe worth a thousand yì
is not made from a single fox's white fur.
How can one only take those of the same way
and reject those who are merely alike?
That is not the way of a universal king.
Thus, heaven and earth are not always bright;
great waters are not always clear;
great fires are not always blazing;
the kingly virtue is not always lofty.
Only then can one lead a thousand people.
As straight as an arrow,
as level as a whetstone,
it is not enough to cover all things.
Thus, narrow streams dry up quickly;
shallow currents exhaust quickly;
barren land does not produce.
If rich blessings
do not extend beyond the palace,
they cannot flow throughout the state.
1.2 "Cultivating the Self Second"
In battle, though the noble man has formations,
courage is the foundation.
In mourning, though there are rites,
grief is the foundation.
For scholars, though there is learning,
conduct is the foundation.
Thus, if the foundation is not firm,
do not strive to enrich the branches.
If those nearby are not close,
do not strive to attract the distant.
If relatives are not attached,
do not strive for external relations.
If affairs lack beginning and end,
do not strive for many undertakings.
If one is ignorant in handling matters,
do not strive to spread hearsay.
Thus, when the ancient kings governed the world,
they surely examined the near to attract the far.
The noble man examines the near,
and the near is cultivated.
Seeing uncultivated conduct,
he reflects it upon himself when seeing criticism.
Thereby, resentment decreases and conduct is cultivated.
Slanderous words
do not enter the ear;
attacking sounds
do not leave the mouth;
thoughts of harming others
do not reside in the heart.
Even if there are slanderous and accusatory people,
they have nothing to rely on.
Thus, the noble man's efforts daily strengthen,
his aspirations daily exceed,
his established vigor daily flourishes.
The way of the noble man is:
in poverty, he shows integrity;
in wealth, he shows righteousness;
toward the living, he shows love;
toward the dead, he shows grief.
These four practices
cannot be falsely reversed in oneself.
What is stored in the heart never exhausts love;
what moves the body never exhausts respect;
what comes from the mouth never exhausts gentleness.
Pervading the four limbs,
connecting to the skin and flesh,
even with white hair and balding crown, yet never ceasing—
is this not only the sage?
One whose will is not strong
will not have wisdom that reaches far.
One whose words are not trustworthy
will not have resolute actions.
One who hoards wealth and cannot share it with others
is not worthy of friendship.
One who does not firmly uphold the Way,
whose knowledge is not broad,
and who cannot discern right from wrong clearly
is not worthy of association.
If the root is not firm,
the branches will surely be precarious.
One who is brave but does not cultivate virtue
will later become lazy.
If the source is muddy,
the stream will not be clear.
One whose actions are not trustworthy
will surely have their reputation tarnished.
Fame does not arise without cause,
and praise does not grow by itself.
When achievements are accomplished and fame is established,
reputation cannot be falsely claimed but must reflect one's true self.
Those who are quick to speak but slow to act,
though eloquent, will not be heeded;
those who boast of their efforts,
though hardworking, will not be appreciated.
The wise understand in heart without elaborate speech,
and they labor without boasting of their merits,
thus their fame spreads throughout the world.
Speech should not aim at quantity but at wisdom,
not at ornamentation but at clarity.
Therefore, those lacking wisdom and clarity within themselves
will find their intentions leading them astray.
Goodness not rooted in the heart will not endure,
actions not justified by oneself will not stand.
Fame cannot be attained through simplicity,
nor reputation established through cunning.
The noble person embodies their actions with their whole being.
If one pursues profit earnestly
but neglects fame carelessly,
such a person has never been found
who can become a true scholar under heaven.
1.3 "On the Influence of Associations - Third"
Mòzǐ, seeing the dyeing of silk, sighed and said:
Dyed in blue, it becomes blue;
dyed in yellow, it becomes yellow.
The dye changes,
and the color changes accordingly.
After five dips,
it becomes five-colored.
Thus, one must be cautious about dyeing.
Not only is this true for dyeing silk;
states also undergo dyeing.
Shùn was dyed by Xǔ Yóu and Bó Yáng,
Yǔ by Gāo Yáo and Bó Yì,
Tāng by Yī Yǐn and Zhòng Huǐ,
and King Wǔ by Tài Gōng and Zhōu Gōng.
These four kings were dyed rightly,
thus they ruled the world,
were established as Sons of Heaven,
and their achievements and fame overshadowed heaven and earth.
When mentioning the righteous and illustrious men of the world,
these four kings are always cited.
Jié of Xià was dyed by Gān Xīn and Tuī Chǐ,
Zhòu of Yīn by Chóng Hóu and È Lái,
King Lì by Lì Gōng Zhǎng Fù and Róng Yí Zhōng,
and King Yōu by Fù Gōng Yí and Cài Gōng Gǔ.
These four kings were dyed wrongly,
thus their states were ruined and they met death,
becoming scorned by the world.
When mentioning the unrighteous and disgraced men of the world,
these four kings are always cited.
Duke Huán of Qí was dyed by Guǎn Zhòng and Bào Shū,
Duke Wén of Jìn by Jiù Fàn and Guō Yǎn,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ by Sūn Shū and Shěn Yǐn,
Hé Lǘ of Wú by Wǔ Yuán and Wén Yì,
and Gōu Jiàn of Yuè by Fàn Lǐ and Dàfū Zhǒng.
These five lords were dyed rightly,
thus they became hegemons among the feudal lords,
and their achievements and fame were passed down to later generations.
Fàn Jí Shè was dyed by Cháng Liǔ Shuò and Wáng Shè,
Zhōng Háng Yín by Jí Qín and Gāo Qiáng,
Fū Chāi of Wú by Wáng Sūn Luò and Tài Zǎi Pǐ,
Zhì Bó Yáo by Zhì Guó and Zhāng Wǔ,
Shàng of Zhōngshān by Wèi Yì and Yǎn Cháng,
and Kāng of Sòng by Táng Yāng and Yòu Bù Lǐ.
These six lords were dyed wrongly,
thus their states were destroyed and lost,
they themselves suffered execution,
their ancestral temples were ruined,
their lineages were cut off without descendants,
their officials were scattered,
and their people were displaced.
When mentioning the greedy, violent, and oppressive men of the world,
these six lords are always cited.
What brings security to a ruler?
It is due to his adherence to principle,
and adherence to principle stems from being dyed rightly.
Thus, a skilled ruler
exerts effort in selecting people,
but is at ease in governing officials.
An incapable ruler
harms his body and exhausts his spirit,
worries and toils in mind,
yet his state becomes more perilous,
and his person more disgraced.
These six lords
did not fail to value their states or love themselves,
but they did not know the essential point.
Not knowing the essential point
means they were dyed wrongly.
Not only states undergo dyeing;
scholars also undergo dyeing.
If one's friends all love righteousness,
are sincere, cautious, and law-abiding,
then one's family prospers daily, one's person becomes more secure, and one's reputation grows more honorable,
and in office, one governs rightly—
such were Duàngān Mù, Qínzǐ, and Fù Yuè.
If one's friends are all boastful and aggressive,
deceitful and cliquish,
then one's family declines daily, one's person becomes more endangered, and one's reputation grows more shameful,
and in office, one governs wrongly—
such were Zǐ Xī, Yì Yá, and Shù Diāo.
The *Book of Songs* says, "One must choose what to immerse in,
one must be cautious about what to immerse in."
This refers to this idea.
1.4 "On the Standard of Law - Fourth"
Mòzǐ said:
Those who undertake tasks in the world
cannot be without a standard of law.
Without a standard of law, yet succeeding in their affairs—
there is no such thing.
Even the scholars who become generals or ministers have their standards,
and even the various artisans at work have their standards.
Artisans use the square for making squares,
the compass for making circles,
the line for straightness,
water for leveling,
and the plumb line for verticality.
Whether skilled or unskilled,
all take these five as standards.
The skilled can hit the mark with them,
while the unskilled, though unable to hit the mark,
by imitating and relying on them in their work,
still surpass their own unaided efforts.
Thus, all artisans in their work
have standards to measure by.
Now, on a grand scale, governing the world,
or next, governing a great state,
yet having no standard to measure by—
this is inferior to the discernment of artisans.
Then what can be taken as the standard for governance?
Should all model themselves after their parents?
There are many parents in the world,
but few are benevolent.
If all model themselves after their parents,
this standard would be unbenevolent.
An unbenevolent standard
cannot serve as a standard.
Should all model themselves after their teachers?
There are many teachers in the world,
but few are benevolent.
If all model themselves after their teachers,
this standard would be unbenevolent.
An unbenevolent standard
cannot serve as a standard.
Should all model themselves after their rulers?
There are many rulers in the world,
but few are benevolent.
If all model themselves after their rulers,
this standard would be unbenevolent.
An unbenevolent standard
cannot serve as a standard.
Thus, parents, teachers, and rulers—these three—
none can serve as the standard for governance.
Then what can be taken as the model for governing?
Hence it is said:
Nothing is better than modeling after Heaven.
Heaven's conduct is broad and selfless,
its bestowals are generous without seeking virtue,
its brightness endures without fading,
thus the sage kings emulate it.
Since they take Heaven as the model,
in every action and undertaking,
they must measure by Heaven,
what Heaven desires, they do;
what Heaven does not desire, they cease.
But what does Heaven desire and dislike?
Heaven surely desires humans to love and benefit each other,
and does not desire humans to hate and harm each other.
How do we know that Heaven desires humans to love and benefit each other,
and does not desire them to hate and harm each other?
Because it universally loves them,
and universally benefits them.
How do we know Heaven universally loves them,
and universally benefits them?
Because it universally possesses them,
and universally nourishes them.
Now all states great and small under heaven
are cities of Heaven.
All people, young and old, noble and humble,
are subjects of Heaven.
Hence none fail to feed oxen and sheep,
raise dogs and pigs,
prepare clean wine and millet offerings,
to reverently serve Heaven.
Is this not universal possession
and universal nourishment?
If Heaven indeed universally possesses and nourishes them,
how can it be said that it does not desire humans to love and benefit each other?
Therefore it is said:
"Those who love and benefit others,
Heaven will surely bless.
Those who hate and harm others,
Heaven will surely curse."
It is said: "Those who kill the innocent
receive inauspicious outcomes.
How can it be said that when people kill each other, Heaven would give them blessings?
Thus Heaven desires humans to love and benefit each other,
and does not desire them to hate and harm each other."
In ancient times, the sage kings Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ,
universally loved the common people under heaven,
leading them to honor Heaven and serve spirits,
they benefited many people,
thus Heaven blessed them,
establishing them as Sons of Heaven,
and all feudal lords under heaven served them as guests.
The tyrant kings Jié, Zhòu, Yōu, and Lì,
universally hated the common people under heaven,
leading them to curse Heaven and insult spirits,
they harmed many people,
thus Heaven cursed them,
causing them to lose their states,
die and be humiliated under heaven,
their descendants reviling them,
which continues to this day without cease.
Thus those who do evil and receive curses
are Jié, Zhòu, Yōu, and Lì.
Those who love and benefit others and receive blessings
are Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ.
There are those who love and benefit others and receive blessings,
and there are those who hate and harm others and receive curses.
1.5 The Seven Calamities - Chapter Five
Mòzǐ said:
The state has seven calamities.
What are the seven calamities?
When city walls and moats cannot be defended,
yet palaces are built,
this is the first calamity.
When enemy states reach the border,
and neighboring states do not rescue,
this is the second calamity.
When people's strength is exhausted on useless works,
and rewards are given to incompetent people,
people's strength is spent on useless things,
and treasures are depleted on entertaining guests,
this is the third calamity.
When officials cling to their salaries,
and wandering scholars cherish friendships,
the ruler cultivates laws to punish ministers,
and ministers are intimidated and dare not remonstrate,
this is the fourth calamity.
When the ruler considers himself sage and wise without consulting affairs,
thinks himself secure and strong without defense preparations,
and neighboring states plot without his awareness,
this is the fifth calamity.
When those trusted are not loyal,
and those loyal are not trusted,
this is the sixth calamity.
When stored grains and millets
are insufficient to feed people,
ministers are insufficient to serve,
rewards cannot bring joy,
and punishments cannot inspire awe,
this is the seventh calamity.
Governing a state with these seven calamities,
will surely lead to loss of the altars of soil and grain.
Defending a city with these seven calamities,
when enemies come, the state will fall.
Where the seven calamities reside,
the state will surely suffer disaster.
All the five grains
are what the people depend on,
and what the ruler uses for sustenance.
Thus if the people have nothing to depend on, the ruler has no sustenance;
if the people have no food, they cannot be employed.
Therefore food production must not be neglected,
land must not be left untilled,
and expenditures must not be unthrifty.
When all five grains are harvested,
the ruler enjoys all five flavors;
if not all are harvested,
then not all flavors are enjoyed.
Failure of one grain is called jǐn,
failure of two grains is called hàn,
failure of three grains is called xiōng,
failure of four grains is called kuì,
failure of all five grains is called jī.
In years of jǐn,
officials from dàfū down reduce their salaries by one-fifth.
In hàn,
they reduce by two-fifths.
In xiōng,
they reduce by three-fifths.
In kuì,
they reduce by four-fifths.
In jī,
they receive no salaries at all,
only sustenance rations.
Thus when xiōng and jī exist in the state,
the ruler removes five-fifths of his tripod meals,
dàfū remove their hanging bells,
scholars do not enter schools,
the ruler's court robes are not remade,
guests from feudal lords,
envoys from neighboring states,
are served plain meals without lavishness.
Side horses are removed from carriages,
roads are not swept,
horses are not fed grain,
maids and concubines do not wear silk,
this announces the extremity of insufficiency.
Now if someone carrying their child to fetch water
lets their child fall into the well,
the mother will surely go and rescue them.
Now in years of xiōng,
people are hungry and starving on the roads,
this distress is heavier than losing a child in a well,
how can it be ignored?
Thus when the year is good,
the people are benevolent and good;
when the year is bad,
the people are stingy and evil.
How can the people be constant in this?
When producers are few,
and consumers many,
then the year cannot be abundant.
Therefore it is said:
"When wealth is insufficient, examine the timing;
when food is insufficient, examine the expenditures."
Thus the ancient people generated wealth according to the season,
strengthened the foundation and used wealth thriftily,
then wealth was sufficient.
Thus even the sage kings of highest antiquity,
could they make the five grains always harvest,
and prevent drought and flood from coming?
Yet they had no people suffering cold and hunger,
why?
They worked urgently in season,
and nourished themselves frugally.
Hence the Xià Shū says:
"Yǔ had seven years of flood."
The Yīn Shū says:
"Tāng had five years of drought."
This shows they encountered severe xiōng and jī.
Yet the people did not suffer cold and hunger,
why?
They generated wealth diligently,
and used it thriftily.
Therefore, if the granaries are not stocked with grain,
one cannot cope with famine.
If the armories are not equipped with weapons,
even if one has righteousness,
one cannot subdue the unrighteous.
If the city walls are not fully prepared,
one cannot defend oneself.
If the mind is not prepared with forethought,
one cannot respond to emergencies.
This is like Qìng Jì lacking the intention to leave,
and thus unable to escape lightly.
Jié lacked preparations against Tāng,
so he was exiled.
Zhòu lacked preparations against King Wǔ,
so he was killed.
Though Jié and Zhòu were honored as sons of heaven,
and possessed the wealth of the entire world,
they were both destroyed by lords of a hundred lǐ.
Why is that?
Because they had wealth and honor but made no preparations.
Thus, preparedness
is of great importance to the state.
Food is the treasure of the state,
weapons are the claws of the state,
and city walls are for self-defense.
These three are the essential tools of the state.
Hence it is said:
By employing them in necessary labor,
and repairing their city walls,
the people toil but are not harmed;
by using regular taxes,
and collecting their dues,
the people expend but do not suffer.
What the people suffer from
is not these.
They suffer from heavy exactions imposed on the common people,
rewarding the undeserving with gifts,
emptying the treasuries,
to prepare for carriages, horses, robes, and rare curiosities.
They suffer from forced labor,
used to build palaces and places of amusement,
and in death, thick coffins are made,
with many burial robes.
In life, they build towers and pavilions,
and in death, they construct tombs.
Thus, the people suffer externally,
while the treasuries are exhausted internally,
those above are never satisfied with their pleasures,
and those below cannot endure their suffering.
Hence, the state, when faced with enemies, is harmed,
and the people, when encountering famine, perish.
These are all faults of inadequate preparedness.
Moreover, food
is what the sages treasure.
Therefore, the "Zhōu Shū" says:
"A state that does not have food for three years
is not a state;
a family that does not have food for three years
means the children are not its children."
This is called the state's preparedness.
1.6 "Cí Guò - The Sixth"
Mòzǐ said:
In ancient times, when people did not know how to build houses,
they lived on hills and mounds,
dwelling in caves.
The dampness below harmed the people,
so the sage kings built houses,
and the method for building houses
was:
"High enough to avoid dampness,
the sides sufficient to ward off wind and cold,
the top adequate to withstand snow, frost, rain, and dew,
and the height of the palace walls
sufficient to distinguish the rites between men and women.
Only this much is necessary;
any expenditure of wealth and labor that does not add benefit
is not done."
Therefore, when the sage kings built houses,
it was for convenience in living,
not for spectacle and pleasure.
When making clothing, belts, and shoes,
it was for comfort of the body,
not to be peculiar.
Thus, frugal in their own persons,
they taught the people,
so the people of the world could be governed,
and resources could be sufficient.
The rulers of today,
in building houses, differ from this.
They heavily tax the people,
forcibly seize their means of clothing and food,
to build houses, towers, and winding structures for display,
adorned with colors and carvings.
Building houses in this way,
those around them all emulate them.
Thus, their wealth is insufficient to cope with famine,
relieve the orphaned and widowed,
so the state is poor and the people difficult to govern.
If the ruler truly desires order in the world and hates chaos,
he must be frugal in building houses.
In ancient times, when people did not know how to make clothing,
they wore hides and tied grass,
which in winter were not light and warm,
and in summer not light and cool.
The sage kings considered this unsuitable for human comfort,
so they taught women to weave,
(Suffering from heavy exactions on the people).
Using silk and hemp,
hemp cloth and silk,
they made clothing for the people.
The method for making clothing was:
in winter, silk garments
sufficient to be light and warm,
in summer, linen garments
sufficient to be light and cool.
Only this much is necessary.
Thus, when the sages made clothing,
it was to fit the body and comfort the skin, and that was enough,
not to glorify the senses or impress the foolish.
At that time,
sturdy carriages and fine horses were not valued,
carvings and ornate patterns were not admired.
Why?
Because they were guided thus.
Thus, the people's resources for clothing and food
were sufficient for each family to cope with drought, flood, and famine.
Why?
Because they understood the means of self-sustenance,
and were not swayed by externals.
Therefore, the people were frugal and easy to govern,
and the ruler used resources sparingly and easily provided.
The treasuries were full,
sufficient to meet emergencies,
weapons were not blunted,
soldiers and people were not overworked,
and they were capable of subduing the rebellious,
so the enterprise of a hegemon could be pursued under heaven.
The kings of today,
in making clothing, differ from this.
What is light and warm in winter,
and light and cool in summer,
is already available.
Yet they heavily tax the people,
forcibly seize their means of clothing and food,
to make garments of brocade and ornate, extravagant patterns.
They cast metal for hooks,
and use pearls and jade for pendants.
Women engage in ornate work,
men in carvings,
for personal wear.
This does not add to warmth;
it merely wastes resources and labor,
all devoted to useless ends.
From this perspective,
their making of clothing
is not for the body,
but all for display.
Thus, the people become decadent and difficult to govern,
and the ruler becomes extravagant and hard to admonish.
With an extravagant ruler
governing a decadent people,
to expect no chaos
is impossible.
If the ruler truly desires order in the world and hates chaos,
he must be frugal in making clothing.
In ancient times when people did not know how to prepare food and drink,
they ate plain food and lived separately.
Thus the sages taught men to plow, cultivate, and plant,
thereby providing food for the people.
As for their food,
it was sufficient only to boost energy, fill emptiness, strengthen the body, and satisfy the stomach.
Hence their use of resources was frugal,
their self-sustenance was thrifty,
and the people were prosperous and the state well-governed.
Now it is not so:
heavy levies are imposed on the people,
to prepare fine foods of livestock,
steamed and roasted fish and turtles,
with large states accumulating hundreds of vessels,
small states accumulating tens of vessels.
Spread over a square zhang,
the eye cannot see it all,
the hand cannot handle it all,
the mouth cannot taste it all.
In winter it freezes,
in summer it spoils.
When the ruler indulges in such food and drink,
those around him emulate him,
thus the wealthy and noble are extravagant,
while the orphaned and widowed suffer cold and hunger.
To wish for no chaos
is impossible.
If the ruler truly desires the world to be well-governed and hates chaos,
he must exercise moderation in food and drink.
In ancient times when people did not know how to make boats and carts,
heavy burdens could not be moved,
and distant places could not be reached.
Thus the sage kings created boats and carts
to facilitate the people's affairs.
Their boats and carts
were complete, sturdy, light, and efficient,
capable of carrying heavy loads over long distances.
They required little expenditure,
yet provided great benefits,
so the people welcomed and benefited from them.
Decrees were not urgent yet were implemented,
the people were not overworked yet had ample supplies,
thus they rallied to the rulers.
The kings of today,
however, make boats and carts differently.
Though complete, sturdy, light, and efficient features are all present,
they heavily tax the people
to decorate the boats and carts,
adorning carts with ornate patterns,
and boats with carvings.
Women abandon their weaving to craft ornate patterns,
so the people suffer cold;
men leave their farming to do carvings,
so the people starve.
When the ruler makes boats and carts like this,
those around him emulate him,
thus the people face both hunger and cold,
leading them to wrongdoing.
More wrongdoing leads to severe punishments,
severe punishments lead to state chaos.
If the ruler truly desires the world to be well-governed and hates chaos,
he must exercise moderation in making boats and carts.
All that revolves between heaven and earth,
encompassed within the four seas,
the nature of the universe,
the harmony of yīn and yáng,
exists without exception,
and even the greatest sage cannot alter it.
How do we know this is so?
The sages have passed down:
for heaven and earth,
we speak of above and below;
for the four seasons,
we speak of yīn and yáng;
for human relations,
we speak of male and female;
for birds and beasts,
we speak of male and female, cock and hen.
This is the true nature of the universe,
and even the former kings,
could not change it.
Even the supreme sages of ancient times,
kept consorts without harming their conduct,
so the people bore no resentment.
With no confined women in the palace,
there were no widowers in the world.
With no confined women inside
and no widowers outside,
the people of the world multiplied.
The rulers of today,
in keeping consorts,
have large states confining thousands of women,
small states hundreds,
so many men in the world are widowers without wives,
and many women are confined without husbands.
Men miss their time,
so the population declines.
If the ruler truly desires the people to multiply and hates their decline,
he must exercise moderation in keeping consorts.
In all these five aspects,
the sages practiced frugality and moderation,
while the petty indulge in excess.
Frugality and moderation lead to prosperity,
excess leads to ruin.
These five must be moderated:
husband and wife moderated, and heaven and earth harmonize;
wind and rain moderated, and the five grains ripen;
clothing moderated, and skin and flesh harmonize.
1.7 "Three Criticisms, Seventh"
Chéng Fán asked Mòzǐ:
"You have said,
'The sage kings did not engage in music.'
Yet when feudal lords wearied of governance,
they rested to the music of bells and drums.
When officials wearied of governance,
they rested to the music of yú and sè.
When farmers plowed in spring and weeded in summer,
harvested in autumn and stored in winter,
they rested to the music of líng and fǒu.
Now you say,
'The sage kings did not engage in music.'
This is like harnessing a horse without unbridling it,
or drawing a bow without relaxing it—
is that not something no being with blood and breath can endure?"
Mòzǐ replied:
"In the past, Yáo and Shùn had the 'Dìqī',
using it as ritual,
and also as music.
When Tāng exiled Jié to the great waters,
encompassed the world and established himself as king,
with tasks accomplished and achievements set,
and no major troubles thereafter,
he adopted the music of the former kings,
and also created his own music,
named 'Hù',
and revised the 'Jiǔ Sháo'.
When King Wǔ defeated the Yīn and killed Zhòu,
encompassed the world and established himself as king,
with tasks accomplished and achievements set,
and no major troubles thereafter,
he adopted the music of the former kings,
and also created his own music,
named 'Xiàng'.
King Chéng of Zhōu adopted the music of the former kings,
and also created his own music,
named 'Zōu Yú'.
In governing the world, King Chéng of Zhōu
was not as good as King Wǔ.
King Wǔ in governing the world
was not as good as Tāng.
Tāng in governing the world
was not as good as Yáo and Shùn.
Thus, the more elaborate their music,
the less effective their governance.
From this we see
that music is not the means to govern the world."
Chéng Fán said:
"You say,
'The sage kings had no music.'
Yet this is also music—
how can you say the sage kings had no music?"
Mòzǐ replied:
"The sage kings' decrees were about sufficiency and insufficiency.
As for the benefit of eating,
knowing to eat when hungry
is wisdom,
yet it is as if without knowledge.
Now if the sage kings had music but little,
it is as if they had none."
2.1 "Exalting the Worthy, First, Eighth"
Mòzǐ said:
"In ancient times, the kings, dukes, and great officers who governed the state
all desired the state's wealth,
the people's multitude,
and the order of punishments and governance.
Yet instead of wealth, they got poverty;
instead of multitude, they got few;
instead of order, they got chaos.
Thus, they fundamentally lost what they desired
and gained what they hated.
What is the reason for this?"
Mòzǐ said:
"It lies in the kings, dukes, and great officers who govern the state
failing to govern by exalting the worthy and employing the capable.
Therefore, if a state has many worthy and good scholars,
then its governance is solid;
if it has few worthy and good scholars,
then its governance is weak.
Thus, the task of the great
is simply to multiply the worthy."
asked:
"So, what method can be used to multiply the number of worthy individuals?"
Mòzǐ replied:
"Suppose you wish to increase the number of skilled archers and charioteers in your state.
You must enrich and ennoble them,
respect and praise them,
and only then will the skilled archers and charioteers in the state become numerous.
How much more should this apply to the virtuous and worthy scholars,
profound in moral conduct,
eloquent in speech and debate,
and broad in knowledge of the Way and its arts?
These are truly the treasures of the state
and the supports of the altars of soil and grain.
They too must be enriched and ennobled,
respected and praised,
and then the good scholars of the state will also become numerous."
Therefore, when the sage kings of antiquity governed,
they declared:
"'Do not enrich the unrighteous,
do not ennoble the unrighteous,
do not be intimate with the unrighteous,
do not keep close to the unrighteous.'"
When the wealthy and noble in the state heard this,
they all withdrew and deliberated, saying:
"What we initially relied upon
was wealth and nobility.
Now our ruler promotes righteousness without avoiding the poor and humble;
therefore, we must practice righteousness."
Those who were intimate [with the ruler] heard this,
and also withdrew to deliberate, saying:
"What we initially relied upon
was intimacy.
Now our ruler promotes righteousness without avoiding the distant;
therefore, we must practice righteousness."
Those who were close [to the ruler] heard this,
and also withdrew to deliberate, saying:
"What we initially relied upon
was closeness.
Now our ruler promotes righteousness without avoiding the remote;
therefore, we must practice righteousness."
Those who were distant heard this,
and also withdrew to deliberate, saying:
"We initially thought that being distant meant having nothing to rely on,
but now our ruler promotes righteousness without avoiding the distant;
therefore, we must practice righteousness."
Until it reached the ministers from distant borders and outskirts, the minor sons at the gates and courtyards, the masses within the state, and the common people from the four frontiers—
upon hearing this, they all vied to practice righteousness.
Why was this so?
It is said:
The means by which the superior employs the subordinates
is one thing;
the means by which the subordinates serve the superior
is one method.
To use an analogy:
Suppose there is a high wall and deep palace.
Once the wall is erected with care,
a single gate is made on top.
If a thief enters,
close the gate by which he entered and search for him,
and the thief will have no way to escape.
Why is this so?
It is because the ruler holds the key.
Therefore, when the sage kings of antiquity governed,
they ranked virtue and exalted the worthy.
Even if they were farmers or artisans in the marketplaces,
if they had ability, they were promoted.
They were given high ranks,
generous emoluments,
assigned to tasks,
and granted decisive authority.
It was said:
"If their rank is not high, the people will not respect them;
if their emoluments are not generous, the people will not trust them;
if their governance decrees are not decisive, the people will not fear them."
Presenting these three things to the worthy
was not a reward for their worthiness,
but to ensure the success of their tasks.
Thus, at that time,
positions were filled according to virtue,
offices were served according to duties,
rewards were determined by labor,
and emoluments were distributed based on merit.
Therefore, officials were not perpetually noble,
and the people were not eternally humble.
Those with ability were promoted,
and those without were demoted.
Promoting public righteousness
and avoiding private grudges—
this is what these words mean.
Therefore, in antiquity, Yáo promoted Shùn from the north of Fúzé,
entrusted him with governance,
and the world was pacified.
Yǔ promoted Yì from among the people of Yīnfāng,
entrusted him with governance,
and the nine provinces were established.
Tāng promoted Yī Yǐn from the kitchens,
entrusted him with governance,
and his plans succeeded.
King Wén promoted Hóng Yāo and Tài Diān from among the hunters,
entrusted them with governance,
and the western lands submitted.
Thus, at that time,
even ministers with high emoluments and尊贵 positions
were all respectful and cautious in their duties,
and even farmers and artisans in the marketplaces
all strove to encourage and uphold righteousness.
Therefore, scholars
are those who assist and succeed [the ruler].
Hence, with scholars, plans are not thwarted,
the body is not wearied,
fame is established and merit achieved,
beauty is displayed and evil does not arise—
all this comes from obtaining scholars.
Therefore, Mòzǐ said:
"In times of success,
worthy scholars must be promoted;
in times of failure,
worthy scholars must be promoted.
If you wish to follow the ways of Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, and Tāng,
you cannot but exalt the worthy.
For exalting the worthy
is the foundation of governance."
2.2 "Exalting the Worthy II, Chapter 9"
Mòzǐ said:
"Now, the kings, dukes, and great men who rule the people, preside over the altars of soil and grain, and govern the state,
wishing to maintain and not lose it—
why do they not understand that exalting the worthy is the foundation of governance?
How do we know that exalting the worthy is the foundation of governance?
It is said:
When the noble and wise govern the foolish and humble, there is order;
when the foolish and humble govern the noble and wise, there is chaos.
Thus we know that exalting the worthy is the foundation of governance.
Therefore, the sage kings of antiquity greatly honored and exalted the worthy and employed the capable.
They did not favor fathers and brothers,
did not show partiality to the rich and noble,
and were not captivated by beauty.
The worthy were promoted and elevated,
enriched and ennobled,
and made officials and leaders.
The unworthy were suppressed and dismissed,
impoverished and humbled,
and made servants and laborers.
Thus, the people were all encouraged by the rewards,
feared the punishments,
and vied to become worthy.
Hence, the worthy were many and the unworthy few—
this is called advancing the worthy.
Then, the sage would listen to their words,
observe their actions,
examine their abilities, and carefully assign them offices—
this is called employing the capable.
Thus, those who could govern the state
were set to govern the state.
Those who could lead offices
were set to lead offices.
Those who could govern towns
were set to govern towns.
All those assigned to govern the state, government offices, and townships—
these were all the worthy of the state.
"When the worthy govern the state,
they attend court early and retire late,
hearing lawsuits and managing governance,
so the state is well-governed and punishments are just.
When the worthy lead offices,
they retire late and rise early,
collecting the profits from passes, markets, mountains, forests, and marshes,
to fill the government stores,
so the government is full and wealth is not dispersed.
When the worthy govern towns,
they go out early and return late,
plowing, sowing, planting, and cultivating,
gathering beans and millet,
so beans and millet are abundant and the people have enough to eat.
Thus, when the state is well-governed, punishments are just;
when the government is full, the myriad people are prosperous.
Above, there are clean wine and millet offerings
to sacrifice to Heaven and ghosts.
Externally, there are hides and silk
to interact with the feudal lords of the four neighbors.
Internally, there is food for the hungry and rest for the weary,
sustaining and nurturing the myriad people.
Externally, there is the means to attract the worthy of the world.
Therefore, above, Heaven and ghosts enrich them;
externally, the feudal lords ally with them;
internally, the myriad people are close to them;
the worthy return to them.
With this, they succeed in planning affairs,
accomplish what they undertake,
are firm in defense,
and strong in offense.
Thus, the way the sage kings of the three dynasties—Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ—ruled the world and corrected the feudal lords
was also by this method."
"Since we call this a principle,
if the method for its implementation remains unknown,
then matters remain as if unaccomplished.
Therefore, it is essential to establish three foundations.
What are these three foundations?
They are:
If official ranks are not high, the people will not respect them;
if emoluments are not generous, the people will not trust them;
if decrees are not decisive, the people will not fear them.
Thus, the ancient sage kings bestowed high ranks,
granted substantial emoluments,
assigned them responsibilities,
and issued decisive orders.
Was this merely to reward their ministers?
It was because they desired the success of their affairs.
The Book of Songs says:
'I tell you of cares and compassion,
instruct you on conferring ranks;
who can handle heat
without using water to wash?'
This means that the rulers and lords of antiquity could not but uphold goodness in inheriting and assisting,
just as one handling heat uses washing
to soothe their hands.
The ancient sage kings only sought to obtain worthy individuals and employ them,
bestowing ranks to honor them,
dividing lands to enfeoff them,
and never wearying of this throughout their lives.
Worthy individuals only sought to obtain enlightened rulers and serve them,
exhausting the strength of their limbs
to undertake the ruler's tasks,
and never tiring of this throughout their lives.
If there was beauty and goodness,
they attributed it to their superiors;
thus, beauty and goodness resided above,
while resentment and criticism remained below;
peace and joy belonged to the ruler,
worry and sorrow to the ministers.
This is how the ancient sage kings governed.
"Now, the kings, dukes, and great men also wish to emulate others in governing by exalting the worthy and employing the capable,
bestowing high ranks upon them,
yet their emoluments do not follow.
To grant high ranks without emoluments
leads to distrust among the people.
They say:
'This is not truly out of love for me,
but rather borrowing and using me.'
How can such borrowed people
become close to their superiors?
Therefore, the former kings said:
'Those who feed on governance
cannot share responsibilities with others;
those who amass wealth
cannot share emoluments with others.'
If responsibilities are not given
and emoluments are not shared,
how then can the worthy individuals of the world come to the side of the kings, dukes, and great men?
If the worthy do not come to the side of the kings, dukes, and great men,
then the unworthy will be at their sides.
With the unworthy at their sides,
their praises will not match worthiness,
and their punishments will not match villainy.
If the kings, dukes, and great men respect this in governing the state and family,
then rewards will inevitably not match worthiness,
and punishments will inevitably not match villainy.
If rewards do not match worthiness and punishments do not match villainy,
then the worthy are not encouraged,
and the villainous are not restrained.
Thus, at home, they are not affectionate and filial to parents;
abroad, they do not respect elders in the village;
in daily life, they lack restraint,
in comings and goings, they lack moderation,
and between men and women, there is no distinction.
Employed in government offices, they steal;
tasked with defending cities, they betray;
when the ruler faces peril, they do not die for him;
when he flees, they do not follow.
Set to adjudicate cases, they are unjust;
assigned to distribute wealth, they are unfair.
Consulted on plans, they achieve nothing;
entrusted with tasks, they accomplish nothing;
in defense, they are not firm;
in attacks, they are not strong.
Thus, even the reasons why the tyrant kings of the Three Dynasties—Jié, Zhòu, Yōu, and Lì—lost their states,
and brought ruin to their altars of grain and soil,
were due to this.
Why?
Because they understood minor matters
but failed to understand major ones.
"Now, if the kings, dukes, and great men have a garment they cannot make,
they must rely on a skilled tailor.
If they have an ox or sheep they cannot slaughter,
they must rely on a skilled butcher.
Thus, in such matters,
the kings, dukes, and great men do not know how to govern by exalting the worthy and employing the capable.
When it comes to the disorder of their state
and the peril of their altars of grain and soil,
they do not know to employ the capable to govern it.
They appoint their relatives;
they appoint those who are wealthy and noble without reason or have handsome faces.
To appoint those who are wealthy and noble without reason or have handsome faces—
must they necessarily be wise and intelligent?
If such are set to govern the state,
then this is employing the unwise to govern the state;
the disorder of the state
can thus be known.
Moreover, if the kings, dukes, and great men appoint someone out of fondness for their appearance,
without examining their wisdom in their hearts,
but act on their affection,
then one who cannot govern a hundred people
is placed in an office of a thousand;
one who cannot govern a thousand people
is placed in an office of ten thousand.
What is the reason for this?
It is said:
'Those in office have high ranks and generous emoluments,
so they are appointed out of fondness for their appearance.'
To place one who cannot govern a thousand people
in an office of ten thousand
is to make the office ten times greater.
The methods of governance require daily attention;
the days spent governing them
do not increase tenfold;
the wisdom applied to govern them
does not increase tenfold;
yet the office is made ten times larger.
Thus, one part is governed, and nine are neglected.
Even if they toil day and night to govern such an office,
it will still remain ungoverned.
What is the reason for this?
It is that the kings, dukes, and great men do not understand governing by exalting the worthy and employing the capable.
Therefore, those who govern by exalting the worthy and employing the capable and achieve order—
this refers to what I have said;
those who govern by demeaning the worthy and bring disorder—
this also refers to what I have said.
"Now, if the kings, dukes, and great men truly wish to govern their states,
to preserve them without loss,
why do they not examine the root of governing by exalting the worthy?
Moreover, that governing by exalting the worthy is the root—
is this not solely the words of Master Mòzǐ?
This is the Way of the sage kings,
the words of the former kings' text 'Jù Nián,'
which transmits the saying:
'Seek sagely rulers and wise men
to assist your person.'
The 'Táng Shì' says:
'We sought the great sage,
to join efforts and unite hearts with him,
in order to govern the world.'
This means that the sages never failed to govern by exalting the worthy and employing the capable.
Thus, the ancient sage kings, because they could carefully govern by exalting the worthy and employing the capable,
without adulteration by other things,
enabled all under heaven to attain their proper places.
In antiquity, Shùn plowed at Lìshān,
made pottery by the riverbanks,
fished at Léizé,
and Yáo found him at the sunny side of Fúzé,
raised him to be the Son of Heaven,
and entrusted him with the governance of the world,
to rule the people of the world.
Yī Zhì
was a private servant of the daughter of the Yǒu Shēn clan,
personally a cook;
Tāng obtained him,
raised him to be his own minister,
and entrusted him with the governance of the world,
to rule the people of the world.
Fù Yuè, clad in coarse cloth and girded with rope,
was hired as a builder at Fùyán;
Wǔ Dīng obtained him,
raised him to be one of the Three Dukes,
and entrusted him with the governance of the world,
to rule the people of the world.
Why did these begin lowly and end noble,
begin poor and end wealthy?
It is because the kings, dukes, and great men understood governing by exalting the worthy and employing the capable.
Thus, the people did not go hungry without food,
cold without clothing,
weary without rest,
or disorderly without governance.
Therefore, the ancient sage kings carefully governed by exalting the worthy and employing the capable,
taking Heaven as their model.
Even Heaven does not distinguish between poverty and wealth, nobility and lowliness, distance and closeness, kinship and estrangement;
it raises the worthy and exalts them,
and suppresses the unworthy and discards them.
"Then who are those who, being noble and wealthy, practiced virtue and thereby obtained their reward?
Who are they?
It is said:
Such as the sage kings of the Three Dynasties of old—Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ—were such men.
For what reason did they obtain their reward?
It is said:
In governing the world,
they loved all universally,
and thereby benefited them,
and further led the myriad people of the world to honor Heaven and serve the spirits,
loving and benefiting the myriad people.
Therefore, Heaven and the spirits rewarded them,
established them as the Sons of Heaven,
to act as parents to the people,
and the myriad people followed and praised them, calling them 'Sage Kings,'
which continues to this day without ceasing.
These are those who, being noble and wealthy, practiced virtue and thereby obtained their reward.
"Then who are those who, being noble and wealthy, practiced violence and thereby incurred their punishment?
Who are they?
It is said:
Such as the violent kings of the Three Dynasties of old—Jié, Zhòu, Yōu, and Lì—were such men.
How do we know it is so?
It is said:
In governing the world,
they hated all universally,
and thereby harmed them,
and further led the people of the world to revile Heaven and insult the spirits,
harming and killing the myriad people.
Therefore, Heaven and the spirits punished them,
causing them to die and suffer execution,
their sons and grandsons to be scattered and separated,
their households to be lost and destroyed,
cut off without posterity,
and the myriad people followed and condemned them, calling them 'Violent Kings,'
which continues to this day without ceasing.
These are those who, being noble and wealthy, practiced violence and thereby incurred their punishment.
"Then who are those who, being close relatives, practiced evil and thereby incurred their punishment?
Who are they?
It is said:
Such as Gǔn of old,
the first son of the Emperor,
who abandoned the Emperor's virtuous ways,
was then punished in the wilderness of Yǔ,
where the hot sun shone without relief,
and the Emperor showed him no love.
This is one who, being a close relative, practiced evil and thereby incurred his punishment.
"Then whom does Heaven employ for their ability?
Who are they?
It is said:
Such as Yǔ, Jì, and Gāo Yáo of old were such men.
How do we know it is so?
The book of the former kings, the 'Lǚ Xíng,' speaks of it, saying:
'The August Emperor inquired carefully of the lower people,
and there were complaints against the Miáo.
He said:
"All the lords and their subordinates below,
though brilliantly intelligent, are not constant,
and the widowers and widows are not protected.
Majesty that is virtuous is true majesty,
enlightenment that is virtuous is true enlightenment."'
Then he appointed the three lords to show compassion and achieve merit for the people.
Bó Yí promulgated the statutes,
making the people wise through penalties.
Yǔ leveled the waters and lands,
and gave names to the mountains and rivers.
Jì promoted sowing and planting,
and the farmers grew fine grains.
The three lords achieved merit,
which extended to the people.'
This speaks of these three sages,
who were careful in their words,
cautious in their actions,
refined in their thoughts,
sought out the hidden affairs and neglected benefits of the world to serve Heaven above,
and thus Heaven enjoyed their virtue.
Applying it below to the myriad people,
the myriad people received their benefits,
endlessly throughout their lives.
Therefore, the words of the former kings say:
'This Way,
greatly applied to the world, does not fall short;
applied in small matters, it does not cause distress;
cultivated and applied, the myriad people receive its benefits,
endlessly throughout their lives.'
The 'Zhōu Sòng' speaks of it, saying:
'The virtue of the sage,
is like the height of Heaven,
like the breadth of Earth.
It shines upon the world,
as firm as the Earth,
as enduring as the mountains.
It does not crack or collapse,
like the light of the sun,
like the brightness of the moon,
constant with Heaven and Earth.'
This means that the virtue of the sage is clear and manifest, vast and great,
solid and firm, cultivated for long endurance.
Therefore, the virtue of the sage
encompasses all that of Heaven and Earth.
"Now the kings, dukes, and great men who wish to rule the world and correct the feudal lords,
if they lack virtue and righteousness,
what will they rely on?
Their argument will necessarily rely on awe and coercive power.
But from where will the kings, dukes, and great men obtain this awe and coercive power?
It comes from sacrificing the people to death.
The people,
greatly desire to live,
and greatly hate to die.
What they desire is not obtained, and what they hate repeatedly comes to them.
From ancient times to the present,
there has never been anyone who could by this means rule the world and correct the feudal lords.
Now if the great men wish to rule the world and correct the feudal lords,
and desire to have their will prevail in the world,
and their names established for posterity,
why do they not recognize that exalting the virtuous is the foundation of government?
This is the profound conduct of the sages."
2.3 "Exalting the Virtuous III"
Master Mòzǐ said:
The kings, dukes, and great men of the world
all desire their states to be wealthy,
their people to be numerous,
and their penal laws to bring order.
Yet they do not understand that governing their states and people by exalting the virtuous
means that the kings, dukes, and great men have fundamentally lost the root of governing by exalting the virtuous.
If the kings, dukes, and great men have fundamentally lost the root of governing by exalting the virtuous,
then can they not take examples to show them?
Suppose now there is a feudal lord here,
governing his state,
who says:
'All the knights in my state who can shoot and drive chariots,
I will reward and honor.
Those knights who cannot shoot and drive chariots,
I will punish and hold in low esteem.'
Ask the knights of that state:
Who will be pleased and who will be afraid?
I believe that certainly the knights who can shoot and drive will be pleased,
and those who cannot will be afraid.
I would then follow with rewards to guide them further, saying:
'All the loyal and trustworthy knights in my state,
I will reward and honor.
Those who are not loyal and trustworthy,
I will punish and hold in low esteem.'
Ask the knights of that state:
Who will be pleased and who will be afraid?
I believe that certainly the loyal and trustworthy knights will be pleased,
and the disloyal and untrustworthy will be afraid.
Now if only they would govern their state and people by exalting the virtuous,
causing those in the state who do good to be encouraged,
and those who do violence to be restrained.
Extending this to governing the world,
causing those in the world who do good to be encouraged,
and those who do violence to be restrained.
Yet formerly, the reason I valued the Way of Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ
—for what reason was it?
Because when they faced the multitude, issued government orders, and ruled the people,
they caused those in the world who did good to be encouraged,
and those who did violence to be restrained.
Thus, this exalting of the virtuous
is the same as the Way of Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ.
Nowadays, the scholars and gentlemen of the world
in their daily lives and speech all advocate honoring the worthy,
but when it comes to governing the masses and administering policies to rule the people,
none know to honor the worthy and employ the capable.
From this, I know that the scholars and gentlemen of the world understand small matters but not great ones.
How do I know this is so?
If the kings, dukes, and great men have livestock property,
and cannot butcher it themselves,
they will surely seek a skilled butcher.
If they have clothing material,
and cannot make it themselves,
they will surely seek a skilled artisan.
When kings, dukes, and great men are in such situations,
even if it involves their own flesh and blood relatives,
or those who are wealthy and noble without reason or have handsome features,
if they truly know these persons are incapable,
they will not employ them.
Why is this?
They fear it would waste their resources.
When kings, dukes, and great men are in such situations,
they do not fail to honor the worthy and employ the capable.
If kings, dukes, and great men have a worn-out horse,
and cannot treat it themselves,
they will surely seek a skilled veterinarian.
If they have a damaged bow,
and cannot string it themselves,
they will surely seek a skilled craftsman.
When kings, dukes, and great men are in such situations,
even if it involves their own flesh and blood relatives,
or those who are wealthy and noble without reason or have handsome features,
if they truly know these persons are incapable,
they will certainly not employ them.
Why is this?
They fear it would waste their resources.
When kings, dukes, and great men are in such situations,
they do not fail to honor the worthy and employ the capable.
But when it comes to their states, it is not so.
The flesh and blood relatives of kings, dukes, and great men, or those wealthy and noble without reason with handsome features,
are promoted.
Then, do kings, dukes, and great men care for their states
less than they care for a damaged bow, a worn-out horse, clothing material, or livestock property?
From this, I know that the scholars and gentlemen of the world all understand small matters but not great ones.
This is like making a mute serve as an envoy,
or a deaf person serve as a music master.
Therefore, when the sage kings of antiquity governed the world,
those they enriched,
those they honored,
were not necessarily the flesh and blood relatives of kings, dukes, and great men, or those wealthy and noble without reason with handsome features.
Thus, in the past, Shùn plowed at Lìshān,
made pottery by the river,
fished at Léizé,
and made lime at Chángyáng.
Yáo found him north of Fúzé,
established him as the Son of Heaven,
entrusted him with the administration of the world,
to govern the people of the world.
In the past, Yīyǐn was the tutor of the daughter of the Shēn family,
and was made a cook.
Tāng found and promoted him,
established him as one of the Three Dukes,
entrusted him with the administration of the world,
to govern the people of the world.
In the past, Fùyuè lived on an island in the northern sea,
upon a circular earth mound,
wearing coarse clothes and a rope belt,
hired as a laborer building the walls at Fùyán.
Wǔdīng found and promoted him,
established him as one of the Three Dukes,
entrusted him with the administration of the world,
to govern the people of the world.
Therefore, when Yáo promoted Shùn,
Tāng promoted Yīyǐn,
and Wǔdīng promoted Fùyuè,
was it because they were flesh and blood relatives, wealthy and noble without reason, or had handsome features?
They only followed their words,
employed their plans,
and practiced their ways,
which above could benefit Heaven,
in the middle could benefit the spirits,
and below could benefit the people.
Therefore, they were elevated and promoted.
The sage kings of antiquity, having carefully examined the honoring of the worthy,
and wishing to implement it in governance,
thus wrote it on bamboo and silk,
carved it on plates and vessels,
to be handed down to later generations.
In the book of the former kings, the "Lǚxíng," it is stated:
"The king said:
Ah!
Come,
you who have states and lands,
I announce to you the principles of punishment.
Now, to pacify the common people,
whom will you choose, O men?
What will you reverence if not punishments?
What measure will you adopt that is not thorough?"
If you can choose men and reverence punishments,
the way of Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ can be attained.
Why is this?
It is because they honored the worthy and attained it.
In the sayings of the former kings' book "Shùnián," it is stated:
It says:
"Seek out the sage, martial, and wise men
to shield and assist your person."
This means that the former kings in governing the world
must select the worthy
to serve as officials and assistants for their groups.
It is said:
Now, the scholars and gentlemen of the world all desire wealth and honor and hate poverty and lowliness.
But how can you obtain wealth and honor and avoid poverty and lowliness?
The answer is:
Nothing is better than being worthy.
What is the way to be worthy?
The answer is:
Those with strength should quickly help others,
those with wealth should earnestly share with others,
those with the Way should encourage and teach others.
If this is done,
then the hungry will get food,
the cold will get clothing,
and the chaotic will get order.
If the hungry get food,
the cold get clothing,
and the chaotic get order,
this brings peace and livelihood.
Now, those whom the kings, dukes, and great men enrich,
those whom they honor,
are all their flesh and blood relatives, or those wealthy and noble without reason with handsome features.
Now, these flesh and blood relatives of kings, dukes, and great men, or those wealthy and noble without reason with handsome features,
how can they necessarily be wise?
If they are not wise,
and are set to govern their states,
then the chaos in their states can be known.
Now, the scholars and gentlemen of the world all desire wealth and honor and hate poverty and lowliness,
but how can you obtain wealth and honor and avoid poverty and lowliness?
The answer is:
Nothing is better than being a flesh and blood relative of kings, dukes, and great men, or one wealthy and noble without reason with handsome features.
But being a flesh and blood relative of kings, dukes, and great men, or one wealthy and noble without reason with handsome features,
this is not something that can be achieved by learning.
If one does not know discrimination,
even with virtues as profound as those of Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ,
one will not be additionally obtained;
and the flesh and blood relatives of kings, dukes, and great men,
even if lame, mute, or deaf,
and violent like Jié and Zhòu,
will not be additionally dismissed.
Therefore, rewards do not correspond to worthiness,
punishments do not correspond to violence,
those who are rewarded have no merit,
and those who are punished have no crime.
This causes the common people to be disheartened and disorganized,
discouraged from doing good,
letting their limbs' strength lie idle,
and not laboring for each other;
allowing surplus wealth to rot and stink,
and not sharing it with each other;
hiding good doctrines,
and not teaching each other.
If this is the case,
then the hungry will not get food,
the cold will not get clothing,
and the chaotic will not get order.
Therefore, in ancient times,
Yáo had Shùn,
Shùn had Yǔ,
Yǔ had Gāo Yáo,
Tāng had his minor officials,
King Wǔ had Hóng Yāo, Tài Diān, Nán Gōng Kuò, and Sǎn Yí Shēng.
Extrapolating from this upwards,
through them, the world was harmonized,
and the common people prospered.
Thus, those nearby were pacified,
and those afar came to submit.
Wherever the sun and moon shone,
wherever boats and carts reached,
wherever rain and dew moistened,
wherever grain was consumed for nourishment,
none needed encouragement or praise.
Moreover, today's kings, dukes, great men, officers, and gentlemen,
who sincerely desire to practice benevolence and righteousness,
seek to become superior scholars,
above wishing to align with the way of the sage kings,
below wishing to benefit the state and its people,
Thus, the doctrine of exalting the worthy
is one that cannot be examined without considering this.
Exalting the worthy
benefits the spirits, ghosts, and the people,
and is the foundation of governance.
3.1 "Exalting Unity I: Chapter Eleven"
Mòzǐ said:
In ancient times, when people first came into being and there was no proper governance,
it is said that
each person had different principles.
Thus, one person meant one principle,
two people meant two principles,
ten people meant ten principles.
The more people there were,
the more principles they called their own.
Hence, each person affirmed their own principles
and denounced those of others,
leading to mutual condemnation.
Thus, within families, fathers, sons, brothers harbored resentment and hatred,
scattering and unable to harmonize.
The people of the world
all used water, fire, poison, and drugs to harm one another,
to the extent that surplus strength was not used for mutual aid,
surplus rotting wealth was not shared,
and beneficial ways were hidden and not taught to others.
The chaos in the world
became like that among birds and beasts.
To understand the reason for the world's chaos,
it arises from the lack of political leaders.
Therefore, the worthy and capable of the world were selected
and established as the Son of Heaven.
Once the Son of Heaven was established,
considering his strength insufficient,
more worthy and capable individuals from the world were selected
and appointed as the Three Dukes.
With the Son of Heaven and the Three Dukes in place,
due to the vastness of the world,
and the difficulty of clearly discerning right from wrong and benefit from harm among people of distant lands and different regions,
which could not be understood one by one,
the land was divided into ten thousand states,
establishing feudal lords and rulers.
Once the feudal lords and rulers were established,
considering their strength insufficient,
more worthy and capable individuals from their states were selected
and appointed as district leaders.
With district leaders in place,
the Son of Heaven issued decrees to the people of the world,
saying:
"Whether you hear good or bad,
report it all to your superiors.
What the superiors deem right, all must deem right;
what the superiors deem wrong, all must deem wrong.
If superiors have faults, admonish them;
if subordinates have merits, recommend them.
To align with superiors and not collude with inferiors—
this is what superiors reward and subordinates praise.
If, upon hearing good or bad,
one fails to report it to superiors,
cannot affirm what superiors affirm,
cannot deny what superiors deny,
fails to admonish superiors' faults,
or recommend subordinates' merits,
colluding with inferiors instead of aligning with superiors—
this is what superiors punish and the people condemn."
Using this for rewards and punishments,
they were clear and careful to ensure trust.
Thus, the village elder
is the benevolent person of the village.
The village elder issues decrees to the village people,
saying:
"Whether you hear good or bad,
must report it to the district head.
What the district head deems right, all must deem right;
what the district head deems wrong, all must deem wrong.
Abandon your improper speech,
and learn the proper speech of the district head.
Abandon your improper conduct,
and learn the proper conduct of the district head."
Then how can the district be said to be in chaos?
Consider what governs the district—
what is it?
The district head can unify the principles of the district,
hence the district is orderly.
The district head
is the benevolent person of the district.
The district head issues decrees to the district people,
saying:
"Whether you hear good or bad,
must report it to the state ruler.
What the state ruler deems right, all must deem right;
what the state ruler deems wrong, all must deem wrong.
Abandon your improper speech,
and learn the proper speech of the state ruler.
Abandon your improper conduct,
and learn the proper conduct of the state ruler."
Then how can the state be said to be in chaos?
Consider what governs the state—
what is it?
The state ruler can unify the principles of the state,
hence the state is orderly.
The state ruler
is the benevolent person of the state.
The state ruler issues decrees to the state people,
saying:
"Whether you hear good or bad,
must report it to the Son of Heaven.
What the Son of Heaven deems right, all must deem right;
what the Son of Heaven deems wrong, all must deem wrong.
Abandon your improper speech,
and learn the proper speech of the Son of Heaven.
Abandon your improper conduct,
and learn the proper conduct of the Son of Heaven."
Then how can the world be said to be in chaos?
Consider what governs the world—
what is it?
The Son of Heaven can unify the principles of the world,
hence the world is orderly.
If the people of the world all align with the One above but
do not align with Heaven,
then calamities have yet to be removed.
Now, if Heaven sends violent winds and bitter rains,
coming incessantly,
this is Heaven's punishment for the people not aligning with Heaven.
Therefore, Mòzǐ said:
The ancient sage kings established the five punishments
to govern their people.
Just as silk threads have a main strand,
and nets have a head rope,
they were used to restrain the people of the world who did not align with their superiors.
3.2 "Exalting Unity II: Chapter Twelve"
Mòzǐ said:
In the present time,
reverting to the era when people first existed without proper leaders,
it is said:
"People in the world have different principles."
Thus, one person, one principle;
ten people, ten principles;
a hundred people, a hundred principles.
The more people there are,
the more principles they call their own.
Hence, each person affirms their own principles
and denies those of others,
leading to mutual condemnation.
Within families, fathers, sons, brothers become enemies,
all harboring intentions to scatter,
unable to harmonize,
to the point of not using surplus strength for mutual aid,
hiding beneficial ways and not teaching them,
hoarding surplus rotting wealth and not sharing it.
The chaos in the world
became like that among birds and beasts.
Without the order of ruler and minister, superior and inferior, elder and younger,
or the rites between father and son, elder and younger brothers,
thus the world fell into chaos.
Understanding that without proper leaders among the people,
to unify the standards of righteousness across the world,
the world would fall into chaos,
therefore, the wise, virtuous, sagacious, and discerning individuals of the world were selected,
and established as the Son of Heaven,
to undertake the task of unifying the standards of righteousness across the world.
Once the Son of Heaven was established,
it was thought that relying solely on his own senses,
he could not alone unify the standards of righteousness across the world,
so the world's commendable, experienced, wise, virtuous, sagacious, and discerning individuals were selected,
and appointed as the Three Dukes,
to join in the task of unifying the standards of righteousness across the world.
Once the Son of Heaven and the Three Dukes were established,
it was thought that the world was vast,
and the people in remote mountains and forests could not be unified,
so the world was divided,
and established into myriad feudal lords and state rulers,
to undertake the task of unifying the standards of righteousness in their respective states.
Once the state rulers were established,
it was again thought that relying solely on their own senses,
they could not unify the standards of righteousness in their states,
so the wise individuals of their states were chosen,
and appointed as generals, ministers, and officials on their left and right,
extending down to the village chiefs,
to join in the task of unifying the standards of righteousness in their states.
The rulers, the Son of Heaven, and the feudal lords,
the proper leaders of the people,
were thus established.
The Son of Heaven issued decrees and implemented teachings,
saying:
"All who hear or see good must report it to their superiors,
and all who hear or see evil must also report it to their superiors.
What the superiors approve must be approved,
and what the superiors disapprove must be disapproved.
If the people have goodness, recommend it;
if the superiors have faults, admonish them.
Unify in righteousness with the superiors,
and do not harbor intentions to form cliques below.
Those whom the superiors capture will be rewarded,
and the myriad people will praise them upon hearing.
If, however, one hears or sees good but does not report it to the superiors,
or hears or sees evil but does not report it to the superiors,
cannot approve what the superiors approve,
cannot disapprove what the superiors disapprove,
cannot recommend the goodness of the people,
cannot admonish the faults of the superiors,
but instead forms cliques below and criticizes the superiors,
those whom the superiors capture will be punished,
and the myriad people will condemn and slander them upon hearing."
Thus, the sage kings of old in their administration of punishments, governance, rewards, and praise,
were extremely clear and careful to ensure accuracy and trustworthiness,
so that all people under heaven
desired the rewards and praise of their superiors,
and feared the condemnation and punishment from above.
Therefore, the village chiefs complied with the governance of the Son of Heaven,
and unified the standards of righteousness in their villages.
Once the village chiefs unified the standards of righteousness in their villages,
they led the myriad people of their villages to align with the township chiefs,
saying:
"All the myriad people of the village
must align with the township chiefs,
and dare not form cliques below.
What the township chiefs approve must be approved,
and what the township chiefs disapprove must be disapproved.
Abandon your unwholesome words,
and learn the wholesome words of the township chiefs.
Abandon your unwholesome actions,
and learn the wholesome actions of the township chiefs."
The township chiefs are indeed the virtuous of the township,
and if all the people of the township emulate the township chiefs,
how can the township not be well-governed?
Consider how the township chiefs govern the township—
for what reason is this so?
It is said:
Only because they can unify the standards of righteousness in their township,
therefore the township is well-governed.
The township chiefs govern their township,
and once the township is well-governed,
they lead the myriad people of the township to align with the state ruler,
saying:
"All the myriad people of the township
must align with the state ruler above,
and dare not form cliques below.
What the state ruler approves must be approved,
and what the state ruler disapproves must be disapproved.
Abandon your unwholesome words,
and learn the wholesome words of the state ruler.
Abandon your unwholesome actions,
and learn the wholesome actions of the state ruler."
The state ruler is indeed the virtuous of the state,
and if all the people of the state emulate the state ruler,
how can the state not be well-governed?
Consider how the state ruler governs the state and the state is well-governed—
for what reason is this so?
It is said:
Only because he can unify the standards of righteousness in his state,
therefore the state is well-governed.
The state ruler governs his state,
and once the state is well-governed,
he leads the myriad people of the state to align with the Son of Heaven,
saying:
"All the myriad people of the state
must align with the Son of Heaven above,
and dare not form cliques below.
What the Son of Heaven approves must be approved,
and what the Son of Heaven disapproves must be disapproved.
Abandon your unwholesome words,
and learn the wholesome words of the Son of Heaven.
Abandon your unwholesome actions,
and learn the wholesome actions of the Son of Heaven."
The Son of Heaven
is indeed the benevolent person of the world.
If all the myriad people of the world emulate the Son of Heaven,
how can the Son of Heaven not govern well?
Consider how the Son of Heaven governs the world—
for what reason is this so?
It is said:
Only because he can unify the standards of righteousness across the world,
therefore the world is well-governed.
Now, if one aligns with the Son of Heaven above,
but does not align with Heaven,
then the calamities from Heaven will still not cease.
Thus, when Heaven sends unseasonable cold and heat,
untimely snow, frost, rain, and dew,
the five grains do not ripen,
the six domestic animals do not thrive,
diseases, calamities, epidemics, and plagues,
violent winds and bitter rains,
come repeatedly and in succession,
these are the punishments sent down by Heaven,
intended to punish those below who do not align with Heaven.
Therefore, the sage kings of old understood what the heavenly spirits desired,
and avoided what the heavenly spirits hated,
in order to promote benefits for the world,
and eliminate harms for the world.
Thus, they led the myriad people of the world,
to fast, bathe, and purify themselves,
and prepare clean wine, millet, and other offerings,
to sacrifice to the heavenly spirits.
In their service to the spirits and gods,
they dared not fail to keep the wine and offerings pure and clean,
the sacrificial animals plump and fat,
the jade tablets, silks, and cloths of appropriate measure,
the spring and autumn sacrifices at the correct times,
the judgment of lawsuits fair and impartial,
the distribution of wealth equitable,
and their conduct diligent and respectful.
It is said:
If they act as proper leaders in this way,
therefore...
above, the heavenly spirits show favor to those who govern as leaders,
below, the myriad people find convenience in their governance.
Where the heavenly spirits show deep favor,
and if one strives diligently in it,
then the blessings of the heavenly spirits can be obtained.
Where the myriad people find convenience,
and if one can strive diligently in it,
then the affection of the myriad people can be gained.
If one governs in this way,
then planning affairs succeeds,
undertaking affairs achieves,
defense inwards is secure,
and campaigns outwards are victorious.
For what reason is this so?
It is said:
Only because they govern by aligning with the above.
Thus, the sage kings of old governed in this way.
Nowadays, people under heaven say:
