"In the present times,
the proper leaders of heaven have not yet been abolished by heaven,
yet the reason why heaven is in disorder,
what is the cause?"
Mòzǐ said:
"In the present times, the establishment of proper leaders
is fundamentally different from ancient practices.
This is like the Miao tribe's implementation of the five punishments.
Formerly, the sage kings instituted the five punishments
to govern heaven,
but when it came to the Miao tribe instituting the five punishments,
they brought disorder to heaven.
Is this because the punishments themselves were bad?
It was their application that was improper.
Therefore, the ancient king's book 'Lǚxíng' states:
'The Miao people did not employ restraint,
but executed punishments arbitrarily,
creating only the five cruel punishments,
calling them law.'
This shows that those who use punishments properly govern the people,
while those who misuse them create five forms of slaughter.
Is this because the punishments themselves were bad?
It was their application that was improper,
thus leading to these five forms of slaughter.
Therefore, the ancient king's book 'Shù Lìng' states:
'The mouth can either produce good or stir up conflict.'
This means that those who use speech properly produce good,
while those who misuse it create slander, harm, banditry, and warfare.
Is this because the mouth itself is bad?
It is its use that is improper,
thus leading to slander, harm, banditry, and warfare.
Therefore, when the ancients established proper leaders,
it was to govern the people.
This is like the warp threads in weaving
or the main rope in a fishing net,
meant to control the wicked and violent in heaven and unify their righteousness.
Thus, the ancient king's book 'Xiāng Nián' states:
'When establishing states and setting up capitals,
creating kings and lords,
it is not for luxury;
appointing ministers, officials, and teachers,
it is not for idleness;
but to distinguish and assign them to govern heaven equally.'
This means that when the ancient spirits and gods established states and set up leaders,
it was not to give them high ranks, generous emoluments, wealth, honor, and leisure,
but to benefit the myriad people, eliminate harms, enrich the poor, increase the few, secure the endangered, and bring order to chaos.
Thus, the sage kings of old governed in this manner.
Now, when kings, lords, and great men administer punishments and governance,
they do the opposite.
They appoint as leaders those who are related or familiar,
making them their assistants,
and setting them up as proper leaders.
The people know that their superiors establish leaders not properly to govern them,
so they all form cliques and hide,
unwilling to identify with their superiors,
thus superiors and subordinates do not share the same principles.
If superiors and subordinates do not share the same principles,
rewards and praise cannot encourage goodness,
and punishments cannot deter violence.
How do we know this is so?
It is said:
If a superior stands to administer the state,
acting as the people's proper leader,
and says:
'This person should be rewarded,
I will reward him.'
But if superiors and subordinates do not share the same principles,
what the superior rewards is what the multitude condemns.
They say:
'Though he associates with the multitude,
he earns their condemnation.'
Thus, even if he receives the superior's reward,
it is not enough to encourage him.
If a superior stands to administer the state,
acting as the people's proper leader,
and says:
'This person should be punished,
I will punish him.'
But if superiors and subordinates do not share the same principles,
what the superior punishes is what the multitude praises.
They say:
'Though he associates with the multitude,
he earns their praise.'
Thus, even if he suffers the superior's punishment,
it is not enough to deter him.
If one stands to administer the state,
acting as the people's proper leader,
and rewards and praise cannot encourage goodness,
while punishments cannot deter violence,
is this not the same as when people first existed without proper leaders?
If having proper leaders is the same as not having them,
then this is not the way to govern the people and unify the multitude.
Therefore, the ancient sage kings exclusively employed identification with superiors to establish leaders,
so superiors and subordinates were sincerely connected.
If the superior had overlooked matters or neglected benefits,
the subordinates could supplement and benefit them;
if the subordinates had accumulated grievances or harms,
the superior could learn and remove them.
Thus, when someone thousands of miles away did good,
even if his household did not fully know,
or his village did not fully hear,
the Son of Heaven could learn and reward him.
When someone thousands of miles away did evil,
even if his household did not fully know,
or his village did not fully hear,
the Son of Heaven could learn and punish him.
Therefore, all people under heaven
were fearful, trembling, and cautious,
daring not to commit wickedness or violence,
saying:
"Heaven's seeing and hearing are divine."
The ancient kings said:
"It is not divinity,
but rather the ability to make others' eyes and ears aid one's seeing and hearing,
make others' mouths aid one's speaking,
make others' minds aid one's thinking,
make others' limbs aid one's actions."
When many aid in seeing and hearing,
what one hears and sees reaches far.
When many aid in speaking,
the influence of one's virtuous words becomes broad.
When many aid in thinking,
one's plans and deliberations are quickly achieved.
When many aid in acting,
one's undertakings are quickly accomplished.
Therefore, the reason the ancient sages could accomplish tasks and achieve success,
leaving their names to posterity,
was due to no other cause or different thing,
but:
only their ability to govern through identification with superiors.
Thus, the ancient king's book 'Zhōusòng' states:
"They come to see that king,
seeking his statutes."
This refers to the ancient feudal lords coming in spring and autumn to court at the Son of Heaven's court,
receiving his strict instructions.
Returning to govern their states,
wherever his governance reached,
none dared not submit.
At that time,
there were none who dared confuse the Son of Heaven's teachings.
The 'Shī' says:
"My horses are piebald,
the six reins glossy.
Galloping and speeding,
everywhere consulting and deliberating."
It also says:
"My horses are black,
the six reins like silk.
Galloping and speeding,
everywhere consulting and planning."
This means that when the ancient feudal lords heard or saw good or evil,
they all sped to report to the Son of Heaven.
Thus, rewards were given to the worthy,
punishments to the violent,
the innocent were not killed,
the guilty were not missed,
and this was the achievement of identification with superiors.
Therefore, Mòzǐ said:
"Nowadays, the kings, lords, great men, and gentlemen of heaven,
if you truly wish to enrich your states,
increase your people,
order your punishments and governance,
and stabilize your altars of soil and grain,
you must not fail to examine the doctrine of identification with superiors,
for this is the foundation of governance."
3.3 "Elevating Uniformity III - Chapter Thirteen"
Mòzǐ said:
The task of the wise
must involve implementing what brings order to the state and its people,
and avoiding what causes chaos to the state and its people.
Now, what is it
that brings order to the state and its people?
When those above administer governance,
if they understand the sentiments of those below, there is order;
if they do not understand the sentiments of those below, there is chaos.
How do we know this is so?
When those above administer governance and understand the sentiments of those below,
they are clear about what the people consider good and bad.
If they are clear about what the people consider good and bad,
then they can reward the good people they identify
and punish the violent people they identify.
When good people are rewarded and violent people punished,
the state will surely be orderly.
When those above administer governance
without understanding the sentiments of those below,
they are not clear about what the people consider good and bad.
If they are not clear about what the people consider good and bad,
then they cannot reward the good people
nor punish the violent people.
When good people go unrewarded and violent people unpunished,
governance like this
will surely lead to chaos among the state's populace.
Therefore, in matters of reward and punishment, understanding the sentiments below
is something that cannot be overlooked.
So how can one plan to understand the sentiments below?
Thus Mòzǐ said:
Only by governing through elevating uniformity to a single standard
can this be achieved.
How do we know that elevating uniformity to a single standard can be used to govern the world?
Why not examine the ancient tales of governance and administration?
In ancient times when Heaven first created people, there were no proper leaders,
and each person acted for themselves.
If each person acted for themselves,
then one person had one standard,
ten people had ten standards,
a hundred people had a hundred standards,
a thousand people had a thousand standards,
until the number of people became countless,
and the so-called standards also became countless.
Everyone considered their own standard right and others' wrong,
hence there were major conflicts and minor disputes.
Therefore, to unify the standards of the world,
they selected the worthy
and established them as the Son of Heaven.
The Son of Heaven, knowing his wisdom and strength insufficient to govern alone,
selected the next best
and established them as the Three Dukes.
The Three Dukes, knowing their wisdom and strength insufficient to assist the Son of Heaven alone,
divided the state and established feudal lords.
The feudal lords, knowing their wisdom and strength insufficient to govern their territories alone,
selected the next best
and established them as ministers and administrators.
The ministers and administrators, knowing their wisdom and strength insufficient to assist their lords alone,
selected the next best
and established them as village leaders and family heads.
Thus when the ancient Son of Heaven established the Three Dukes, feudal lords, ministers, and village leaders,
it was not for their wealth, status, or leisure that they were chosen,
but to have them assist in governing disorder and administering punishments.
Therefore, in ancient times when states were founded and capitals established,
kings and lords were set up,
assisted by ministers, officers, and instructors,
not for self-indulgence,
but to distinguish and enable them to assist in governing and illuminating the world.
Now, why do those above fail to govern those below,
and those below fail to serve those above?
This is because upper and lower harm each other.
Why does this happen?
Because standards differ.
If those with different standards form factions,
and those above consider someone good,
the factions will slander them.
Even if such a person receives rewards from above,
they face slander from the people,
so those who do good may not necessarily be encouraged by visible rewards.
If those above consider someone violent,
and intend to punish them,
even if such a person receives punishment from above,
they enjoy praise from the people,
so those who do violence may not necessarily be deterred by visible punishments.
Thus, the rewards and praise from above cannot sufficiently encourage good,
and the slander and punishments cannot sufficiently deter violence.
Why does this happen?
Because standards differ.
So how can we unify the standards of the world?
What can be done?
Thus Mòzǐ said:
"Why not try having family heads issue commands to their families,
saying:
'If you see those who love and benefit the family, you must report it;
if you see those who hate and harm the family, you must also report it.
If you report those who love and benefit the family,
you are likewise one who loves and benefits the family;
those above will reward you,
and the people will praise you.
If you see those who hate and harm the family and do not report them,
you are likewise one who hates and harms the family;
those above will punish you,
and the people will condemn you.'
Thus everyone in the family
wants to obtain the rewards and praise of their superiors,
and avoid their condemnation and punishment.
Therefore, with good words,
the family head can reward the good people he identifies
and punish the violent people he identifies.
With good people rewarded
and violent people punished,
the family will surely be orderly.
Now, what is it
that brings order to the family?
Only governing through elevating uniformity to a single standard.
"With the family already orderly,
is this the complete way of governing the state?
Not yet.
The families in the world are numerous,
and each considers its own family right and others' wrong,
hence there are major disorders
and minor disputes.
Therefore, have the family heads unify their families' standards
by elevating uniformity to the state's lord.
The state's lord also issues commands to the state's people,
saying:
'If you see those who love and benefit the state, you must report it;
if you see those who hate and harm the state, you must also report it.
If you report those who love and benefit the state,
you are likewise one who loves and benefits the state;
those above will reward you,
and the people will praise you.
If you see those who hate and harm the state and do not report them,
you are likewise one who hates and harms the state;
those above will punish you,
and the people will condemn you.'
Thus everyone in the state
wants to obtain the rewards and praise of their superiors,
and avoid their condemnation and punishment.
Therefore, the people report what they see as good
and report what they see as bad.
The state's lord rewards the good people he identifies
and punishes the violent people he identifies.
With good people rewarded and violent people punished,
the state will surely be orderly.
Now, what is it
that brings order to the state?
Only governing through elevating uniformity to a single standard.
"With the state already orderly,
is this the complete way of governing the world?
Not yet.
The states in the world are numerous,
and each considers its own state right and others' wrong,
hence there are major wars
and minor disputes.
Therefore, have the state's lords select their states' standards
by elevating uniformity to the Son of Heaven.
The Son of Heaven also issues commands to the world's people,
saying:
'If you see those who love and benefit the world, you must report it;
if you see those who hate and harm the world, you must also report it.
If you report those who love and benefit the world,
you are likewise one who loves and benefits the world;
those above will reward you,
and the people will praise you.
If you see those who hate and harm the world and do not report them,
you are likewise one who hates and harms the world;
those above will punish you,
and the people will condemn you.'
Thus everyone in the world
wants to obtain the rewards and praise of their superiors,
and avoid their condemnation and punishment.
Therefore, they report what they see as good and bad.
The Son of Heaven rewards the good people he identifies
and punishes the violent people he identifies.
With good people rewarded and violent people punished, the world will surely be orderly.
Now, what is it
that brings order to the world?
Only governing through elevating uniformity to a single standard.
"When the world is already well-governed,
the Son of Heaven further consolidates the righteousness of the world,
to align upward with Heaven.
Therefore, the doctrine of upward alignment,
when applied by the Son of Heaven,
can govern the world;
when used by feudal lords,
it can govern their states;
when employed by family heads,
it can govern their households.
Thus, when broadly applied, governing the world is not deficient;
when narrowly used, ruling a state or family is not obstructed—
this is what is meant by the Way.
Hence it is said:
'Governing the states of the world is like governing one household;
directing the people of the world is like directing one man.'
If one thinks that only Mòzǐ has this while the former kings lacked it,
is that so?
It is actually the same.
The sage kings all governed through upward alignment,
hence the world was well-ordered.
How do we know this is so?
The words in the former kings' text 'Great Declaration' state thus,
saying:
'If petty men witness deceitful craftiness and only hear of it,
but do not report it,
their crime is equal.'
This means that those who see depravity and do not report it
are equally guilty as the depraved.
"Thus, when the ancient sage kings governed the world,
those they selected to serve as their aides were all excellent,
and there were many external assistants to broaden their sight and hearing.
Hence, when planning affairs with others,
they gained insights before others;
when undertaking tasks with others,
they achieved success before others;
their praise and reputation
were spread by others first.
Only by being trustworthy in person and diligent in action
did they attain such benefits.
There is an ancient saying:
'One eye seeing
is not as good as two eyes seeing;
one ear hearing
is not as good as two ears hearing;
one hand grasping
is not as strong as two hands.'
Only by being trustworthy in person and diligent in action
can such benefits be achieved.
Therefore, when the ancient sage kings governed the world,
if there was a worthy person a thousand miles away,
even if not all in his village had heard or seen him,
the sage king would still reward him.
If there was a violent person within a thousand miles,
even if not all in his village had heard or seen him,
the sage king would still punish him.
So, did they rely solely on the sage king's keen ears and clear eyes?
How could one glance see clearly a thousand miles away,
or one hearing perceive sounds a thousand miles distant?
The sage king did not go to see personally,
nor approach to listen directly,
yet he made rebels, rioters, thieves, and robbers roam the world with nowhere to stand firmly—
why?
It is because governing through upward alignment is excellent."
Therefore, Mòzǐ said:
"Those who make the people align upward,
if they do not love the people deeply,
the people cannot be directed.
It is said:
One must love them deeply to direct them,
establish trust to sustain them,
use wealth and honor to guide them forward,
and clear punishments to regulate them afterward.
Governing in this way,
even if they wish not to align with me,
it will be impossible."
Thus Mòzǐ said:
"Now, the kings, dukes, great men, officers, and gentlemen of the world,
if they sincerely desire to practice benevolence and righteousness,
seek to become superior officers,
aspire above to match the Way of the sages,
and below to benefit the state and its people,
must therefore examine the doctrine of upward alignment.
Upward alignment is the foundation of governance
and the essence of ruling a state."
4.1 "Universal Love I - Chapter Fourteen"
The sage takes governing the world as his task;
he must know the origin of disorder
to be able to govern it;
not knowing the origin of disorder,
he cannot govern.
It is like a doctor treating a person's illness:
he must know the origin of the illness
to treat it;
not knowing the origin of the illness,
he cannot treat it.
How is governing disorder any different?
One must know the origin of disorder
to govern it;
not knowing the origin of disorder,
one cannot govern.
The sage takes governing the world as his task;
he must examine the origin of disorder.
So, what is the origin of disorder?
It arises from lack of mutual love.
When ministers and sons are unfilial to rulers and fathers,
that is called disorder.
A son loving himself but not his father
harms the father to benefit himself;
a younger brother loving himself but not his elder brother
harms the brother to benefit himself;
a minister loving himself but not his ruler
harms the ruler to benefit himself—
this is called disorder.
Similarly, if a father is not affectionate to his son,
an elder brother not to his younger brother,
a ruler not to his minister,
this too is called disorder in the world.
A father loving himself
but not his son
harms the son to benefit himself;
an elder brother loving himself
but not his younger brother
harms the brother to benefit himself;
a ruler loving himself
but not his minister
harms the minister to benefit himself.
Why is this?
All arise from lack of mutual love.
Even with thieves and robbers in the world,
it is the same.
A thief loves his own house,
but not others' houses,
so he steals from others to benefit his own;
a robber loves his own person,
but not others' persons,
so he harms others to benefit himself.
Why is this?
All stem from lack of mutual love.
Even with ministers disrupting each other's families or feudal lords attacking each other's states,
it is the same.
Each minister loves his own family,
but not others' families,
so he disrupts others' families to benefit his own;
each feudal lord loves his own state,
but not others' states,
so he attacks others' states to benefit his own.
All disorders in the world
are encompassed here.
Examine where this originates:
all arise from lack of mutual love.
If everyone in the world loved each other mutually,
loving others as themselves,
would there still be unfilial people?
Viewing father, elder brother, and ruler as oneself, how could unfiliality be practiced?
Would there still be unaffectionate people?
Viewing sons, younger brothers, and ministers as oneself,
how could unaffection be practiced?
Thus, unfiliality and unaffection would cease.
Would there still be thieves and robbers?
Viewing others' houses as one's own,
who would steal?
Viewing others' persons as one's own,
who would rob?
Thus, thieves and robbers would cease.
Would there still be ministers disrupting families or feudal lords attacking states?
Viewing others' families as one's own,
who would disrupt?
Viewing others' states as one's own,
who would attack?
Thus, ministers disrupting families and feudal lords attacking states would cease.
If everyone in the world loved mutually,
states would not attack each other,
families would not disrupt each other,
thieves and robbers would vanish,
rulers and ministers, fathers and sons would all be filial and affectionate—
thus the world would be well-governed.
Therefore, the sage who takes governing the world as his task
must inevitably prohibit hatred and encourage love.
Hence, universal mutual love leads to order,
while mutual hatred leads to disorder.
Therefore, Mòzǐ said:
"We must encourage loving others—
for this reason."
4.2 "Universal Love II" (Chapter 15)
Master Mòzǐ said:
"What benevolent persons take as their task
is surely to promote the benefits of the world
and eliminate the harms of the world,
this being what they take as their task."
Then what are the benefits of the world?
What are the harms of the world?
Master Mòzǐ said:
"Now, as for states attacking one another,
families usurping one another,
individuals injuring one another,
rulers not being gracious and ministers not being loyal,
fathers not being affectionate and sons not being filial,
elder and younger brothers not being harmonious -
these are the harms of the world."
Then from where do these harms arise?
Do they arise from mutual love?
Master Mòzǐ said:
"They arise from the lack of mutual love.
Now feudal lords only know to love their own states,
not loving others' states,
therefore they do not hesitate to mobilize their states to attack others' states.
Now family heads only know to love their own families,
not loving others' families,
therefore they do not hesitate to mobilize their families to usurp others' families.
Now individuals only know to love their own persons,
not loving others' persons,
therefore they do not hesitate to mobilize themselves to injure others' persons.
Thus when feudal lords don't love one another,
they inevitably battle in the fields.
When family heads don't love one another,
they inevitably usurp one another.
When individuals don't love one another,
they inevitably injure one another.
When rulers and ministers don't love one another,
they are not gracious and loyal.
When fathers and sons don't love one another,
they are not affectionate and filial.
When brothers don't love one another,
they are not harmonious.
When all people in the world don't love one another,
the strong inevitably control the weak,
the many inevitably plunder the few,
the rich inevitably insult the poor,
the noble inevitably disdain the humble,
the cunning inevitably deceive the foolish.
All calamities, usurpations, resentments, and hatreds in the world
arise
from the lack of mutual love.
Therefore benevolent persons condemn this."
Since they condemn this,
how do they change it?
Master Mòzǐ said:
"Change it with the way of universal mutual love and mutual benefit."
Then what is the way of universal mutual love and mutual benefit?
Master Mòzǐ said:
"Regard others' states
as one regards one's own state;
regard others' families
as one regards one's own family;
regard others' persons
as one regards one's own person.
Thus when feudal lords love one another,
they don't battle in the fields.
When family heads love one another,
they don't usurp one another.
When individuals love one another,
they don't injure one another,
When rulers and ministers love one another, they are gracious and loyal;
when fathers and sons love one another, they are affectionate and filial;
when brothers love one another, they are harmonious.
When all people in the world love one another,
the strong don't control the weak,
the many don't plunder the few,
the rich don't insult the poor,
the noble don't disdain the humble,
the cunning don't deceive the foolish.
All calamities, usurpations, resentments, and hatreds in the world can be prevented from arising
because they arise from mutual love;
therefore benevolent persons praise this."
However, the scholars of today
gentlemen say:
"Yes,
universal love would be good.
Nevertheless,
it is something difficult and impractical in the world."
Master Mòzǐ said:
"The scholars and gentlemen of the world
simply don't understand its benefits and discern its reasons.
Now as for attacking cities and battling in the fields,
sacrificing oneself for fame -
these are things all common people in the world find difficult.
But if the ruler delights in them,
then officers and masses can do them.
How much more universal mutual love and mutual benefit,
which are different from these!
Those who love others
will inevitably be loved by others in return;
those who benefit others
will inevitably be benefited by others in return.
Those who hate others
will inevitably be hated by others in return;
those who harm others
will inevitably be harmed by others in return.
What difficulty is there in this?
It's simply that superiors don't adopt it as policy,
and officers don't practice it as conduct."
"Formerly, Duke Wén of Jìn liked his officers to wear poor clothing,
so the ministers of Duke Wén
all wore sheepskin robes,
leather sword belts,
plain silk caps,
coarse cloth garments,
and entered wearing hempen sandals to see the ruler,
and went out wearing them to walk in court.
What is the reason for this?
The ruler delighted in it,
so the ministers could do it.
Formerly, King Líng of Chǔ liked his officers to have slender waists,
so the ministers of King Líng
all restricted themselves to one meal a day,
exhaled before tightening their belts,
leaned against walls to stand up,
after one year,
the court had dark and sallow complexions.
What is the reason for this?
The ruler delighted in it,
so the ministers could do it.
Formerly, King Gōujiàn of Yuè liked his officers to be courageous,
training and drilling his ministers to be unified,
set a boat on fire,
and tested his officers, saying:
'All the treasures of Yuè are here!'
King Yuè personally beat the drum to urge his officers forward,
when the officers heard the drum sound,
breaking ranks and charging, dying by rushing into the fire -
there were over a hundred men on left and right,
then King Yuè sounded the gong to make them withdraw."
Therefore Master Mòzǐ said:
"As for eating little, wearing poor clothing, and sacrificing oneself for fame -
these are things all common people in the world find difficult.
But if the ruler delights in them,
then the masses can do them.
How much more universal mutual love and mutual benefit, which are different from these!
Those who love others
will also be loved by others in return.
Those who benefit others
will also be benefited by others in return.
Those who hate others
will also be hated by others in return.
Those who harm others
will also be harmed by others in return.
What difficulty is there in this?
It's simply that superiors don't adopt it as policy,
and officers don't practice it as conduct."
Yet the scholars and gentlemen of today say:
"Indeed,
universal love would be excellent.
Nevertheless,
it is an impracticable ideal,
like trying to carry Mount Tài across the Jiāng and Jì rivers."
Master Mòzǐ replied:
"This analogy is flawed.
To carry Mount Tài across the Jiāng and Jì rivers
would require supreme strength,
yet from ancient times to the present,
no one has ever accomplished it.
But universal mutual love and mutual benefit are different—
the sage kings of old practiced them.
How do we know this?
In ancient times, Yǔ regulated the world,
digging the Xīhé and Yúdòu in the west
to drain the waters of the Qú, Sūn, and Huáng rivers.
In the north, he built dikes at Fáng, Yuán, and Gū,
diverting waters to Hòuzhīdǐ and Hūchízhīdòu,
creating the Dǐzhù Rapids,
and cutting through the Lóngmén mountains,
to benefit the people of Yān, Dài, the Hú and Mò tribes, and the Xīhé region.
In the east, he drained the flooded plains,
contained the Měngzhū marshes,
and channeled the waters into nine canals,
controlling the floods of the eastern lands
to benefit the people of Jìzhōu.
In the south, he managed the Jiāng, Hàn, Huái, and Rǔ rivers,
making them flow eastward
into the Five Lakes,
to benefit the people of Chǔ, Jīng, Yuè, and the southern tribes.
This describes Yǔ's deeds,
and I now advocate universal love.
In the past, King Wén ruled the western land,
shining like the sun and moon,
his light spreading in all directions,
illuminating the western territory.
He did not allow large states to bully small ones,
nor the multitude to oppress the widowed and orphaned,
nor the powerful to seize the grain and livestock of farmers.
Heaven looked down upon King Wén's compassion,
so that the aged without children
could live out their years in security,
the isolated without brothers
could find their place among the living,
and the young who lost their parents
had support to grow up.
This describes King Wén's deeds,
and I now advocate universal love.
When King Wǔ sacrificed at Mount Tài,
the ancient text records:
"O Mount Tài!
The devout descendant, the King of Zhōu, performs this rite.
The great endeavor is accomplished;
the benevolent arise
to protect the peoples of Shāng, Xià, and the barbarian tribes.
Though I have close kin,
they are not as valuable as the benevolent.
If the myriad regions err,
the fault lies with me alone."
This describes King Wǔ's deeds,
and I now advocate universal love."
Therefore, Master Mòzǐ said:
"The scholars and gentlemen of today,
who sincerely desire the world's wealth
and hate its poverty,
who desire its order
and hate its chaos,
should practice universal mutual love
and mutual benefit.
This is the way of the sage kings,
the path to world order,
and must be diligently pursued."
4.3 "Universal Love, Part 3"
Master Mòzǐ said:
"The task of the benevolent
is surely to seek to promote the world's benefits
and eliminate the world's harms."
But in the present age,
what are the greatest harms in the world?
He said:
"When large states attack small ones,
great families disrupt small ones,
the strong rob the weak,
the many oppress the few,
the cunning deceive the simple,
the noble disdain the humble—
these are the harms of the world.
Add to these rulers who are unkind,
ministers who are disloyal,
fathers who are unloving,
sons who are unfilial—
these too are the harms of the world.
And now the common people,
armed with weapons, poison, fire, and water,
mutually injure and harm one another—
this also is a harm of the world.
Let us trace the origin of these numerous harms:
From where do they arise?
Do they arise from loving and benefiting others?
Surely one must say they do not,
but rather from hating and harming others.
If we distinguish those in the world who hate and harm others,
are they universalists
or particularists?
Surely one must say they are particularists.
Then does particularism indeed give rise to the great harms of the world?"
Therefore, Master Mòzǐ said:
"Particularism is wrong.
To condemn something
requires offering an alternative.
If one condemns without an alternative,
it is like trying to extinguish fire with water—
the argument will surely be invalid."
Therefore, Master Mòzǐ said:
"Replace particularism with universalism.
But why can universalism replace particularism?
He said:
If one treated others' states as one's own,
who would mobilize their state to attack another's?
For others would be as oneself.
If one treated others' cities as one's own,
who would mobilize their city to assault another's?
For others would be as oneself.
If one treated others' families as one's own,
who would mobilize their family to disrupt another's?
For others would be as oneself.
Thus, if states and cities did not attack each other,
and families did not disrupt or harm one another,
would this be a harm to the world
or a benefit?
Surely one must say it is a benefit.
Let us trace the origin of these numerous benefits:
From where do they arise?
Do they arise from hating and harming others?
Surely one must say they do not,
but rather from loving and benefiting others.
If we distinguish those in the world who love and benefit others,
are they particularists
or universalists?
Surely one must say they are universalists.
Then does universalism indeed give rise to the great benefits of the world?"
Therefore, Master Mòzǐ said:
"Universalism is right.
And earlier I stated:
'The task of the benevolent
is surely to seek to promote the world's benefits
and eliminate the world's harms.'
Now I trace the origin of the great benefits in the world to universalism,
and the origin of the great harms to particularism."
Therefore, Master Mòzǐ said:
"That particularism is wrong and universalism is right
is evident from this reasoning.
Now I seek to promote the world's benefits
by adopting universalism as the standard.
Thus, the sharp-eared and clear-sighted assist each other in hearing and seeing,
the strong-limbed aid each other in action and labor,
and those with the Way diligently teach one another.
Thus, the aged without wives or children
have support to live out their years.
The young orphans without parents
have reliance to grow up.
If only we adopt universalism as the standard,
such are its benefits.
Yet I do not understand why all who hear of universalism in the world reject it—
what is the reason for this?"
Yet the scholars of the world who criticize universal love have not ceased their arguments,
and still say:
"Universal love may be good,
but
how can it be put into practice?"
Mòzǐ replied:
"If it truly cannot be practiced,
even I would criticize it.
But how can something good be impracticable?
Let us consider both views by presenting
two hypothetical gentlemen:
one holding particularist views,
the other upholding universal love.
Thus the particularist would say:
'How could I treat my friend's needs as my own,
or my friend's family as my family?'
Therefore, when he sees his friend in need,
he will not feed the hungry,
clothe the cold,
nurse the sick,
nor bury the dead.
Such are the words
and deeds of the particularist.
The universalist speaks differently
and acts differently, saying:
'I have heard that to be a noble scholar in the world,
one must treat friends' needs as one's own,
and friends' families as one's family.'
Only then can one become a noble scholar.
Therefore, when he sees his friend in need,
he feeds the hungry,
clothes the cold,
nurses the sick,
and buries the dead.
Such are the words
and deeds of the universalist.
Now these two types of men,
do they not contradict each other in word and oppose each other in deed?
Suppose these two men
keep their word faithfully
and act resolutely,
making word and deed agree
like matching tally halves,
with no word left unfulfilled by action.
Then I dare ask: if on some vast plain
a man dons armor and helmet
to go to battle,
facing uncertain survival,
or if a high official is sent on distant missions to Bā, Yuè, Qí, or Jīng,
with his return uncertain—
who knows if he will come back?
In such cases, whom would one choose?
When entrusting the care of one's parents,
and the welfare of one's wife and children,
to another's care,
would one choose a universalist
or a particularist?
I believe in such situations,
no one in the world, however foolish,
even while criticizing universal love,
would choose anyone but a universalist.
Thus people denounce universal love in speech
but choose it in practice—
this shows how words and actions contradict.
I do not understand why the scholars of the world,
upon hearing of universal love,
all condemn it.
Yet the scholars who criticize universal love still persist, saying:
"Perhaps this principle applies to choosing friends,
but not to choosing rulers?"
"Let us consider both views by presenting
two hypothetical rulers:
one practicing universal love,
the other particularism.
Thus the particularist ruler would say:
'How can I treat my people's needs as my own?
This goes against human nature.
Human life on earth
is brief indeed,
like galloping steeds glimpsed through a crack.'
Therefore, when he sees his people suffering,
he will not feed the hungry,
clothe the cold,
nurse the sick,
nor bury the dead.
Such are the words
and deeds of the particularist ruler.
The universalist ruler speaks differently
and acts differently, saying:
'I have heard that to be an enlightened ruler,
one must put the people's welfare first
and one's own last.'
Only then can one become an enlightened ruler.
Therefore, when he sees his people suffering,
he feeds the hungry,
clothes the cold,
nurses the sick,
and buries the dead.
Such are the words
and deeds of the universalist ruler.
Now these two types of rulers,
do they not contradict each other in word and oppose each other in deed?
Suppose these two rulers
keep their word faithfully
and act resolutely,
making word and deed agree
like matching tally halves,
with no word left unfulfilled by action.
Then I dare ask: in a year of plague
when many people suffer from toil, cold, and hunger,
dying in ditches and gullies
in great numbers—
if one must choose between these two rulers,
whom would one follow?
I believe in such situations,
no one in the world, however foolish,
even while criticizing universal love in rulers,
would choose anyone but the universalist ruler.
Thus people denounce universal love in speech
but choose it in practice—
this shows how words and actions conflict.
I do not understand why the scholars of the world,
upon hearing of universal love, all condemn it."
Yet the scholars of the world who oppose universal love continue to voice their objections,
saying:
"Universal love may be benevolent
and righteous.
Nevertheless,
how can it be practiced?
I compare the impracticability of universal love
to lifting Mount Tài and leaping over the Jiāng and Hé rivers.
Thus, universal love
is merely a wishful ideal—
how could it possibly be something achievable?"
Mòzǐ replied:
"As for lifting Mount Tài to leap over the Jiāng and Hé rivers,
from ancient times to the present,
since the birth of humanity, this has never been accomplished.
But now, mutual love and mutual benefit
were personally practiced by the six ancient sage kings themselves.
How do we know the six ancient sage kings personally practiced them?"
Mòzǐ said:
"Although I did not live in the same age as they,
hearing their voices directly,
nor seeing their countenances,
I know it from what they recorded on bamboo and silk,
engraved on metal and stone,
carved on plates and vessels,
and passed down to later generations.
The 'Great Oath' states:
'King Wén was like the sun and moon,
shining over the four quarters
and the western land.'
This speaks of King Wén's vast universal love for the world,
comparing him to the sun and moon impartially shining upon all under heaven without bias—
this is King Wén's universality.
Thus, the universal love Mòzǐ advocates
takes King Wén as its model.
Moreover, it is not only the 'Great Oath' that affirms this;
the 'Oath of Yǔ' likewise testifies to it.
Yǔ declared:
'Assembled multitudes,
all listen to my words:
It is not that I, the humble one, dare to instigate rebellion,
but the ignorant Miao tribe
invites Heaven's punishment.
Thus, I lead you, lords of various states,
to campaign against the Miao.'
Yǔ's campaign against the Miao
was not to seek greater wealth and honor,
nor to secure blessings and emoluments,
nor to delight his senses,
but to promote the benefit of the world
and eliminate its harms—
this is Yǔ's universality.
Thus, the universal love Mòzǐ advocates
takes Yǔ as its model.
Moreover, it is not only the 'Oath of Yǔ' that affirms this;
the 'Declaration of Tāng' likewise testifies to it.
Tāng said:
'I, the humble one Lǚ,
dare to use a black bull
to report to High Heaven and Earth:
"Now there is a great drought,
which should fall upon my person.
I do not know how I have offended Heaven above and Earth below.
I dare not conceal the good,
nor dare I pardon the guilty,
for all is discerned in the Emperor's heart.
If the myriad regions have crimes,
let them fall upon my person.
If my person has crimes,
let them not extend to the myriad regions."'
This shows that Tāng, honored as the Son of Heaven
and possessing all under heaven,
yet did not fear to offer himself as sacrifice
to pray to the Lord on High and the spirits—
this is Tāng's universality.
Thus, the universal love Mòzǐ advocates
takes Tāng as its model.
Moreover, it is not only the 'Oath of Yǔ' and 'Declaration of Tāng' that affirm this;
the Zhōu 'Odes' likewise testify to it.
The Zhōu 'Odes' say:
'The kingly way is vast,
unbiased and impartial.
The kingly way is level,
impartial and unbiased.
Straight as an arrow,
smooth as a whetstone,
it is trodden by the noble,
and watched by the common.'
Do my words not speak of the Way?
In ancient times, King Wén and King Wǔ governed justly,
distributing rewards equally to the worthy and punishments to the violent,
without favoring kin or brothers.
This is the universality of Wén and Wǔ.
Thus, the universal love Mòzǐ advocates
takes Wén and Wǔ as its model.
I do not understand why all under heaven, upon hearing of universal love, reject it—
what is the reason?
Yet the objections of those in the world who oppose universal love still do not cease,
saying:
"Could it be detrimental to the interests of parents
and harmful to filial piety?"
Mòzǐ said:
"Let us examine the intentions of filial sons planning for their parents.
I do not know whether a filial son planning for his parents
wishes others to love and benefit them,
or wishes others to hate and harm them?
Judging by reason,
he surely wishes others to love and benefit them.
Then how should I proceed to achieve this?
If I first engage in loving and benefiting others' parents,
will others then reciprocate by loving and benefiting my parents?
Or if I first engage in hating and harming others' parents,
will others then reciprocate by loving and benefiting my parents?
Surely, I must first engage in loving and benefiting others' parents,
then others will reciprocate by loving and benefiting my parents.
Thus, the mutual conduct of filial sons
is indeed inevitable.
Is it not necessary to first engage in loving and benefiting others' parents?
Or do you consider the filial sons of the world imprudent
and insufficient to serve as models?
Let us examine what the ancient kings recorded in the 'Major Odes,' which states:
'No word goes unanswered,
no virtue unrewarded.
When you throw me a peach,
I return you a plum.'
This means that those who love others will surely be loved,
and those who hate others will surely be hated.
I do not understand why the scholars of the world, upon hearing of universal love, reject it—
what is the reason?"
Do they consider it too difficult to practice?
Yet there have been even more difficult things that were accomplished.
Formerly, King Líng of Jīng loved slender waists.
During his reign,
the men of Jīng ate no more than one meal,
needed support to rise,
and leaned on walls to walk.
Thus, restricted eating was extremely difficult,
yet they did it because King Líng delighted in it,
and within a generation the people transformed—
they sought to please their superior.
Formerly, King Gōujiàn of Yuè loved bravery.
He trained his officers for three years,
and knowing their understanding was still insufficient,
set fire to his boats
and ordered the advance.
His officers fell in the front lines,
dying in fire and water,
too many to count.
At that time,
without the drum they would not retreat—
the men of Yuè could be called trembling with zeal.
Thus, burning oneself was extremely difficult,
yet they did it because King Gōujiàn delighted in it,
and within a generation the people transformed—
they sought to please their superior.
Formerly, Duke Wén of Jìn loved coarse clothing.
During his reign,
the men of Jìn
wore robes of heavy cloth,
sheepskin coats,
caps of plain silk,
and coarse hemp shoes
to enter and see Duke Wén,
and exit to tread his court.
Thus, wearing coarse clothing was extremely difficult,
yet they did it because Duke Wén delighted in it,
and within a generation the people transformed—
they sought to please their superior.
Therefore, restricted eating, burning oneself, and coarse clothing
are among the most difficult things under heaven,
yet when the superior delighted in them,
the people transformed within a generation.
Why?
Because they sought to please their superior.
Now as for mutual love
and mutual benefit,
these are beneficial and easy to practice,
beyond calculation.
I believe the only lack is a superior who delights in them.
If there were a superior who delighted in them,
encouraging with rewards and praise,
and intimidating with penalties and punishments,
I believe people's turn to mutual love and mutual benefit
would be like fire rising and water flowing downward—
unstoppable under heaven.
Therefore, universal love is the way of the sage kings,
the means by which kings, dukes, and great men find security,
and the reason why the clothing and food of the myriad people are sufficient.
Hence, a gentleman should examine universal love and strive to practice it.
As a ruler, one must be benevolent;
as a minister, one must be loyal;
as a father, one must be kind;
as a son, one must be filial;
as an elder brother, one must be friendly;
as a younger brother, one must be respectful.
Therefore, if a gentleman wishes to be a benevolent ruler, loyal minister, kind father, filial son, friendly elder brother, or respectful younger brother,
universal love must be practiced.
This is the way of the sage kings and of great benefit to the myriad people.
5.1 "Condemnation of Offensive War I - Chapter 17"
Mòzǐ said:
In ancient times, kings, dukes, and great men desired gain and hated loss,
desired security and hated danger,
so offensive warfare must be condemned.
Suppose there is a man who enters another's orchard
and steals their peaches and plums.
Upon hearing of it, everyone condemns him,
and when caught by the authorities, he is punished.
Why is this?
Because he harms others to benefit himself.
As for those who steal others' dogs, pigs, chickens, or piglets,
their injustice is even greater than entering an orchard to steal peaches and plums.
Why is this?
Because they harm others more.
The more they harm others,
the greater their inhumanity becomes,
and the heavier their guilt.
As for those who enter others' stables
and take their horses or cattle,
their injustice is even greater than stealing dogs, pigs, chickens, or piglets.
Why is this?
Because they harm others even more.
The more they harm others,
the greater their inhumanity becomes,
and the heavier their guilt.
As for those who kill an innocent person,
strip them of their clothes, and take their spears and swords,
their injustice is even greater than entering a stable and taking horses or cattle.
Why is this?
Because they harm others the most.
The more they harm others,
the greater their inhumanity becomes,
and the heavier their guilt.
In such cases,
all gentlemen under heaven know to condemn it,
calling it unjust.
But now when it comes to the great injustice of attacking states,
they do not know to condemn it;
instead, they praise it,
calling it just.
How can this be called knowing the distinction between justice and injustice?
Killing one person is called unjust
and must incur one death penalty.
Following this reasoning,
killing ten people is ten times unjust
and must incur ten death penalties.
Killing a hundred people is a hundred times unjust
and must incur a hundred death penalties.
In such cases,
all gentlemen under heaven know to condemn it,
calling it unjust.
But now the great injustice of attacking states
is not known and condemned;
instead, it is praised,
called just.
Truly, they do not know it is unjust,
hence they record such words to leave to posterity.
If they knew it was unjust,
what reason would they have to record such injustice for posterity?
Suppose there is a person here
who, seeing a little black, calls it black,
but seeing much black, calls it white.
Then we would surely consider this person unable to distinguish black from white.
Tasting a little bitterness, they call it bitter,
but tasting much bitterness, they call it sweet.
Then we would surely consider this person unable to distinguish sweet from bitter.
Now, when minor wrongs are committed,
they know to condemn them.
But when major wrongs like attacking states are committed,
they do not know to condemn them;
instead, they praise them,
calling them just.
Can this be called knowing the distinction between justice and injustice?
Thus we know that the gentlemen under heaven
are confused in distinguishing justice from injustice.
5.2 "Condemnation of Offensive War II - Chapter 18"
Mòzǐ said:
In ancient times, kings, dukes, and great men who governed states
truly desired careful judgment in praise and blame,
appropriateness in rewards and punishments,
and no faults in penalties and administration.
Therefore, offensive warfare should not be waged.
Now, if armies are raised,
in winter they fear the cold,
in summer they fear the heat—
this cannot be done in winter or summer.
In spring, it disrupts the people's plowing, planting, and cultivation;
in autumn, it disrupts the people's harvesting.
If just one season is wasted,
the number of people who die from hunger, cold, and starvation
is incalculable.
Now, let us calculate the army's equipment:
bamboo arrows, feathered banners, tents, armor, shields, and sword hilts—
the number that rot, break, and become unusable
is incalculable.
As for spears, halberds, dagger-axes, swords, and chariots—
the number that break, shatter, rot, and become unusable
is incalculable.
As for oxen and horses: fat when they depart,
lean when they return,
or dying and not returning at all—
their number is incalculable.
As for the long and distant roads,
where grain supplies are cut off and not continuous,
the number of people who die
is incalculable.
As for their unsettled living conditions,
irregular eating and drinking,
lack of moderation in hunger and fullness,
the number of people who fall ill and die on the road
is incalculable.
Army losses are numerous and incalculable;
total annihilation of armies is incalculable.
Then the number of spirits who lose their sacrifices
is also incalculable.
The state issues orders,
seizes the people's resources,
and destroys the people's benefits on such a large scale.
Why then do they do it?
They say:
"I covet the fame of victory in attack
and the profits gained,
so I do it."
Mòzǐ said:
Consider what they gain from victory—
it is of no use.
Consider what they obtain—
it is far less than what they lose.
Now, to attack a city of three lǐ in inner walls and seven lǐ in outer walls,
even if they could take it without sharp weapons
and without killing, merely by obtaining it empty,
this would be so.
Yet many must be killed, certainly tens of thousands,
at least thousands,
before a city of three lǐ in inner walls and seven lǐ in outer walls can be obtained.
Now, a state with ten thousand chariots,
whose empty cities number in the thousands,
cannot all be occupied;
whose vast lands number in the tens of thousands,
cannot all be opened up.
Thus, land is what they have in surplus,
and subjects are what they lack.
Now to exhaust the lives of their subjects
and intensify the sufferings of high and low
to contend for empty cities
is to discard what they lack
and increase what they already have in surplus.
To govern in this way
is not to attend to the state's affairs.
Those who advocate offensive warfare say:
"To the south, the kings of Jīng and Yuè,
to the north, the rulers of Qí and Jìn,
when first enfeoffed across the land,
the extent of their territories
had not yet reached several hundred lǐ,
and the multitude of their followers
had not yet reached several hundred thousand.
Due to the cause of offensive warfare,
the breadth of their lands came to span several thousand lǐ,
and the multitude of their followers came to number several million.
This is why offensive warfare is swift."
Mòzǐ said:
Even if four or five states might gain benefits from it,
it is still called an unrighteous way.
It is like a physician administering medicine to sick people.
Suppose there is a physician here
who mixes his invocational medicines and administers them to all the sick people under heaven.
If ten thousand people take this,
and only four or five physicians benefit from it,
it is still called ineffective medicine.
Thus, a filial son would not feed it to his parents,
nor would a loyal minister feed it to his lord.
In ancient times, when states were enfeoffed across the land,
for the distant, based on what was heard by ear,
for the near, based on what was seen by eye,
those who perished due to offensive warfare were too numerous to count.
How do we know this is so?
In the east, there was the state of Jǔ.
It was a very small state,
sandwiched between large states,
and did not respectfully serve the great.
The great states likewise did not follow and show care or benefit to it.
Thus, to the east, the Yuè people encroached and reduced its territory,
and to the west, the Qí people annexed and possessed it.
Considering why Jǔ perished between Qí and Yuè,
it was due to this offensive warfare.
Even in the south, Chén and Cài,
the reason they perished between Wú and Yuè,
was also due to offensive warfare.
Even in the north, Jūyī and Bùzhùhé,
the reason they perished between Yān, Dài, Hú, and Mò,
was also due to offensive warfare.
Therefore:
(Thus, offensive warfare must be condemned) Mòzǐ said:
The ancients had a saying:
"If planning yields no result,
then use the past to know the future,
use the apparent to know the hidden."
If planning is like this,
one can obtain understanding.
Advocates of offensive warfare say:
"They could not gather and use their multitudes,
thus they perished.
I can gather and use my multitudes,
and with this wage offensive warfare across the land,
who would dare not submit?"
Mòzǐ said:
Even if you can gather and use your multitudes,
how can you compare to the ancient Wú's Hé Lǘ?
Ancient Wú's Hé Lǘ trained his soldiers for seven years,
armored and bearing weapons, they marched three hundred lǐ before encamping,
stationed at Cùlín,
emerged through the narrow path of Míng'ài,
fought at Bǎijǔ,
penetrated the state of Chǔ and made Sòng and Lǔ pay homage.
But when it came to Fū Chāi himself,
he went north to attack Qí,
encamped at Wénshàng,
fought at Àilíng,
greatly defeated the Qí people and forced them to flee to Tàishān.
He went east to attack Yuè,
crossed the three rivers and five lakes,
and forced them to flee to Kuàijī.
None of the nine barbarian states failed to submit.
Yet afterward, he could not reward the orphans,
distribute alms to the masses,
relied on his own strength,
boasted of his achievements,
praised his own wisdom,
neglected instruction,
then built the Gūsū Tower,
which after seven years was still unfinished.
When it reached this point,
then Wú had hearts turning away and weary.
Yuè King Gōu Jiàn, seeing that the high and low in Wú were not in harmony,
gathered his multitudes to avenge his enemy.
He entered the northern outer wall,
captured the great boats,
surrounded the royal palace,
and thus the state of Wú perished.
Formerly, Jìn had six generals,
and among them, none was as strong as Zhì Bó.
Considering the breadth of his lands,
the multitude of his followers,
he sought to resist the feudal lords to build a heroic name.
(The swiftness of offensive warfare) ,
thus he selected his claw-and-tooth officers,
arrayed his multitudes of boats and chariots,
attacked and possessed the Zhōngháng clan.
Thinking his strategy was already sufficient,
he further attacked the Fàn clan and greatly defeated them.
Merging three families into one, he did not stop,
but further besieged Zhào Xiāngzǐ in Jìnyáng.
When it reached this point,
then Hán and Wèi also conspired together, saying:
"The ancients had a saying:
'When the lips are gone, the teeth are cold.'
If the Zhào clan perishes in the morning,
we follow in the evening.
If the Zhào clan perishes in the evening,
we follow in the morning.
The Odes say:
'If the fish does not strive in water,
what will it reach on land?'" Thus, the rulers of these three states united their efforts,
opened their gates and cleared the roads,
donned armor and raised soldiers,
Hán and Wèi from the outside,
the Zhào clan from the inside,
attacked Zhì Bó,
and greatly defeated him.
Therefore, Mòzǐ said:
The ancients had a saying:
"The gentleman does not use water as a mirror,
but uses people as a mirror.
Using water as a mirror, one sees one's face;
using people as a mirror, one knows fortune and misfortune."
Now, if one considers offensive warfare beneficial,
then why not examine the case of Zhì Bó?
This shows it is not fortunate but ominous,
as can already be understood.
5.3 "Condemnation of Offensive Warfare Part 3 - Chapter 19"
Mòzǐ said:
What is it that the world today praises as good?
What explanation is given?
Is it that it benefits Heaven above,
benefits ghosts in the middle,
and benefits humans below,
thus it is praised?
Or is it not that it benefits Heaven above,
benefits ghosts in the middle,
and benefits humans below,
thus it is praised?
Even the most foolish person below
would surely say:
"It is because it benefits Heaven above,
benefits ghosts in the middle,
and benefits humans below,
thus it is praised."
What the world today collectively upholds
is the law of the sage kings.
Yet today, many feudal lords still mostly engage in attack, conquest, and annexation,
which is having the name of praising righteousness,
without examining its reality.
This is like a blind person agreeing with others on the names of white and black,
but unable to distinguish the actual things.
How can that be called discrimination?
Therefore, when the wise of ancient times planned for the world,
they necessarily considered righteousness carefully before acting.
Thus, in action, they had no doubts,
swiftly achieved success,
obtained what they desired,
and complied with the benefits of Heaven, ghosts, and the common people.
This is the way of the wise.
Therefore, the benevolent men of ancient times who possessed the world
necessarily opposed the doctrines of the great states,
unified the harmony of the world,
brought together all within the four seas,
then led the common people of the world
in agriculture and served the Lord on High, mountains, rivers, and spirits as subjects.
Benefiting people more,
their achievements were thus greater.
Therefore, Heaven rewarded them,
ghosts enriched them,
people praised them,
made them noble as the Son of Heaven,
rich in possessing the world,
their fame equal to heaven and earth,
and to this day, it has not ceased.
This is the way of the wise,
the reason the former kings possessed the world.
Now the kings, dukes, and great men, the feudal lords of the world, do not act thus.
They are sure to dispatch their officers and warriors,
array their troops in chariots and boats,
equip them with strong armor and sharp weapons,
and set off to attack innocent states.
Invading their borders and territories,
they cut down their grain crops,
fell their trees,
destroy their inner and outer city walls,
fill in their moats and ponds,
slaughter their sacrificial animals,
burn down their ancestral temples,
massacre their common people,
exterminate their old and weak,
and seize their precious vessels.
Urging their soldiers forward into battle,
they command:
"To die in the line of duty is the highest honor;
to kill many is the next;
to be wounded is the lowest.
And as for those who break ranks or flee in defeat—
their crime is punishable by death without pardon!"
Thus they terrify their troops.
Now, to annex states and overthrow armies,
to brutalize the common people,
and to disrupt the legacy of the sages—
do they intend this to benefit Heaven?
To take Heaven's people
and attack Heaven's cities—
this is to slaughter Heaven's populace,
strip and shake the positions of the spirits,
overturn the altars of soil and grain,
and steal and kill the sacrificial animals.
This, then, does not align with the benefits of Heaven above.
Do they intend this to benefit the spirits?
To kill the spirits,
exterminate the masters of ghosts and spirits,
abolish the former kings,
brutalize the common people,
and cause the people to scatter and flee—
this does not align with the benefits of the spirits in the middle.
Do they intend this to benefit the people?
To kill people
in the name of benefiting them is preposterous.
Moreover, calculating the costs,
this is the root of harm to life;
the exhaustion of the wealth and resources of the people under Heaven is incalculable.
Thus, this does not align with the benefits of the people below.
Now, consider the mutual disadvantages for armies:
generals lacking courage,
officers lacking dedication,
weapons lacking sharpness,
training lacking practice,
armies lacking numbers,
troops lacking harmony,
authority lacking deterrence,
harm lacking duration,
conflict lacking urgency,
cohesion lacking strength,
resolve lacking firmness,
and allied states harboring doubts.
When allied states harbor doubts,
then the enemy arises with schemes, and morale wanes.
If all these conditions are fully present
and one persists in military campaigns,
then the state loses its soldiers,
and the people abandon their livelihoods.
Now, observe the claims of states that favor aggressive warfare:
if they raise a moderate army,
the number of gentlemen and commoners must be several thousand,
with followers multiplied to a hundred thousand,
before it is sufficient to mobilize as an army.
The long campaigns last several years,
the short ones several months.
Thus, the rulers have no leisure to attend to governance,
the officers no leisure to manage their offices,
the farmers no leisure to sow and reap,
the women no leisure to spin, weave, and sew.
This means the state loses its soldiers,
and the people abandon their livelihoods.
Moreover, with their chariots and horses worn out,
their tents and canopies,
the provisions for the three armies,
and the preparations of armor and weapons—
if even one-fifth is recovered,
it is still considered a generous surplus.
Yet further, with the losses and dispersals on the roads,
the roads being long and distant,
food supplies failing to reach them,
meals not taken at proper times,
servants and soldiers suffering from hunger, cold, freezing, starvation, and illness,
and those who die and are discarded in ditches and valleys—
their numbers are beyond calculation.
This is how it brings harm to people,
a profound calamity for the world.
Yet the kings, dukes, and great men delight in and carry this out—
this is to delight in the brutal destruction of the common people of the world.
Is it not perverse?
Now, among the war-loving states of the world,
Qí, Jìn, Chǔ, and Yuè—
if these four states were to achieve their ambitions in the world,
they would all have populations ten times their current size,
and still be unable to fully utilize their land.
This shows a shortage of people and a surplus of land.
Yet now, for the sake of contending over land, they instead brutalize one another.
This, then, is to deplete what is insufficient and aggravate what is surplus.
Now those rulers fond of offensive warfare
adorn their arguments to criticize Master Mòzǐ, saying:
"You consider offensive warfare to be unjust,
but is it not beneficial to things?
In ancient times, Yǔ campaigned against the Yǒumiáo,
Tāng attacked Jié,
King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
and all were established as sage kings.
What is the reason for this?"
Master Mòzǐ said:
"You have not examined the categories of my words,
nor understood the reasons behind them.
What they did was not what is called 'attack',
but what is called 'punishment'.
In ancient times, the Sānmíao were in great chaos,
Heaven ordered their destruction.
The sun demon appeared at night,
it rained blood for three mornings,
a dragon was born in the temple,
dogs cried in the markets,
ice formed in summer,
the earth split open to the springs,
the five grains underwent changes,
and the people were greatly terrified.
Gāoyáng then commanded Yǔ at the Xuángōng,
Yǔ personally held Heaven's auspicious mandate,
to campaign against the Yǒumiáo.
Lightning repeatedly struck with awe,
there was a spirit with a human face and bird body,
waiting as if holding a jade tablet,
seizing the auspicious signs of the Yǒumiáo.
The Miáo army fell into great chaos,
and afterwards they nearly perished.
After Yǔ had conquered the Yǒumiáo,
he regulated the mountains and rivers,
distinguished the hierarchy of things,
established control over the four extremities,
and spirits and people did not disobey,
the world then became tranquil.
This was Yǔ's campaign against the Yǒumiáo.
Coming to the Xià's Jié,
Heaven showed stern commands:
the sun and moon were untimely,
cold and heat arrived mixed together,
the five grains withered and died,
ghosts called out in the capital,
cranes cried for over ten nights.
Heaven then commanded Tāng at the Biāogōng,
to receive the great mandate over Xià:
'The virtue of Xià is in great chaos,
I have already ended their mandate from Heaven,
go and punish them,
I will surely make you equal to the task.'
Tāng then dared to lead his multitudes,
marching toward the borders of Xià.
The Lord on High then secretly and violently destroyed the cities of Xià.
Shortly after,
a spirit came to report:
'The virtue of Xià is in great chaos,
go and attack them,
I will surely make you greatly equal to the task.
I have received the mandate from Heaven,
Heaven orders Róng to set fire at the northwestern corner between the cities of Xià.'
Tāng led Jié's multitudes to conquer Xià,
assembled the feudal lords at Bó,
presented the proclamation of Heaven's mandate,
communicating it to the four directions,
and no feudal lord under heaven dared not submit.
This was Tāng's punishment of Jié.
Coming then to the Shāng king Zhòu,
Heaven did not enjoy his virtue,
sacrifices were conducted at the wrong times,
ten suns appeared together in the middle of the night,
it rained earth at Bó,
the nine tripods moved from their positions,
female demons appeared at night,
ghosts chanted at night,
there were women who turned into men,
Heaven rained flesh,
thorns grew on the state's highways,
and the king indulged himself wantonly.
A red bird held a jade tablet in its beak,
descending upon Zhōu's Qíshè,
saying:
'Heaven orders King Wén of Zhōu to attack Yīn and possess the state.'
Tàidiān came to submit,
the river produced the green chart,
the earth produced the chéng huáng.
King Wǔ undertook the task,
dreamed of three spirits,
saying:
'We have already drowned Yīn's Zhòu in the virtue of wine,
go and attack him,
we will surely make you greatly equal to the task.'
King Wǔ then attacked the madman,
turned Shāng into Zhōu,
Heaven bestowed upon King Wǔ the banner of the yellow bird.
After the king had conquered Yīn,
completed the gifts of the Lord on High,
distributed the worship of various spirits,
sacrificed to Zhòu's former kings,
communicated with the four barbarians,
and none under heaven did not submit,
then he continued Tāng's legacy.
This was King Wǔ's punishment of Zhòu.
If we examine these three sage kings,
it was not what is called 'attack',
but what is called 'punishment'.
Then those rulers fond of offensive warfare
adorn their arguments to criticize Master Mòzǐ, saying:
"You consider offensive warfare to be unjust,
but is it not beneficial to things?
In ancient times, Chǔ's Xióng Lí was first enfeoffed in the area of Suī Mountain,
Yuè's king Jǐn Kuī came from Yǒujù,
first establishing the state of Yuè,
Táng Shū and Lǚ Shàng established the states of Qí and Jìn.
These all had territories of several hundred lǐ,
now because of annexing states,
they have divided the world into four and possess it.
What is the reason for this?"
Master Mòzǐ said:
"You have not examined the categories of my words,
nor understood the reasons behind them.
In ancient times, when the Son of Heaven first enfeoffed the feudal lords,
there were over ten thousand.
Now because of annexing states,
over ten thousand states have been destroyed,
and only these four states remain independent.
This is like a physician who gives medicine to over ten thousand people,
and only four are cured,
then he cannot be called a good physician.
Then those rulers fond of offensive warfare further adorn their arguments, saying:
"It is not that I find gold, jade, children, women, and land insufficient,
I wish to establish a reputation for righteousness in the world,
and attract feudal lords with virtue."
Master Mòzǐ said:
Now if there is one who can establish a reputation for righteousness in the world,
and attract feudal lords with virtue,
the submission of the world can be expected immediately.
The world has been engaged in offensive warfare for a long time,
like a child servant driving a carriage.
Now if there is one who can sincerely imitate and first benefit the feudal lords of the world,
when a large state acts unjustly,
then all share the concern;
when a large state attacks a small state,
then all join in rescuing it;
when a small state's city walls are incomplete,
they must see to their repair;
when cloth and grain are lacking, then supply them;
when currency and silk are insufficient, then provide them.
With this to offer to large states,
then the rulers of small states will be pleased.
Others labor while I am at ease,
then my armor and weapons will be strong.
Be generous and kind,
relax what is urgent,
and the people will surely move to you.
Change offensive warfare to govern my state,
and the results will surely double.
Measure the expenses of mobilizing my army,
to assist the exhausted feudal lords,
then I can surely obtain benefits.
Supervise with correctness,
make righteousness my reputation,
I must strive to be generous to my multitudes,
be trustworthy to my army,
with this to assist the armies of the feudal lords,
then I will be invincible under heaven,
and the benefits will be innumerable.
This is beneficial to the world,
but the kings, dukes, and great men do not understand and employ it,
this can be said to be ignorance of the great task of benefiting the world.
Therefore, Master Mòzǐ said:
Now all the kings, dukes, great men, officers, and gentlemen under heaven,
if in their hearts they truly wish to promote the benefits of the world,
and eliminate the harms of the world,
should consider that frequent offensive warfare
is truly a great harm to the world.
Now if one wishes to practice benevolence and righteousness,
strive to be a superior officer,
above wishing to accord with the way of the sage kings,
below wishing to accord with the benefits of the state and its people,
then one must consider the doctrine of condemning offensive warfare,
and cannot fail to examine this.
6.1 "Economy of Expenditure I - Chapter Twenty"
When a sage administers a state,
he can double its benefits.
When he extends his governance to the whole world,
he can double the benefits of the world.
This doubling
does not come from acquiring territory externally,
but from within the state itself,
by eliminating useless expenditures,
which is sufficient to double them.
When a sage king governs,
in issuing orders, initiating projects, employing the people, and using resources,
there is nothing he does that does not add to their utility.
Thus, resources are used without waste,
the people's virtue is not burdened with toil,
and the benefits he promotes are many.
Why are clothing and furs made?
For protection against cold in winter,
and against heat in summer.
In the principles of making garments,
those that add warmth in winter and coolness in summer
are promoted.
Those that do not add such benefits
are eliminated.
Why are houses built?
For protection against wind and cold in winter,
and against heat and rain in summer.
In building houses,
those that are sturdy
are promoted.
Those that are not
are eliminated.
Why are armor, shields, and the five weapons made?
To guard against invaders, riots, and thieves.
If there are invaders, riots, or thieves,
those with armor, shields, and the five weapons will prevail;
none will fail,
hence the sage creates armor, shields, and the five weapons.
In making armor, shields, and the five weapons,
those that are lightweight, sharp, sturdy, and hard to break
are promoted.
Those that are not
are eliminated.
Why are boats and carts made?
Carts to travel over hills and land,
boats to navigate rivers and valleys,
to facilitate benefits from all directions.
In the principles of making boats and carts,
those that are lightweight and efficient
are promoted.
Those that are not
are eliminated.
In creating all these things,
there is nothing done that does not add to their utility,
thus resources are used without waste,
the people's virtue is not burdened with toil,
and the benefits promoted are many.
If we eliminate the rulers' fondness for amassing pearls, jade, birds, beasts, dogs, and horses,
and use those resources to increase the numbers of clothing, houses, armor, shields, the five weapons, boats, and carts,
would that not double the quantity?
Then it is not difficult.
So what is hard to double?
Only the population is hard to double.
Yet the population can be doubled.
In the past, the sage kings established a law stating:
"A man at twenty years of age
shall not dare to avoid starting a family.
A woman at fifteen years of age
shall not dare to avoid serving a man."
This was the law of the sage kings.
After the sage kings passed away,
the people became unrestrained.
Those who wished to start a family early
might do so at twenty,
while those who wished to start late
might do so at forty.
Comparing the early and the late,
they lag behind the sage kings' law by ten years.
If all women bear children after three years of marriage,
they could have two or three children.
Is this not a way to make people start families early and thus double the population?
But it is not so now.
Today's rulers
have many ways to reduce the population.
They make the people toil,
their taxes are heavy,
the people's wealth is insufficient,
and those who die from cold and hunger are countless.
Moreover, the rulers raise armies to attack neighboring states,
with campaigns lasting as long as a year,
or as short as several months,
during which men and women long do not see each other—
this is a way to reduce the population.
Add to that those who die from unsettled living conditions, irregular meals, and resulting illnesses,
as well as those who die in invasions and seizures,
in sieges and battles in the fields,
and the numbers are countless.
Is this not how today's rulers employ numerous methods to reduce the population?
The sage in governance simply avoids these,
and is it not through numerous methods that the sage in governance increases the population?
Therefore, Mòzǐ said:
"Eliminate useless expenditures—
this is the way of the sage kings,
and a great benefit to the world."
6.2 "Moderation in Use, Part 2"
Mòzǐ said:
"The wise kings and sages of ancient times who ruled the world and corrected the lords
loved the people with utmost loyalty,
benefited the people with profound generosity,
combining loyalty and trustworthiness,
while also showing them the benefits,
so they were never weary throughout their lives,
nor did they tire until their deaths.
The reason the wise kings and sages of ancient times ruled the world and corrected the lords
was this.
Thus, the sage kings of old established the laws of moderation in use, saying:
'All the various artisans of the world,
wheelwrights, cart-makers, leatherworkers, potters, smiths, carpenters, and craftsmen,
shall each engage in what they can do.'
And:
'Whatever is sufficient to supply the people's needs
shall be done; any added cost that does not benefit the people shall cease.'
The sage kings of old established the laws on food and drink, saying:
'Enough to fill the emptiness, sustain the energy,
strengthen the limbs,
and make the ears and eyes sharp—
that is sufficient.'
They did not seek the ultimate in blending the five flavors,
the harmony of fragrances,
nor procure rare and exotic items from distant lands.
How do we know this is so?
In ancient times, when Yáo governed the world,
he pacified the south as far as Jiāozhǐ,
reached Yōudū in the north,
and extended east and west to where the sun rises and sets,
and all submitted.
Yet when it came to his own indulgences,
he did not have two kinds of millet,
nor more than one soup with meat,
ate from earthenware bowls,
drank from earthenware cups,
and used a dipper for serving.
The ceremonial rituals of bowing, rising, and social etiquette
the sage kings did not practice.
The sage kings of old established the laws on clothing, saying:
'In winter, darkish-red or purplish-black garments that are lightweight and warm;
in summer, hemp or grass-cloth garments that are lightweight and cool—
that is sufficient.'
Any added cost that does not benefit the people
the sage kings did not undertake.
The sage kings of old, because fierce birds and cunning beasts harmed the people,
taught the people to carry arms.
Wearing swords daily,
they could pierce upon thrusting,
cut upon striking,
and withstand side blows without breaking—
such were the benefits of swords.
Armor, as clothing, was lightweight and efficient,
moving with the soldier and obedient—
such were the benefits of armor.
Carts were for carrying heavy loads over long distances,
riding in them was safe,
pulling them was smooth,
safe so as not to harm people,
smooth for quick arrival—
such were the benefits of carts.
The sage kings of old, because wide rivers and broad valleys could not be crossed,
thus made efficient boats and oars,
sufficient to ferry across—that was all.
Even when the highest officials or lords arrived,
the boats and oars were not changed,
the ferrymen did not adorn themselves—
