such were the benefits of boats.
The sage kings of old established the laws on moderate funerals, saying:
'Three layers of clothing,
enough to let the flesh decay;
a coffin three inches thick,
enough to let the bones decay.
A dug grave not deep enough to reach water,
and not allowing odors to escape—
that is sufficient.
Once the dead are buried,
the living should not prolong mourning with grief.'"
In ancient times when humans were first born and had no dwellings,
they dwelled in caves dug into hills and mounds.
The sage kings pondered this,
considering such cave dwellings:
They could shield against wind and cold in winter.
But when summer arrived,
the lower parts became damp,
while the upper parts were steamed by heat,
fearing this would harm people's vitality,
thus they created dwellings for benefit.
So then, what should be the method for building dwellings?
Mòzǐ said:
Their sides can defend against wind and cold,
their tops can defend against snow, frost, rain, and dew,
their interiors clean,
suitable for sacrificial rites,
and the walls sufficient to separate men and women—
that is all.
Any additional expense that does not benefit the people
the sage kings would not undertake.
6.3 "Moderation in Use Part 3"
Missing.
6.4 "Moderation in Funerals Part 1"
Missing.
6.5 "Moderation in Funerals Part 2"
Missing.
6.6 "Moderation in Funerals Part 3"
Mòzǐ said:
The benevolent person's planning for the world
is no different from a filial son's planning for his parents.
Now, when a filial son plans for his parents,
what does he do?
He says:
"If my parents are poor, I work to enrich them;
if they have few people, I work to increase them;
if the multitude is chaotic, I work to bring order."
In these endeavors,
there may be insufficient strength, inadequate resources, or lack of wisdom, then one stops,
but none dare spare any remaining effort,
conceal plans, or neglect benefits
without acting for their parents.
These three tasks—
this is how a filial son plans for his parents,
precisely like this.
Even when a benevolent person plans for the world,
it is also just like this.
He says:
If the world is poor, work to enrich it;
if the people are few, work to increase them;
if the multitude is chaotic, work to bring order.
In these endeavors,
there may be insufficient strength, inadequate resources, or lack of wisdom, then one stops,
but none dare spare any remaining effort,
conceal plans, or neglect benefits
without acting for the world.
These three tasks—
this is how a benevolent person plans for the world,
precisely like this.
Now, since the sage kings of the three ancient dynasties have passed away,
the world has lost righteousness.
Later generations of gentlemen
some consider lavish funerals and prolonged mourning as benevolent,
righteous,
and the duty of a filial son.
Others consider lavish funerals and prolonged mourning as not benevolent or righteous,
nor the duty of a filial son.
These two types of people
contradict each other in speech,
and oppose each other in action,
yet both say:
"We are following the ways of Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ."
Yet their words contradict,
and their actions oppose.
Here, later generations of gentlemen are all perplexed by the words of these two.
If perplexed by the words of these two,
then let us try applying them in governing the state and the myriad people to observe:
How do lavish funerals and prolonged mourning align with these three benefits?
Suppose we follow their words,
adopt their plans—
can lavish funerals and prolonged mourning truly enrich the poor, increase the few, stabilize danger, and bring order to chaos?
If so, it is benevolent,
righteous,
the duty of a filial son,
and those who advise others must encourage it.
(Who in the world dominates),
The benevolent would seek to promote it throughout the world,
encouraging people to praise it,
never abolishing it.
Or suppose we follow their words,
adopt their plans—
can lavish funerals and prolonged mourning truly not enrich the poor, increase the few, stabilize danger, or bring order to chaos?
Then it is not benevolent, not righteous, not the duty of a filial son.
Those who advise others must discourage it.
The benevolent would seek to eliminate it from the world,
abolishing it and having people condemn it,
never practicing it lifelong.
Thus, promoting the benefits of the world
and eliminating the harms of the world—
if the state and its people are not well-governed now,
it has never been so from ancient times to the present.
How do we know this is so?
Today's scholars and gentlemen
still largely doubt whether lavish funerals and prolonged mourning are right or wrong, beneficial or harmful.
Therefore, Mòzǐ said:
Then let us examine it.
Now, if we follow the proponents of lavish funerals and prolonged mourning,
applying it in state affairs:
For the funerals of kings, dukes, and great men,
they say coffins must be multiple,
burial must be lavish,
shrouds must be numerous,
embroideries must be abundant,
and tombs must be massive.
For the deaths of commoners and lowly people,
it nearly exhausts the household.
For the deaths of feudal lords,
it empties the treasuries,
then adorns the body with gold, jade, pearls, and gems,
with silk ribbons and ties,
burying chariots and horses in the tomb,
and additionally many canopies, tripods, drums, tables, vessels, spears, swords, feathers, hides,
all interred with the deceased.
As if satisfied, they follow with burials of the living,
saying:
For the Son of Heaven, those killed to accompany him
number hundreds at most,
tens at least.
For generals and senior officials, those killed to accompany them
number tens at most,
a few at least.
What are the methods for conducting mourning?
They say:
Weeping without restraint in sound,
wearing mourning garments with flowing tears,
dwelling in a lean-to,
sleeping on grass with a clod as a pillow.
Moreover, they urge each other to force fasting unto hunger,
wearing thin clothes unto cold,
until the face becomes sunken,
the complexion dark and sallow,
ears and eyes not sharp,
hands and feet not strong,
rendering them useless.
They also say:
The superior scholar's conduct of mourning
must require support to rise,
a cane to walk,
maintained for three years.
If such words are followed as law,
such ways practiced,
if kings, dukes, and officials act thus,
they surely cannot attend court early and leave late,
manage the five offices and six bureaus,
clear vegetation,
or fill granaries.
If farmers act thus,
they surely cannot go out early and return late,
plowing, sowing, and planting.
If artisans act thus,
they surely cannot build boats and carts,
or make utensils.
If women act thus,
they surely cannot rise early and retire late,
spinning, weaving, and sewing.
Consider lavish burials as burying much wealth,
and prolonged mourning as long prohibiting work.
Wealth already produced
is supported and buried.
Those who could produce more
are long restrained.
Seeking wealth through this
is like forbidding farming yet expecting harvest—
the means to wealth are unattainable.
Thus, seeking to enrich the state through this is already impossible.
To wish to increase the population,
do you think it is possible?
This argument is again untenable.
Now, if those who advocate elaborate funerals and prolonged mourning were to govern,
when the ruler dies, they mourn for three years;
when parents die, they mourn for three years;
when a wife or the eldest son dies, these five cases
all require mourning for three years.
Then for uncles, brothers, and other sons,
close relatives and clan members mourn for five months;
for aunts, sisters, and maternal relatives, they mourn for several months.
Thus, the emaciation from grief must have its regulations.
Causing the face to become sunken,
the complexion dark and sallow,
the ears and eyes not sharp,
the hands and feet not strong and vigorous—
they become unfit for use.
It is also said:
Superior officers conducting mourning
must be supported to rise,
and use a cane to walk,
maintaining this for three years.
If such laws and words,
such practices and ways,
lead to such hunger and deprivation,
then the people will not withstand the cold in winter,
nor the heat in summer,
and those who fall ill and die will be countless.
This greatly disrupts the relations between men and women.
To seek to increase the population this way
is like making someone carry a sword and hoping for longevity;
the theory of increasing the population cannot be achieved.
Thus, the desire to increase the population is already impossible.
To wish to govern penal administration,
do you think it is possible?
This argument is again untenable.
Now, if those who advocate elaborate funerals and prolonged mourning were to govern,
the state would surely become poor,
the population would surely decrease,
and penal administration would surely fall into disorder.
If such laws and words,
such practices and ways,
cause those above to follow them,
they will be unable to attend to governance;
if those below follow them,
they will be unable to engage in work.
If those above do not attend to governance,
penal administration will surely fall into disorder;
if those below do not engage in work,
the resources for clothing and food will surely be insufficient.
If they are insufficient,
a younger brother seeking help from his elder brother and failing to get it
will inevitably resent his elder brother;
a son seeking from his parents and failing to get it,
an unfilial son will surely resent his parents;
a minister seeking from his ruler and failing to get it,
a disloyal minister will surely rebel against his superior.
Thus, depraved and wicked people,
going out without clothes,
coming in without food,
internally harboring resentment,
all become licentious and violent,
and cannot be restrained.
Hence, there are many robbers and thieves, and few who are orderly.
With many robbers and thieves and few orderly people,
to seek order this way
is like making someone turn around three times and expecting them not to betray you;
the theory of order cannot be achieved.
Thus, the desire to govern penal administration is already impossible.
To wish to prevent large states from attacking small ones,
do you think it is possible?
This argument is again untenable.
Thus, in the past, after the sage kings had passed away,
the world lost righteousness,
and the feudal lords contended by force.
In the south, there were the kings of Chǔ and Yuè,
and in the north, the rulers of Qí and Jìn.
They all trained their troops
to make conquest and annexation their governance over the world.
Therefore, the reason large states do not attack small ones is that
the small states have ample stores,
their city walls are well-maintained,
and there is harmony between superiors and inferiors,
so large states are reluctant to attack them.
If there are no stores,
city walls are not maintained,
and there is no harmony between superiors and inferiors,
then large states are eager to attack them.
Now, if those who advocate elaborate funerals and prolonged mourning were to govern,
the state would surely become poor,
the population would surely decrease,
and penal administration would surely fall into disorder.
If poor,
there will be nothing to store.
If the population is small,
there will be few to repair city walls and moats.
If there is disorder,
then going out to battle will not lead to victory,
and defending will not be secure.
To seek to prevent large states from attacking small ones this way
is already impossible.
To wish to seek blessings from the Lord on High, ghosts, and spirits,
do you think it is possible?
This argument is again untenable.
Now, if those who advocate elaborate funerals and prolonged mourning were to govern,
the state would surely become poor,
the population would surely decrease,
and penal administration would surely fall into disorder.
If poor,
then the sacrificial grains and wines will not be pure and clean.
If the population is small,
then there will be few to serve the Lord on High, ghosts, and spirits.
If there is disorder,
then sacrifices will not be offered in a timely and proper manner.
Now, if serving the Lord on High, ghosts, and spirits is further restricted,
governing in this way,
the Lord on High, ghosts, and spirits would look down from above and say:
"Having such people
or not having such people—
which is better?"
They would say:
"Having such people
or not having such people—
there is no difference."
Then the Lord on High, ghosts, and spirits would send down calamities, punishments, and abandon them,
and would that not be just what they deserve?
Therefore, the ancient sage kings established burial laws, saying:
"A coffin of paulownia wood three inches thick
is sufficient to let the body decay.
Three layers of shrouds
are enough to cover the corpse.
As for the burial,
it should not reach the springs below,
nor let the odor escape above.
The mound should be no larger than the area of three furrows,
and that is all."
Once the dead are buried,
the living must not mourn for long
but should quickly return to work,
each doing what they can
to benefit one another.
This is the law of the sage kings.
Now, those who uphold elaborate funerals and prolonged mourning say:
"Even if elaborate funerals and prolonged mourning cannot enrich the poor, increase the population, stabilize danger, or bring order to chaos,
still, this is the way of the sage kings."
Mòzǐ said:
Not so.
In the past,
Yáo went north to teach the eight Dí tribes,
died on the way,
and was buried on the northern side of Qiōngshān.
He had three layers of shrouds,
a coffin of coarse wood,
bound with vine,
and only after the pit was filled did they weep,
filling the grave without raising a mound.
After the burial,
oxen and horses trod over it.
Shùn went west to teach the seven Róng tribes,
died on the way,
and was buried in Nánjǐ's market.
He had three layers of shrouds,
a coffin of coarse wood,
bound with vine.
After the burial,
the market people walked over it.
Yǔ went east to teach in Yuè,
died on the way,
and was buried on Kuàijī Mountain.
He had three layers of shrouds,
a paulownia coffin three inches thick,
bound with vine,
the planks not joined tightly,
and the passage not leading to a pit.
The depth of the excavated ground
did not reach the springs below,
nor let the odor escape above.
After the burial,
the remaining soil was piled on top,
forming a mound no larger than the area of three furrows,
and that was all.
If we observe these three sage kings,
then elaborate funerals and prolonged mourning are indeed not the way of the sage kings.
For these three kings,
all honored as Sons of Heaven,
rich in possessing the world,
how could they have worried about insufficient resources?
Yet they adopted such burial laws.
Nowadays, the kings, dukes, and great men in conducting burials
differ from this.
They must have an outer coffin and an inner coffin,
with leather straps wrapped three times,
and when jade discs are already prepared,
along with spears, swords, tripods, drums, pots, jars, embroidered silks, plain white silk, ten thousand sets of large harnesses, carriages, horses, and female musicians all provided,
they say it is necessary to build a rammed-earth tomb passageway,
and the burial mound rivals a mountain.
This halts the people's labors,
and exhausts the people's wealth,
beyond all calculation.
Its uselessness is such as this.
Therefore, Mòzǐ said:
Previously, I originally stated that
if one considers their words,
employs their plans,
and evaluates elaborate funerals and prolonged mourning,
can they truly enrich the poor, increase the few, stabilize danger, and bring order to chaos?
Then it would be benevolent,
righteous,
and the duty of a filial son.
For those who advise others,
they must encourage this.
But if one considers following their words,
employing their plans,
and if people practice elaborate funerals and prolonged mourning,
yet it truly cannot enrich the poor, increase the few, stabilize danger, or bring order to chaos,
then it is not benevolent,
not righteous,
and not the duty of a filial son.
For those who advise others,
they must discourage this.
Thus, seeking to enrich the state,
they instead become poor;
desiring to increase the population,
they instead become few;
wishing to govern punishments and administration,
they instead fall into chaos.
Seeking to prohibit large states from attacking small ones,
is already impossible;
wishing to seek blessings from the Lord Above and the ghosts and spirits,
they instead incur misfortune.
Looking upward to the ways of Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ,
they actually oppose them;
looking downward to the affairs of Jié, Zhòu, Yōu, and Lì,
they match perfectly.
If we view it from this perspective,
then elaborate funerals and prolonged mourning
are not the way of the sage kings.
Now those who uphold elaborate funerals and prolonged mourning say:
"If elaborate funerals and prolonged mourning
are indeed not the way of the sage kings,
then why do the gentlemen of the central states persist in doing it without cease and hold to it without abandoning it?"
Mòzǐ said:
This is what is called accommodating their habits and deeming their customs righteous.
In the past, east of Yuè there was the country of Gàomù,
where when the first son was born,
they dismembered and ate him,
calling it "beneficial for younger brothers."
When the grandfather died,
they carried the grandmother on their back and abandoned her,
saying:
"One cannot live with a ghost's wife."
The rulers above made this their policy,
the people below made it their custom,
practicing it without cease,
holding to it without abandoning it.
Then, is this truly the way of benevolence and righteousness?
This is what is called accommodating their habits and deeming their customs righteous.
South of Chǔ there was the country of Yánrén,
where when their parents died,
they let the flesh decay and discarded it,
then buried the bones,
only then becoming filial sons.
West of Qín there was the country of Yíbǐng,
where when their parents died,
they gathered firewood and burned them,
sending the smoke upward,
calling it "ascending to the distant,"
only then becoming filial sons.
The rulers above made this their policy,
the people below made it their custom,
practicing it without cease,
holding to it without abandoning it.
Then, is this truly the way of benevolence and righteousness?
This is what is called accommodating their habits and deeming their customs righteous.
If we view it from these three countries,
then it is too frugal.
If we view it from the gentlemen of the central states,
then it is too lavish.
Like that is too lavish,
like this is too frugal,
so then burial should have moderation.
Thus, clothing and food
are benefits for the living,
and yet there still must be moderation;
burial
is a benefit for the dead,
so why should it alone lack moderation?
Mòzǐ established the laws for burial as follows:
A coffin three inches thick,
sufficient to hold the decaying bones;
three layers of clothing,
sufficient to cover the decaying flesh;
dig the earth to a depth
where below there is no seepage,
and the vapors do not escape above;
the mound should be just enough to mark the place,
then stop.
Weep when going and weep when returning,
then return to work on clothing and food resources,
assist in sacrifices,
to express filial piety to parents.
Therefore it is said:
Mòzǐ's method
does not neglect the benefits of the dead and the living,
this is it.
Therefore Mòzǐ said:
Now the scholars and gentlemen of the world,
if in their hearts they truly wish to practice benevolence and righteousness,
seek to become superior scholars,
above wish to conform to the way of the sage kings,
below wish to benefit the state and its people,
then they should regard the governance of frugal funerals
as something they must examine carefully.
7.1 "The Will of Heaven, Part One - Chapter Twenty-Six"
Mòzǐ said:
Now the scholars and gentlemen of the world
know the small but do not know the great.
How do we know this?
We know it from how they conduct themselves in families.
If someone in a family offends the head of the household,
there is still the neighbor's house to escape to.
Yet relatives, brothers, and acquaintances
mutually warn and caution each other,
all saying:
"We cannot but be cautious,
we cannot but be careful.
How can one live in a family, offend the head, and still be acceptable?"
Not only is this true for those in families,
but even those in states are the same.
If someone in a state offends the ruler,
there is still a neighboring state to escape to.
Yet relatives, brothers, and acquaintances
mutually warn and caution each other,
all saying:
"We cannot but be cautious,
we cannot but be careful.
Who can live in a state, offend the ruler, and still be acceptable?"
This is a case where there is somewhere to escape to,
and yet the mutual warnings are this earnest.
How much more, where there is nowhere to escape to,
should the mutual warnings be even more earnest to be acceptable?
Moreover, there is a saying:
"On a clear day,
if one offends,
where can one escape to?"
The answer is:
There is nowhere to escape to.
For Heaven cannot be avoided in forests, valleys, or secluded, uninhabited places;
it will clearly see all.
Yet the scholars and gentlemen of the world regarding Heaven
are negligent and do not know to mutually warn each other.
This is how I know the scholars and gentlemen of the world know the small but not the great.
Then what does Heaven desire and what does it hate?
Heaven desires righteousness and hates unrighteousness.
Then leading the people of the world to practice righteousness,
means I am doing what Heaven desires.
I do what Heaven desires,
and Heaven will do what I desire.
Then what do I desire and what do I hate?
I desire blessings and prosperity and hate calamities and misfortunes.
Then if I lead the people of the world to practice unrighteousness,
I am doing what Heaven does not desire.
I do what Heaven does not desire,
and Heaven will do what I do not desire.
Then I am leading the people of the world into calamities and misfortunes.
Then how do we know that Heaven desires righteousness and hates unrighteousness?
The answer is:
With righteousness in the world, there is life;
without righteousness, there is death.
With righteousness, there is wealth;
without righteousness, there is poverty.
With righteousness, there is order;
without righteousness, there is chaos.
Then since Heaven desires life and hates death,
desires wealth and hates poverty,
desires order and hates chaos,
this is how we know Heaven desires righteousness and hates unrighteousness.
It is said:
Moreover, righteousness
is governance.
There is no instance of inferiors governing superiors,
but necessarily of superiors governing inferiors.
Therefore, commoners exert themselves in their tasks,
yet cannot govern according to their own will;
they are governed by the gentry.
The gentry exert themselves in their tasks,
yet cannot govern according to their own will;
they are governed by generals and ministers.
Generals and ministers exert themselves in their tasks,
yet cannot govern according to their own will;
they are governed by the three lords and feudal princes.
The three lords and feudal princes exert themselves in administration,
yet cannot govern according to their own will;
they are governed by the Son of Heaven.
The Son of Heaven cannot govern according to his own will;
he is governed by Heaven.
That the Son of Heaven governs the three lords, feudal princes, gentry, and commoners
is clearly understood by the gentlemen of the world.
But that Heaven governs the Son of Heaven
is not clearly understood by the common people of the world.
Thus, the sage kings of the three ancient dynasties—Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ—
wishing to make clear that Heaven governs the Son of Heaven,
explicitly instructed the common people of the world.
Hence, they all fed oxen and sheep, reared dogs and swine,
purified the millet and wine offerings,
and sacrificed to the Lord-on-High, spirits, and deities,
seeking to pray for blessings from Heaven.
I have never heard of anyone in the world praying to the Son of Heaven for blessings;
this is how I know that Heaven governs the Son of Heaven.
Thus, the Son of Heaven
is the most honorable in the world,
the wealthiest in the world.
Therefore, those who desire wealth and honor
must follow the will of Heaven and cannot disobey it.
Those who obey the will of Heaven,
practicing universal love and mutual benefit,
will necessarily be rewarded.
Those who oppose the will of Heaven,
practicing partial hatred and mutual harm,
will necessarily be punished.
Then, who are those who obey the will of Heaven and are rewarded?
Who are those who oppose the will of Heaven and are punished?
Mòzǐ said:
The sage kings of the three ancient dynasties—Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ—
are those who obeyed the will of Heaven and were rewarded.
The tyrannical kings of the three ancient dynasties—Jié, Zhòu, Yōu, and Lì—
are those who opposed the will of Heaven and were punished.
Then, why were Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ rewarded?
Mòzǐ said:
In their affairs, they revered Heaven above,
served the spirits in the middle,
and loved people below.
Thus, the will of Heaven declared:
"These are the ones who love whom I love and benefit whom I benefit.
Their love for others is extensive,
their benefit to others is profound."
Therefore, they were made honorable as Sons of Heaven,
wealthy with the world,
and their descendants continued for ten thousand generations.
Their goodness is praised in tradition,
their influence spread throughout the world,
and they are praised to this day,
called "Sage Kings."
Then, why were Jié, Zhòu, Yōu, and Lì punished?
Mòzǐ said:
In their affairs, they blasphemed Heaven above,
deceived the spirits in the middle,
and despised people below.
Thus, the will of Heaven declared:
"These are the ones who hate whom I love and harm whom I benefit.
Their hatred for others is extensive,
their harm to others is profound."
Therefore, they were not allowed to live out their natural lifespans,
their reigns did not last,
and they are condemned to this day,
called "Tyrannical Kings."
Then, how do we know that Heaven loves the common people of the world?
Because it enlightens them universally.
How do we know it enlightens them universally?
Because it possesses them universally.
How do we know it possesses them universally?
Because it feeds them universally.
How do we know it feeds them universally?
It is said:
Within the four seas,
all the grain-eating people
feed oxen and sheep, rear dogs and swine,
purify the millet and wine offerings,
and sacrifice to the Lord-on-High, spirits, and deities.
Since Heaven has people in its cities,
why would it not love them?
Moreover, I say that killing one innocent person
necessarily brings one calamity.
Who kills the innocent?
It is people.
Who sends the calamity?
It is Heaven.
If Heaven did not love the common people of the world,
why would it send calamities when people kill each other?
This is how I know that Heaven loves the common people of the world.
Those who obey the will of Heaven
practice righteous governance.
Those who oppose the will of Heaven
practice forceful governance.
Then, what does righteous governance entail?
Mòzǐ said:
Large states do not attack small states,
great families do not seize small families,
the strong do not plunder the weak,
the noble do not arrogantly oppress the humble,
the cunning do not deceive the foolish.
This necessarily benefits Heaven above,
benefits the spirits in the middle,
and benefits people below.
With these three benefits, nothing is not benefited.
Thus, the world bestows upon them beautiful names,
calling them "Sage Kings."
Forceful governance is the opposite of this.
Their words contradict this,
their actions oppose this,
like galloping in opposite directions.
Large states attack small states,
great families seize small families,
the strong plunder the weak,
the noble arrogantly oppress the humble,
the cunning deceive the foolish.
This does not benefit Heaven above,
does not benefit the spirits in the middle,
does not benefit people below.
With these three harms, nothing is benefited.
Thus, the world bestows upon them evil names,
calling them "Tyrannical Kings."
Mòzǐ said:
I have the will of Heaven,
just as a wheelwright has his compass,
a carpenter has his square.
The wheelwright and carpenter hold their compass and square
to measure the squareness and roundness of the world,
saying what matches is correct,
what does not match is wrong.
Now, the books of the gentlemen of the world are too numerous to record,
their words are beyond complete reckoning.
They persuade the feudal lords above
and the various scholars below,
yet they are far from righteousness and benevolence.
How do I know this?
I say:
I have the clear standard of the world to measure them.
7.2 The Will of Heaven, Part Two
Mòzǐ said:
Now, the gentlemen of the world who desire to practice benevolence and righteousness
must examine where righteousness comes from.
Since it is said that one must examine where righteousness comes from,
then where does righteousness come from?
Mòzǐ said:
Righteousness does not come from the foolish and humble;
it necessarily comes from the noble and wise.
How do we know that righteousness does not come from the foolish and humble,
but necessarily comes from the noble and wise?
It is said:
Righteousness
is good governance.
How do we know that righteousness is good governance?
It is said:
When the world has righteousness, there is order;
when it lacks righteousness, there is chaos.
Thus, we know that righteousness is good governance.
The foolish and humble
cannot govern the noble and wise;
the noble and wise
can govern the foolish and humble.
This is how I know that righteousness does not come from the foolish and humble,
but necessarily comes from the noble and wise.
Then, who is noble?
Who is wise?
It is said:
Heaven is noble,
Heaven is wise.
Thus, righteousness indeed comes from Heaven.
Now the people of the world say:
"It is evident that the Son of Heaven is more noble than the feudal lords,
and the feudal lords are more noble than the high officials.
This is clearly understood.
However, I do not know that Heaven is more noble and wise than the Son of Heaven."
Mòzǐ said:
The reason I know that Heaven is more noble and wise than the Son of Heaven
is as follows:
It is said:
When the Son of Heaven does good,
Heaven can reward him.
When the Son of Heaven commits violence,
Heaven can punish him.
When the Son of Heaven suffers from illness or calamity,
he must fast and bathe,
prepare pure wine, millet, and sacrificial offerings,
to sacrifice to Heaven and the spirits,
then Heaven can remove them.
But I do not know that Heaven prays for blessings from the Son of Heaven;
this is why I know that Heaven is more noble and wise than the Son of Heaven.
Moreover, the reason I know that Heaven is more noble and wise than the Son of Heaven
is not limited to this alone.
I also know it from the teachings in the books of the ancient kings that illuminate Heaven's way without cease.
It says:
"Heaven is wise and intelligent,
overseeing the rulers below."
This saying indicates that Heaven is more noble and wise than the Son of Heaven.
Do you not also know that there is something more noble and wise than Heaven?
The answer is:
Heaven is the most noble,
Heaven is the most wise,
and that is all.
Thus, righteousness indeed comes from Heaven.
Therefore, Mòzǐ said:
Now the gentlemen of the world,
who truly wish to honor the Way and benefit the people,
and fundamentally examine the roots of benevolence and righteousness,
must not be negligent of the will of Heaven.
Since it is believed that the will of Heaven must not be neglected,
then what does Heaven desire and what does it detest?
Mòzǐ said:
The will of Heaven
does not desire large states to attack small states,
great families to disrupt small families,
the strong to plunder the weak,
the many to oppress the few,
the cunning to scheme against the simple,
the noble to arrogate over the humble—
these are what Heaven does not desire.
Not only this,
but it desires that those with strength help each other,
those with the Way teach each other,
and those with wealth share with each other.
It also desires that those above diligently attend to governance,
and those below diligently engage in their work.
If those above diligently attend to governance,
then the state will be well-ordered.
If those below diligently engage in their work,
then resources will be sufficient.
If the state is well-ordered
and resources are sufficient,
then those above will have the means to prepare pure wine, millet, and sacrificial offerings
to sacrifice to Heaven and the spirits;
externally, they will have jade discs, pearls, and jewels
to exchange with the four neighboring states,
so that grievances among feudal lords do not arise,
and conflicts on the borders do not occur;
internally, they will have the means to feed the hungry and relieve the weary,
nurturing and caring for all the people,
then rulers and ministers, superiors and inferiors will be kind and loyal,
and fathers, sons, elder and younger brothers will be affectionate and filial.
Therefore, only by clearly understanding and complying with the will of Heaven,
and upholding it to spread its light throughout the world,
will punishments and governance be orderly,
the people harmonious,
the state wealthy,
resources sufficient,
and all the people well-clothed and well-fed,
peaceful and free from worries.
Thus, Mòzǐ said:
Now the gentlemen of the world,
who truly wish to follow the Way and benefit the people,
and fundamentally examine the roots of benevolence and righteousness,
must not be negligent of the will of Heaven.
Moreover, the Son of Heaven's possession of the world
is no different from the feudal lords' possession of their territories.
Now, when feudal lords possess their territories,
do they desire their officials and people to harm each other?
If now, residing in a large state, one attacks small states,
or residing in a great family, one disrupts small families,
and seeks rewards and praise thereby,
in the end, it will not be attainable,
and punishment will surely come.
Heaven's possession of the world
is not different from this.
If now, residing in a large state, one attacks small states,
or residing in a large city, one assaults small cities,
and seeks blessings and prosperity from Heaven thereby,
blessings and prosperity will ultimately not be obtained,
and calamity will surely come.
Moreover, if one does not do what Heaven desires,
but does what Heaven does not desire,
then Heaven will also not do what humans desire,
but will do what humans do not desire.
What is it that humans do not desire?
It is said:
Illness and calamity.
If one does not do what Heaven desires,
but does what Heaven does not desire,
this is leading all the people of the world into calamity.
Therefore, the sage kings of old clearly understood what Heaven and the spirits desired,
and avoided what Heaven and the spirits detested,
in order to promote benefits for the world
and eliminate harms to the world.
Thus, Heaven regulated cold and heat,
harmonized the four seasons,
timed yin and yang, rain and dew appropriately,
ripened the five grains,
prospered the six livestock,
so that epidemics, disasters, plagues, and famines did not occur.
Therefore, Mòzǐ said:
Now the gentlemen of the world,
who truly wish to follow the Way and benefit the people,
and fundamentally examine the roots of benevolence and righteousness,
must not be negligent of the will of Heaven.
Moreover, in the world, there are those who are unkind and inauspicious,
such as:
"When a son does not serve his father,
a younger brother does not serve his elder brother,
a minister does not serve his ruler."
Thus, the gentlemen of the world collectively call them inauspicious.
Now, Heaven embraces the world and loves it,
nurtures all things to benefit them;
even the tip of a hair,
if not created by Heaven,
yet the people benefit from it—
this can be said to be profound.
Yet, they alone do not repay Heaven,
and do not know that this is unkind and inauspicious.
This is what I mean by gentlemen understanding the small but not the great.
Moreover, the reason I know that Heaven deeply loves the people
is as follows:
It created the sun, moon, stars, and constellations
to illuminate and guide them;
established the four seasons of spring, autumn, winter, and summer
to regulate them;
sent down snow, frost, rain, and dew
to grow and mature the five grains, hemp, and silk,
enabling the people to obtain and benefit from them;
arranged mountains, rivers, and valleys,
distributed and assigned all affairs;
appointed kings, dukes, marquises, and earls
to oversee the good and evil of the people, rewarding the worthy and punishing the violent;
bestowed metals, wood, birds, and beasts,
and engaged in the production of the five grains, hemp, and silk,
to provide the people with clothing and food resources.
From ancient times to the present,
there has never been a lack of these.
Suppose there is a person here
who joyfully loves his child,
exhausting all efforts to benefit him,
and when the child grows up,
does not repay his father's care—
then the gentlemen of the world would collectively call him unkind and inauspicious.
Now, Heaven embraces the world and loves it,
nurtures all things to benefit them;
even the tip of a hair,
if not created by Heaven,
yet the people benefit from it—
this can be said to be profound.
Yet, they alone do not repay Heaven,
and do not know that this is unkind and inauspicious.
This is what I mean by gentlemen understanding the small but not the great.
Moreover, the reason I know Heaven loves the people profoundly
is not limited to this alone.
It is said that those who kill the innocent
are given misfortune by Heaven.
Who are the ones that kill the innocent?
It is said: humans.
Who is it that gives them misfortune?
It is said: Heaven.
If Heaven did not love the people profoundly,
why would it be said that when humans kill the innocent, Heaven gives them misfortune?
This is how I know that Heaven loves the people profoundly.
Moreover, the reason I know Heaven loves the people profoundly
is not limited to this alone.
It is said that those who love and benefit others,
follow the will of Heaven,
and receive Heaven's rewards—
such cases exist.
Those who hate and harm others,
oppose the will of Heaven,
and receive Heaven's punishments—
such cases also exist.
Now, those who love and benefit others,
follow the will of Heaven,
and receive Heaven's rewards—
who are they?
It is said:
They are like the sage kings of the three ancient dynasties: Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ.
What did Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ engage in?
It is said:
They engaged in inclusivity,
not in division.
Inclusivity means:
when in a large state, not attacking small states;
when in a great family, not disrupting small families;
the strong not plundering the weak;
the many not oppressing the few;
the cunning not scheming against the simple;
the noble not arrogantly despising the humble.
Observing their actions,
they benefit Heaven above,
benefit spirits in the middle,
and benefit humans below.
These three benefits leave nothing unbenefited—
this is called the virtue of Heaven.
Gathering the fine names of the world and bestowing them upon them,
it is said:
This is benevolence,
righteousness,
loving and benefiting others,
following the will of Heaven,
and receiving Heaven's rewards.
Not only this,
but it is also written on bamboo and silk,
engraved on metal and stone,
carved on plates and vessels,
and passed down to descendants of later generations.
It is said:
For what purpose will this be?
It will be to recognize those who love and benefit others,
follow the will of Heaven,
and receive Heaven's rewards.
The "Huáng Yǐ" ode states:
"The Lord said to King Wén,
I cherish your bright virtue,
not raising your voice or changing your countenance,
not relying on might or severity,
unknowing and unperceiving,
you follow the rules of the Lord."
The Lord praised his adherence to the rules,
thus raising up the Yin to reward him,
making him honored as the Son of Heaven,
rich in possessing the world,
with fame and reputation enduring to this day.
Therefore, those who love and benefit others,
follow the will of Heaven,
and receive Heaven's rewards—
can indeed be known.
Now, those who hate and harm others,
oppose the will of Heaven,
and receive Heaven's punishments—
who are they?
It is said:
They are like the tyrant kings of the three ancient dynasties: Jié, Zhòu, Yōu, and Lì.
What did Jié, Zhòu, Yōu, and Lì engage in?
It is said:
They engaged in division,
not in inclusivity.
Division means:
when in a large state, attacking small states;
when in a great family, disrupting small families;
the strong plundering the weak;
the many oppressing the few;
the cunning scheming against the simple;
the noble arrogantly despising the humble.
Observing their actions,
they do not benefit Heaven above,
do not benefit spirits in the middle,
and do not benefit humans below.
These three harms leave nothing unharmed—
this is called the offense against Heaven.
Gathering the disgraceful names of the world and bestowing them upon them,
it is said:
This is not benevolence,
not righteousness.
Hating and harming others,
opposing the will of Heaven,
and receiving Heaven's punishments.
Not only this,
but their deeds are also written on bamboo and silk,
engraved on metal and stone,
carved on plates and vessels,
and passed down to descendants of later generations.
It is said:
For what purpose will this be?
It will be to recognize those who hate and harm others,
oppose the will of Heaven,
and receive Heaven's punishments.
The "Dà Míng" ode states:
"Zhòu behaved arrogantly in his dwelling,
unwilling to serve the Lord on High,
abandoning the spirits of his ancestors and not sacrificing to them.
He even said:
I have the mandate,
without need for diligent effort."
Heaven also abandoned Zhòu and did not protect him.
Examining why Heaven abandoned Zhòu and did not protect him—
it is because he opposed the will of Heaven.
Therefore, those who hate and harm others,
oppose the will of Heaven,
and receive Heaven's punishments—
can indeed be known.
Therefore, Mòzǐ's possession of the will of Heaven
is no different from a wheelwright having a compass
or a carpenter having a square.
Now, when a wheelwright holds his compass,
he uses it to measure the roundness or non-roundness of the world.
He says:
"What fits my compass is called round;
what does not fit my compass is called not round."
Thus, round and not round can both be known.
What is the reason for this?
It is because the standard for roundness is clear.
The carpenter also holds his square,
using it to measure the squareness or non-squareness of the world.
He says:
"What fits my square is called square;
what does not fit my square is called not square."
Thus, square and not square can both be known.
What is the reason for this?
It is because the standard for squareness is clear.
Therefore, Mòzǐ's possession of the will of Heaven
is to measure, on the one hand, the governance and administration of the kings, lords, and great men of the world,
and on the other, the writings and speeches of the common people.
Observing their actions:
if they follow the will of Heaven,
they are called good actions;
if they oppose the will of Heaven,
they are called not good actions.
Observing their speeches:
if they follow the will of Heaven,
they are called good speeches;
if they oppose the will of Heaven,
they are called not good speeches.
Observing their governance and administration:
if they follow the will of Heaven,
they are called good governance;
if they oppose the will of Heaven,
they are called not good governance.
Therefore, set this up as the law,
establish this as the standard,
and use it to measure the benevolence or non-benevolence of the kings, lords, great men, ministers, and officials of the world—
it is like distinguishing black from white.
Therefore, Mòzǐ says:
Now, the kings, lords, great men, and gentlemen of the world,
if you truly wish to follow the Way and benefit the people,
and fundamentally understand the root of benevolence and righteousness,
you must not fail to follow the will of Heaven.
Following the will of Heaven
is the standard of righteousness.
7.3 "The Will of Heaven, Part Three, Chapter Twenty-Eight"
Master Mòzǐ said:
"What is the reason for the disorder in the world?"
What explanation can be given for it?
It is because the gentlemen of the world understand small matters but do not understand great ones.
How do we know they understand small matters but not great ones?
We know it from their failure to understand the will of Heaven.
How do we know they fail to understand the will of Heaven?
We know it from their conduct in managing households.
Now if a person living in a household offends,
there is still another household
to which they can escape.
Yet fathers still admonish their sons,
elder brothers admonish their younger brothers,
saying:
"Be cautious, be careful!"
If one is not cautious and careful while managing a household,
how much more so when managing a state?"
Now if a person living in a state offends,
there is still another state
to which they can escape.
Yet fathers still admonish their sons,
elder brothers admonish their younger brothers,
saying:
"Be cautious, be careful!"
When managing a state for others,
one cannot but be cautious and careful."
Now all people live under Heaven and serve Heaven,
yet if they offend against Heaven,
there is nowhere to escape.
Nevertheless, no one knows to warn each other about this.
From this I know they are ignorant about great matters.
Therefore Master Mòzǐ said:
"Be cautious, be careful!"
You must do what Heaven desires,
and eliminate what Heaven hates.
What does Heaven desire,
and what does it hate?
Heaven desires righteousness and hates unrighteousness.
How do we know this is so?
Because righteousness means justice.
How do we know righteousness means justice?
When there is righteousness in the world, there is order;
when there is no righteousness, there is chaos.
From this I know righteousness means justice.
However, in matters of justice,
the lower never corrects the higher;
it must always be the higher that corrects the lower.
Therefore, common people cannot govern themselves;
they are governed by officials.
Officials cannot govern themselves;
they are governed by ministers.
Ministers cannot govern themselves;
they are governed by feudal lords.
Feudal lords cannot govern themselves;
they are governed by the three high ministers.
The three high ministers cannot govern themselves;
they are governed by the Son of Heaven.
The Son of Heaven cannot govern himself;
he is governed by Heaven.
Now the gentlemen of the world
all understand that the Son of Heaven governs the world,
but they do not understand that Heaven governs the Son of Heaven.
Therefore, the sages of old clearly explained to people:
"When the Son of Heaven does good,
Heaven can reward him.
When the Son of Heaven commits errors,
Heaven can punish him.
If the Son of Heaven's rewards and punishments are inappropriate,
if his judgments are unfair,
then disasters and calamities will occur in the world,
and frost and dew will fall unseasonably.
The Son of Heaven must then fatten his cattle, sheep, dogs, and pigs,
prepare pure offerings of millet and wine,
and pray to Heaven for blessings.
I have never heard of Heaven praying to the Son of Heaven for blessings.
From this I know Heaven is more weighty and honorable than the Son of Heaven.
Therefore, righteousness does not come from the foolish and humble,
but must come from the honorable and wise.
Who is honorable?
Who is wise?
Heaven is honorable,
Heaven is wise.
Thus, righteousness indeed comes from Heaven.
Now if the gentlemen of the world wish to practice righteousness,
they cannot but follow Heaven's will.
What does it mean to follow Heaven's will?
It means to love all people in the world equally.
How do we know Heaven loves all people equally?
We know it because Heaven nourishes all equally.
How do we know Heaven nourishes all equally?
From ancient times to the present,
no matter how distant or isolated the country,
all fatten their cattle, sheep, dogs, and pigs,
prepare pure offerings of millet and wine,
to reverently sacrifice to God, mountains, rivers, and spirits.
From this we know Heaven nourishes all equally.
If Heaven nourishes all equally,
it must love all equally.
For example, the rulers of Chǔ and Yuè:
the King of Chǔ is nourished by the entire territory of Chǔ,
so he loves the people of Chǔ;
the King of Yuè is nourished by the entire territory of Yuè,
so he loves the people of Yuè.
Now Heaven is nourished by the entire world,
so I know it loves all people in the world equally.
Moreover, Heaven's love for the people
is not limited to this alone.
In all states of the world today,
among all grain-eating people,
if one innocent person is killed,
there must be one inauspicious event.
Who kills the innocent?
It is a human.
Who sends the inauspicious event?
It is Heaven.
If Heaven truly did not love these people,
why would it send inauspicious events when humans kill the innocent?
Moreover, Heaven's love for the people is profound,
Heaven's love for the people is universal,
this can be known.
How do we know Heaven loves the people?
I know it from the fact that the worthy necessarily reward the good and punish the violent.
How do we know the worthy necessarily reward the good and punish the violent?
I know it from the sage kings of the three ancient dynasties.
The sage kings Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ of the three dynasties loved all people in the world equally,
benefited them accordingly,
changed the minds of their people,
and led them to reverence God, mountains, rivers, and spirits.
Heaven, because they loved those whom Heaven loves,
and benefited those whom Heaven benefits,
added rewards to them,
placed them in the highest position,
established them as Sons of Heaven to serve as models,
and called them 'sages.'
This is evidence that Heaven rewards the good.
The violent kings Jié, Zhòu, Yōu, and Lì of the three dynasties hated all people in the world equally,
harmed them accordingly,
changed the minds of their people,
and led them to insult and despise God, mountains, rivers, and spirits.
Heaven, because they did not love those whom Heaven loves but hated them,
and did not benefit those whom Heaven benefits but harmed them,
added punishments to them,
causing fathers and sons to be separated,
states to perish,
altars of land and grain to be lost,
and sorrow to reach their own persons.
Thus, all the common people of the world joined in condemning them,
and for ten thousand generations their descendants
continue to condemn them without cease,
calling them 'failed kings.'
This is evidence that Heaven punishes the violent.
Now if the gentlemen of the world wish to practice righteousness,
they cannot but follow Heaven's will.
It is said:
Those who follow the will of Heaven
are inclusive.
Those who oppose the will of Heaven
are divisive.
The way of inclusiveness
is righteous governance.
The way of divisiveness
is rule by force.
It is asked:
What is righteous governance like?
It is answered:
The great do not attack the small,
the strong do not bully the weak,
the many do not harm the few,
the cunning do not deceive the simple,
the noble do not despise the humble,
the rich do not scorn the poor,
the young do not rob the old.
Thus, among the various states under Heaven,
none use water, fire, poison, or weapons to harm one another.
Such actions benefit Heaven above,
benefit the spirits in the middle,
and benefit people below.
With these three benefits, there is nothing not benefited—
this is called the virtue of Heaven.
Therefore, all who engage in this
are wise,
benevolent and righteous,
loyal and kind,
loving and filial.
Thus, they gather and accumulate all the good names under Heaven upon themselves.
Why is this so?
Because they follow the will of Heaven.
It is asked:
What is rule by force like?
It is answered:
The great attack the small,
the strong bully the weak,
the many harm the few,
the cunning deceive the simple,
the noble despise the humble,
the rich scorn the poor,
the young rob the old.
Thus, the various states under Heaven
are using water, fire, poison, and weapons to harm one another.
Such actions do not benefit Heaven above,
do not benefit the spirits in the middle,
do not benefit people below.
With these three non-benefits, there is nothing benefited—
this is called the villainy of Heaven.
Therefore, all who engage in this
are rebels and rioters,
thieves and bandits,
neither benevolent nor righteous,
neither loyal nor kind,
neither loving nor filial.
Thus, they gather and accumulate all the evil names under Heaven upon themselves.
Why is this so?
Because they oppose the will of Heaven.
Therefore, Mòzǐ established Heaven
as the standard and law,
just as the wheelwright has his compass,
and the carpenter has his square.
Now, the wheelwright uses the compass,
the carpenter uses the square—
thereby they know the distinction between round and square.
Thus, Mòzǐ established Heaven
as the standard and law,
and I thereby know that the gentlemen and nobles of the world are far from righteousness.
How do I know they are far from righteousness?
In the world today,
the rulers of great states arrogantly say:
"We rule a great state;
if we do not attack small states,
how can we be considered great?"
Therefore, they dispatch their sharp-toothed warriors,
array their boat and chariot troops,
to attack and punish innocent states.
They invade their borders,
cut down their crops,
fell their trees,
destroy their city walls to fill their moats,
burn their ancestral temples,
and slaughter their sacrificial animals.
Those among the people who resist are executed,
while those who do not are bound and taken captive.
Men are made into slaves and convicts,
women into grain-pounders and brewers.
Yet, these rulers who love aggression
do not realize this is unrighteous.
They announce to the neighboring lords:
"I have attacked a state, destroyed its army, and killed its generals—so many men."
And the neighboring lords also do not realize this is unrighteous;
they prepare their furs and silks,
open their treasuries,
and send envoys to feast and congratulate.
Thus, these rulers who love aggression
further fail to realize this is unrighteous.
They record it on bamboo and silk,
store it in their archives.
Their descendants,
wishing to follow their ancestors' ways,
will say:
"Why not open our treasury
and examine our ancestors' righteous laws?"
They will not speak of King Wén and King Wǔ's governance.
If governance is like this,
they will say:
"Our ancestors attacked states, destroyed armies, and killed generals—so many men."
Thus, the rulers who love aggression do not realize this is unrighteous,
and the neighboring lords do not realize this is unrighteous.
Therefore, aggression and warfare continue generation after generation without end.
This is what I call ignorance of great matters.
As for what they call knowing small matters,
what is that like?
Suppose there is a person
who enters another's orchard
and steals their peaches, plums, melons, or ginger.
The authorities will punish them,
and the public will condemn them.
Why?
Because
they did not share the labor
but took the fruits—
they took what did not belong to them.
How much more so for one who climbs over another's wall
to seize their children?
Or breaks into another's treasury
to steal their gold, jade, and valuables?
Or jumps into another's stable
to steal their oxen and horses?
And how much more for killing a single innocent person?
Now, when kings, dukes, and great men govern,
if someone kills an innocent person,
climbs walls to seize children,
breaks into treasuries to steal gold, jade, and valuables,
jumps into stables to steal oxen and horses,
or enters orchards to steal peaches, plums, melons, and ginger—
the kings, dukes, and great men punish them.
Even the governance of ancient rulers like Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ
would not differ in this.
Yet today, the lords under Heaven
still engage in invasion, aggression, and annexation—
this is like killing not one innocent person,
but tens of millions;
like climbing walls to seize children
and breaking into treasuries to steal gold, jade, and valuables
not once, but tens of millions of times;
like jumping into stables to steal oxen and horses
and entering orchards to steal peaches, plums, melons, and ginger
not once, but tens of millions of times.
And they call this righteousness.
Therefore, Mòzǐ said:
Those who confuse righteousness
are no different from those who confuse black and white, sweet and bitter.
Suppose there is a person
who, when shown a little black, calls it black,
but when shown much black, calls it white.
They will say, "My eyes are confused;
I cannot distinguish black from white."
Suppose there is a person
who, when tasting a little sweetness, calls it sweet,
but when tasting much sweetness, calls it bitter.
They will say, "My mouth is confused;
I cannot distinguish sweet from bitter."
Now, when kings, dukes, and great men govern,
if someone kills a person in their own state,
they prohibit it.
Yet if they kill many people in a neighboring state,
they consider it great righteousness.
Is this any different from confusing black and white, sweet and bitter?
Therefore, Mòzǐ established Heaven
as the standard and law.
It is not only Mòzǐ who takes the will of Heaven as the law;
the ancient kings' book, the "Great Odes," says likewise:
"God said to King Wén,
'I cherish your bright virtue.
Do not raise your voice or show your countenance;
do not rely on Xia or change the rules.
Without knowledge or awareness,
follow the laws of God.'"
This admonishes King Wén to take the will of Heaven as the law
and follow the laws of God.
Moreover, the gentlemen and nobles of the world today
who truly wish to practice benevolence and righteousness,
seek to become superior scholars,
align above with the way of the sage kings,
and below with the benefits of the state and its people—
must examine the will of Heaven and cannot neglect it.
The will of Heaven
is the classic of righteousness.
8.1 "Explaining Ghosts I, Chapter 29"
Missing.
8.2 "Explaining Ghosts Part II Chapter 30"
Missing.
8.3 "Explaining Ghosts Part III Chapter 31"
Master Mòzǐ said:
When the sage kings of the three ancient dynasties had passed away,
the world lost righteousness,
and feudal lords used force to dominate.
Thus, the relationship between rulers and ministers, superiors and inferiors, became devoid of kindness and loyalty;
fathers, sons, brothers, and elders lost their compassion, filial piety, fraternal duty, and integrity;
officials were not diligent in governance;
and commoners were not diligent in their work.
People engaged in violence, banditry, and theft,
using weapons, poison, fire, and water,
waylaying innocent travelers on roads and paths,
and seizing others' carriages, horses, clothes, and furs for personal gain.
All these disorders began from this,
causing the world to fall into chaos.
Why did this happen?
It was because people were confused about whether ghosts and spirits exist or not,
and failed to understand that ghosts and spirits can reward the worthy and punish the wicked.
If now the people of the world could believe that ghosts and spirits can reward the worthy and punish the wicked,
then how could the world be in chaos?
Now those who claim there are no ghosts say:
"Ghosts and spirits
do not exist at all."
They teach this from morning till night throughout the world,
confusing the masses,
making everyone doubt the distinction between the existence and non-existence of ghosts and spirits,
thus causing the world to fall into chaos.
Therefore, Master Mòzǐ said:
Today's kings, dukes, great men, and gentlemen,
if they truly wish to promote the benefits of the world
and eliminate its harms,
must clearly examine the distinction between the existence and non-existence of ghosts and spirits,
for this cannot be left unexamined.
Since the distinction between the existence and non-existence of ghosts and spirits
must be examined,
then how should we
clearly investigate this matter?
Master Mòzǐ said:
The way to investigate whether something exists or not in the world
must be based on the actual evidence of what the masses have heard and seen.
If someone has heard or seen it,
they will certainly believe it exists.
If no one has heard or seen it,
they will certainly believe it does not exist.
If so, why not go into any village or community and ask?
From ancient times to the present,
since the beginning of humankind,
if there have been those who have seen the forms of ghosts and spirits,
or heard the voices of ghosts and spirits,
then how can it be said that ghosts and spirits do not exist?
If no one has heard or seen them,
then how can it be said that ghosts and spirits exist?
Now those who claim there are no ghosts say:
"Those in the world who claim to have seen or heard ghosts and spirits
are too numerous to count.
But who has actually seen or heard whether ghosts and spirits exist or not?"
Master Mòzǐ said:
If we take what many have seen together
and what many have heard together,
then the case of Dù Bó from ancient times is an example.
King Xuān of Zhōu killed his minister Dù Bó unjustly.
Dù Bó said:
"My lord has killed me unjustly.
If the dead are without consciousness,
then let it be.
But if the dead are conscious,
within three years,
I will surely make my lord know it."
In the third year,
King Xuān of Zhōu gathered the feudal lords for a hunt at Pǔtián.
There were several hundred chariots,
thousands of foot soldiers,
and the fields were filled with people.
At noon,
Dù Bó appeared on a white horse in a plain carriage,
dressed in red robes and cap,
holding a red bow,
and grasping red arrows.
He pursued King Xuān of Zhōu,
shot into his chariot,
piercing his heart and breaking his spine,
killing him in the chariot,
where he fell over his bow case and died.
At that time,
those among the Zhōu people who were present all saw it,
and those far away all heard of it,
and it was recorded in the Spring and Autumn Annals of Zhōu.
Rulers used this to instruct their ministers,
and fathers used this to warn their sons,
saying:
"Be cautious and careful,
for all who kill the innocent
will incur misfortune.
The punishment of ghosts and spirits
is as swift as this!"
Judging from the account in this book,
the existence of ghosts and spirits
can hardly be doubted.
Not only is the account in this book true.
In the past, Duke Mù of Qín was in his temple at midday,
when a spirit entered the gate and stood to the left.
It had a human face and bird's body,
wearing plain robes with three bands,
and its face was perfectly square.
Duke Mù of Qín saw it
and became terrified,
fleeing.
The spirit said:
"Do not fear.
The Emperor on High enjoys your bright virtue,
and has sent me to grant you nineteen more years of life,
so that your state may prosper and flourish,
your descendants multiply,
and you will not lose them."
Duke Mù of Qín bowed twice and knocked his head on the ground,
saying:
"May I ask the spirit's name?"
It replied:
"I am Gōumáng."
If we take what Duke Mù of Qín personally witnessed as evidence,
then the existence of ghosts and spirits
can hardly be doubted.
Not only is the account in this book true.
In the past, Duke Jiǎn of Yān killed his minister Zhuāngzǐ Yí unjustly.
Zhuāngzǐ Yí said:
"My lord has killed me unjustly.
If the dead are without consciousness, so be it.
But if the dead are conscious,
within three years,
I will surely make my lord know it."
After one year,
the people of Yān were racing to the ancestral temple.
The ancestral temple of Yān
was like the Shèjì altar of Qí,
the Sānglín of Sòng,
and the Yúnmèng of Chǔ,
where men and women gathered to watch.
At noon,
as Duke Jiǎn of Yān was racing along the road to the ancestral temple,
Zhuāngzǐ Yí raised a red staff and struck him,
killing him in his chariot.
At that time,
those among the Yān people who were present all saw it,
and those far away all heard of it,
and it was recorded in the Spring and Autumn Annals of Yān.
The feudal lords passed on the story, saying:
"All who kill the innocent
will incur misfortune.
The punishment of ghosts and spirits
is as swift as this!"
Judging from the account in this book,
the existence of ghosts and spirits
can hardly be doubted.
Not only is the account in this book true.
In the past, during the time of Duke Wén of Sòng, Bào,
there was a minister named Zhù Guàngū who was in charge of sacrifices to the malevolent spirit.
The priest came out leaning on a staff
and said to him:
"Guàngū,
why are the jade tablets and discs not of full measure?
Why are the wine, millet, and other offerings not pure and clean?
Why are the sacrificial animals not complete and fat?
Why are the spring, autumn, winter, and summer sacrifices not offered at the proper times?
Is it you who are doing this,
or is it Bào?"
Guàngū replied:
"Bào is young and weak,
still in swaddling clothes.
How could Bào know about this?
I, the official Guàngū, alone am responsible."
The priest raised his staff and struck him,
killing him on the altar.
At that time,
those among the Sòng people who were present all saw it,
and those far away all heard of it,
and it was recorded in the Spring and Autumn Annals of Sòng.
The feudal lords passed on the story, saying:
"All who are not reverent and careful in sacrifices
will incur the punishment of ghosts and spirits,
which is as swift as this!"
Judging from the account in this book,
the existence of ghosts and spirits
can hardly be doubted.
Not only are the statements in such books as these reliable,
but in the past, among the ministers of Lord Zhuāng of Qí,
there were those named Wáng Lǐguó and Zhōng Lǐ Jiǎo.
These two men
were engaged in a lawsuit for three years without a verdict being reached.
The Lord of Qí considered putting them to death,
but feared that they might be innocent;
he also considered releasing them,
but feared that he might let the guilty escape.
So he had the two men share one sheep,
and swear an oath at the state altar of Qí.
The two men agreed.
Thereupon, a ditch was dug,
the sheep was slain and its blood sprinkled.
After the statement of Wáng Lǐguó had been read through to the end,
and that of Zhōng Lǐ Jiǎo had not yet reached half,
the sheep rose up and butted him,
breaking his leg.
The spirit of the altar, leaping upon him, struck him down,
and he died at the place of the oath.
At that time,
among the followers of the people of Qí, none failed to see it,
and those far away all heard of it.
It was recorded in the Spring and Autumn Annals of Qí.
The feudal lords passed it on and said:
"All who make oaths and do not adhere to their sincerity
will receive punishment from the ghosts and spirits,
swift and severe as this."
Looking at it from the statements in such books,
how can the existence of ghosts and spirits
be doubted?
Therefore, Master Mòzǐ said:
Even in deep valleys, broad forests, and secluded, uninhabited places,
one's conduct must not be without caution,
for there are ghosts and spirits watching.
Now, those who hold that there are no ghosts say:
"How can the perceptions of the common people's ears and eyes
be sufficient to resolve doubts?
Why, in aspiring to be noble gentlemen in the world,
would one still believe in the perceptions of the common people's ears and eyes?"
Master Mòzǐ said:
If you consider the perceptions of the common people's ears and eyes
to be insufficiently reliable,
and not fit to resolve doubts,
do you not know that the sage kings of the three dynasties of old—Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ—
are sufficient to serve as models?
Thus, from the average person upward, all say:
"The sage kings of the three dynasties of old
are sufficient to serve as models."
If the sage kings of the three dynasties of old are sufficient to serve as models,
then let us examine the affairs of these sage kings.
When King Wǔ attacked the Shāng and executed Zhòu,
he had the feudal lords divide the sacrifices,
saying:
"Let those closely related receive the inner sacrifices,
and those more distant receive the outer sacrifices."
Thus, King Wǔ necessarily believed that ghosts and spirits exist,
which is why he attacked the Shāng and executed Zhòu,
and had the feudal lords divide the sacrifices.
If there were no ghosts and spirits,
then what sacrifices would King Wǔ have to divide?
Not only is this true of King Wǔ's affairs,
for the sage kings always bestowed rewards at the ancestral temple,
and carried out punishments at the altar of the soil.
Why were rewards given at the ancestral temple?
To report the fairness of the distribution.
Why were punishments carried out at the altar of the soil?
To report the impartiality of the judgment.
Not only are the statements in such books as these reliable,
but also the sage kings of the three dynasties—Yú, Xià, Shāng, and Zhōu—
when they first established their states and built their capitals,
said they must select the central altar of the state
to establish as the ancestral temple;
they must choose trees that are tall and lush,
to set up as the sacred grove;
they must select the state's elders who are kind, filial, chaste, and good,
to serve as invocators and temple directors;
they must choose from the six domestic animals those that are plump, sleek, and pure in color,
to serve as sacrificial victims;
for jade tablets and discs,
they matched them according to their resources as the standard;
they must select the fragrant and ripe grains among the five cereals,
to make the sweet wine and millet offerings;
thus, the sweet wine and millet offerings
varied with the abundance of the year.
Therefore, when the ancient sage kings governed the world,
they necessarily put ghosts and spirits before the people—
this is the reason.
Hence it is said:
When government offices select and prepare items,
they must first prepare sacrificial vessels and robes,
all stored in the treasury;
invocators, temple directors, and officials all take their positions at court;
sacrificial animals are not kept with ordinary herds.
Thus, the sage kings of old administered their governance in this way.
The sage kings of old necessarily regarded ghosts and spirits as their priority,
and their devotion to ghosts and spirits was profound.
Fearing that later generations might not know this,
they wrote it on bamboo and silk,
to pass down to later generations.
Worried that it might decay or be lost,
and later generations would have no record,
they engraved it on plates and vessels,
and carved it in metal and stone,
to emphasize it.
Fearing that later generations might not reverence it to obtain blessings,
in the books of the former kings,
the words of the sages,
on every foot of silk,
in every chapter of writing,
repeatedly speak of the existence of ghosts and spirits,
emphasizing it again and again.
What is the reason for this?
It is because the sage kings made it their priority.
Now, those who hold that there are no ghosts say:
"Ghosts and spirits
certainly do not exist."
This contradicts the priority of the sage kings.
To contradict the priority of the sage kings
is not the way of a gentleman.
Now, the words of those who hold that there are no ghosts say:
"In the books of the former kings,
surely not a foot of silk,
not a chapter of writing,
repeatedly speaks of the existence of ghosts and spirits,
emphasizing it again and again.
So which books actually have this?"
Master Mòzǐ said:
The Zhōu Shū and the Dà Yǎ have it.
The Dà Yǎ says:
"King Wén is above,
shining in heaven.
Though Zhōu is an old state,
its mandate is renewed.
Is not Zhōu illustrious?
The Emperor's mandate is timely.
King Wén ascends and descends,
at the left and right of the Emperor.
Majestic King Wén,
his fair fame never ceases."
If there were no ghosts and spirits,
then after King Wén died,
how could he be at the left and right of the Emperor?
This is how I know that the Zhōu Shū speaks of ghosts.
Moreover, if only the Zhōu Shū speaks of ghosts,
and the Shāng Shū does not,
then it would not be sufficient to serve as a model.
So let us examine the Shāng Shū,
which says:
"Alas!
In ancient times, during the Xià,
when calamity had not yet come,
all beasts and insects,
even the flying birds,
none did not follow their examples.
How much more so for those with human faces—
how dare they have different hearts?
The ghosts and spirits of the mountains and rivers
also dared not be unpeaceful.
If they could be reverent and sincere,
they would unite all under heaven,
and protect the lands below."
Consider why the ghosts and spirits of the mountains and rivers dared not be unpeaceful:
it was to assist and plan for Yǔ.
This is how I know that the Shāng Shū speaks of ghosts.
Moreover, if only the "Shāng Shū" mentions ghosts,
while the "Xià Shū" does not,
then it would not suffice to serve as a standard.
In that case, let us first examine the "Xià Shū".
The "Yǔ Shì" states:
"The great battle took place at Gān,
where the king commanded the six officials on his left and right,
to descend and listen to the oath in the central army,
saying:
'The Yǒuhù clan insolently defies the Five Elements,
neglects and abandons the Three Fundamentals,
and Heaven thereby cuts off their mandate.
It is also said:
By midday,
today I and the Yǒuhù clan contend for the fate of a single day.
And you, ministers, officials, and common people,
it is not that I desire your fields, lands, or treasured soil,
but I am carrying out Heaven's punishment.
Those on the left who do not fulfill their duties on the left,
those on the right who do not fulfill their duties on the right,
if they do not obey the command.
Charioteers who do not manage your horses properly,
if they do not obey the command.
Therefore, rewards are given at the ancestral temple,
and punishments are carried out at the earth altar.'"
What does "rewards at the ancestral temple" mean?
It signifies the impartial distribution of mandates.
What does "punishments at the earth altar" mean?
It signifies the fairness in hearing legal cases.
Thus, the ancient sage kings certainly regarded ghosts and spirits as rewarding the worthy and punishing the violent,
which is why rewards must be at the ancestral temple,
and punishments must be at the earth altar.
This is how I know that the "Xià Shū" mentions ghosts.
Therefore, first the "Xià Shū",
then the "Shū" of Shāng and Zhōu,
speak repeatedly of the existence of ghosts and spirits,
emphasizing it again and again.
What is the reason for this?
It is because the sage kings attended to it.
Judging from the accounts in these texts,
the existence of ghosts and spirits,
how can it be doubted?
In ancient times, it was said on the auspicious day Dīngmǎo,
Zhōu offered prayers to the earth and local spirits,
sacrificed at the earth altar to ancestors,
to extend their years and lifespan.
If there were no ghosts and spirits,
how could they have extended their years and lifespan?
Therefore, Mòzǐ said:
If indeed ghosts and spirits can reward the worthy and punish the violent,
then this should be implemented in the state,
applied to all the people,
truly as a way to govern the state and benefit the people.
If it is thought otherwise, officials governing the offices would not be clean and honest,
men and women would have no distinctions,
and ghosts and spirits would see it.
When people commit violence, robbery, disorder, theft,
using weapons, poison, water, or fire to harm innocent people on the roads,
seizing others' carriages, horses, clothes, and furs for their own gain,
there are ghosts and spirits who observe it.
Thus, officials governing the offices dare not be unclean or dishonest,
upon seeing good, they dare not fail to reward,
upon seeing violence, they dare not fail to punish.
When people commit violence, robbery, disorder, theft,
using weapons, poison, water, or fire to harm innocent people on the roads,
seizing carriages, horses, clothes, and furs for their own gain,
it ceases because of this,
and thus none dare to be unrestrained.
In dark and secluded places,
considering the clarity of ghosts and spirits,
and in the open where there is even one person,
they fear punishment from above,
thus the world is well-governed.
Therefore, the clarity of ghosts and spirits,
cannot be evaded in dark marshes, mountains, forests, or deep valleys,
the clarity of ghosts and spirits will surely know it.
The punishment of ghosts and spirits,
cannot be withstood by wealth, honor, numerical strength, courage, martial prowess, strong armor, or sharp weapons,
the punishment of ghosts and spirits will surely overcome it.
If it is thought otherwise,
formerly King Jié of Xià, noble as the Son of Heaven,
rich in possessing all under Heaven,
above reviled Heaven and insulted ghosts,
below brought calamity and death to the people of the world,
opposed God and attacked the virtuous conduct of Yuánshān Dì,
thus Heaven sent Tāng to carry out clear punishment upon him.
Tāng with ninety chariots,
in formations like birds and wild geese,
Tāng rode in a great carriage,
attacked and descended upon the multitude at Zhūsuì,
and the king captured Tuīchǐ and Dàxì.
Thus, formerly King Jié of Xià, noble as the Son of Heaven,
rich in possessing all under Heaven,
had men of courage, Tuīchǐ and Dàxì,
who could tear apart rhinoceroses and tigers alive,
and kill with a pointed finger.
The people were numerous in the millions and billions,
filling the marshes and hills.
Yet he could not thereby ward off the punishment of ghosts and spirits.
This is what I call the punishment of ghosts and spirits,
which cannot be withstood by wealth, honor, numerical strength, courage, martial prowess, strong armor, or sharp weapons,
as seen here.
Moreover, it is not only this case that is so.
Formerly King Zhòu of Yīn, noble as the Son of Heaven,
rich in possessing all under Heaven,
above reviled Heaven and insulted ghosts,
below brought calamity and death to the people of the world.
He cast aside the elderly,
murdered children,
burned the innocent,
and disemboweled pregnant women.
The masses, elders, widowers, and widows,
wailed with no one to turn to.
Thus, Heaven sent King Wǔ to carry out clear punishment upon him.
King Wǔ with a hundred selected chariots,
four hundred tiger-like warriors,
first with the envoys of various states observing the army,
battled the Yīn people at Mùyě.
The king captured Fèizhōng and Èlái,
and the multitude rebelled and fled.
King Wǔ pursued them into the palace,
under the万年梓 tree,
beheaded Zhòu and tied him with a red ring,
hung him on a white banner,
to execute him as a warning to the feudal lords of the world.
Thus, formerly King Zhòu of Yīn, noble as the Son of Heaven,
rich in possessing all under Heaven,
had men of courage, Fèizhōng and Èlái,
who could capture rhinoceroses and tigers alive,
and kill with a pointed finger.
The people were numerous in the millions and billions,
filling the marshes and hills.
Yet he could not thereby ward off the punishment of ghosts and spirits.
This is what I call the punishment of ghosts and spirits,
which cannot be withstood by wealth, honor, numerical strength, courage, martial prowess, strong armor, or sharp weapons,
as seen here.
Moreover, the "Qín Ài" says:
"Obtaining blessings, no matter how small; exterminating the clan, no matter how great."
This means that what ghosts and spirits reward,
no matter how small, is surely rewarded;
what ghosts and spirits punish,
no matter how great, is surely punished.
Now those who hold that there are no ghosts say:
"Does this not disregard the benefits to one's parents,
and harm the practice of filial piety?"
Mòzǐ said:
The ghosts spoken of in ancient and modern times,
are none other than:
ghosts of Heaven,
