also ghosts and spirits of mountains and rivers,
and also those who become ghosts after death.
Now there are cases where a son dies before his father,
or a younger brother dies before his elder brother.
Although it may be so,
according to the constant principles of the world,
it is said that those born first die first.
If so,
then those who die first are either father or mother,
or elder brother or sister-in-law.
Now we prepare clean wine, millet, and offerings,
to reverently and carefully perform sacrifices.
If indeed ghosts and spirits exist,
this would allow our parents, sisters-in-law, and brothers to eat and drink,
would that not be greatly beneficial?
If indeed ghosts and spirits do not exist,
this would merely be spending the resources for wine, millet, and offerings.
Even if it is spent,
it is just poured into a dirty ditch and discarded,
but within, the clan,
and outside, the village,
can all partake of the food and drink.
Even if ghosts and spirits do not exist,
this can still foster joy and gather the crowd,
and gain closeness in the village.
Now those who hold that there are no ghosts say:
"Ghosts and spirits,
certainly do not exist,
therefore we do not provide the resources for wine, millet, offerings, and sacrifices.
It is not that we now begrudge the resources for wine, millet, offerings, and sacrifices,
but what would we gain from it?"
This contradicts above the texts of the sage kings,
and within contradicts the conduct of filial sons among the people.
Yet to be considered superior gentlemen in the world,
this is not the way to be a superior gentleman.
Therefore, Mòzǐ said:
Now when we perform sacrifices,
it is not merely pouring them into a dirty ditch and discarding them,
but above, to seek blessings from ghosts and spirits,
below, to foster joy and gather the crowd,
and gain closeness in the village.
If spirits exist,
then this allows our parents and brothers to eat,
would this not be a beneficial affair for the world?"
Therefore, Mòzǐ said:
Now the kings, dukes, great men, officers, and gentlemen of the world,
if they truly desire to promote the benefits of the world
and eliminate the harms of the world,
should regard the existence of ghosts and spirits
as something that cannot but be revered and made clear,
for it is the way of the sage kings.
8.4 "Against Music I" (Chapter 32)
Mòzǐ stated:
The task of benevolent people
must be to seek to promote the benefits of the world
and eliminate the harms of the world.
They take this as the model for the world:
if it benefits people, they do it;
if it does not benefit people, they stop.
Moreover, when benevolent people plan for the world,
they do not do so for what is beautiful to their eyes,
pleasing to their ears,
sweet to their mouths,
or comfortable for their bodies.
To thereby harm and seize the people's resources for food and clothing
is something benevolent people do not do.
Therefore, the reason Mòzǐ condemns music
is not that the sounds of great bells, drums, zithers, pipes, and flutes are considered unpleasing,
nor that the colors of carved and ornate patterns are considered unbeautiful,
nor that the tastes of roasted and grilled meats are considered unsavory,
nor that living in high towers, sturdy pavilions, and deep dwellings is considered uncomfortable.
Although the body knows their comfort,
the mouth knows their sweetness,
the eyes know their beauty,
and the ears know their pleasure,
yet, when examined above, they do not align with the affairs of the sage kings;
when measured below, they do not align with the benefits of the myriad people.
Therefore, Mòzǐ said:
Engaging in music is wrong.
Now, when kings, dukes, and great men create musical instruments
for the affairs of the state,
it is not merely like scooping stagnant water or breaking down a ruined wall to do so,
but they must heavily tax the myriad people
to produce the sounds of great bells, drums, zithers, pipes, and flutes.
If, then, the use of musical instruments
were like the sage kings' creation of boats and carts,
then I would not dare condemn it.
In ancient times, the sage kings also heavily taxed the myriad people
to make boats and carts.
After they were completed,
they said:
"How shall we use them?"
The answer was:
"Boats are used on water,
carts are used on land,
so that gentlemen can rest their feet,
and commoners can relieve their shoulders and backs."
Thus, when the myriad people contributed wealth
and offered it to them,
they did not dare feel resentful.
Why?
Because it ultimately aligned with the people's benefits.
If, then, musical instruments also aligned with the people's benefits like this,
I would not dare condemn them.
The people have three calamities:
the hungry cannot get food,
the cold cannot get clothing,
the weary cannot get rest.
These three are the great calamities of the people.
If, then, we strike great bells,
beat loud drums,
strum zithers,
blow pipes and flutes,
and brandish shields and axes for them,
how can the people obtain the resources for food and clothing?
I believe this is certainly not so.
Moreover, putting this aside,
if now a large state attacks a small state,
a great house assaults a small house,
the strong rob the weak,
the many oppress the few,
the cunning deceive the simple,
the noble arrogate over the humble,
and banditry, rebellion, theft, and robbery arise together,
unable to be stopped,
if then we strike great bells,
beat loud drums,
strum zithers,
blow pipes and flutes,
and brandish shields and axes,
how can the chaos in the world
be brought to order?
I believe this is certainly not so.
Therefore, Mòzǐ said:
Suppose we heavily tax the myriad people
to produce the sounds of great bells, drums, zithers, pipes, and flutes,
seeking to promote the benefits of the world
and eliminate the harms of the world,
it would be of no help.
Therefore, Mòzǐ said:
Engaging in music is wrong.
Now, if kings, dukes, and great men merely stay on high towers and sturdy pavilions to look down,
the bells are like inverted tripods;
if they are not struck,
what pleasure can be gained from them?
The argument is that they must be struck.
But if they are to be struck,
they will certainly not use the old or the slow.
The old and the slow
have ears and eyes that are not sharp,
limbs that are not fully strong,
voices that are not harmonious,
and eyes that do not shift clearly.
They must use those in their prime,
relying on their sharp ears and eyes,
their fully strong limbs,
their harmonious voices,
and their clear-shifting eyes.
If men are made to do it,
it wastes the time for farming and planting;
if women are made to do it,
it wastes the work of spinning and weaving.
Now, when kings, dukes, and great men engage in music,
they harm and seize the people's time for food and clothing to foster music,
and this is extensive.
Therefore, Mòzǐ said:
Engaging in music is wrong.
Now, the sounds of great bells, drums, zithers, pipes, and flutes
are already fully prepared;
if kings, dukes, and great men solemnly play and listen alone,
what pleasure can be gained from them?
The argument is that they must share it with others.
If shared with gentlemen, listening to it
wastes the gentlemen's governance;
if shared with commoners, listening to it
wastes the commoners' work.
Now, when kings, dukes, and great men engage in music,
they harm and seize the people's resources for food and clothing to foster music,
and this is extensive.
Therefore, Mòzǐ said:
Engaging in music is wrong.
In the past, Duke Kāng of Qí promoted the "Wàn" music,
and the ten thousand performers could not wear short coarse clothes,
nor eat chaff and dregs.
It was said:
"If food and drink are not fine,
the face and complexion are not worth looking at;
if clothing is not beautiful,
the body and demeanor are not worth viewing."
Thus, they must eat fine grains and meat,
and wear embroidered silks.
These are people who do not engage in producing resources for food and clothing,
but always feed on others.
Therefore, Mòzǐ said:
Now, when kings, dukes, and great men engage in music,
they harm and seize the people's resources for food and clothing to foster music,
and this is extensive.
Therefore, Mòzǐ said:
Engaging in music is wrong.
Now humans are fundamentally different from birds, beasts, deer, and insects.
The birds, beasts, deer, and insects of today
use their feathers and fur as clothing,
their hooves and claws as trousers and shoes,
and rely on water and grass for food and drink.
Thus, the males need not engage in farming and cultivation,
nor the females in spinning and weaving,
yet their means of clothing and food are naturally provided.
Humans differ from this:
those who rely on their labor survive,
those who do not rely on their labor do not survive.
If the gentlemen do not diligently attend to governance,
then punishments and administration become chaotic;
if the common people do not diligently work,
then wealth and resources become insufficient.
If the scholars and gentlemen of today consider my words incorrect,
then let us briefly enumerate the duties of the world,
and observe the harm of music.
The kings, dukes, and great men rise early and retire late,
hearing lawsuits and governing affairs—
this is their duty.
The scholars and gentlemen exhaust the strength of their limbs,
and devote the wisdom of their thoughts,
internally managing the government offices,
externally collecting the profits from passes, markets, mountains, forests, marshes, and weirs,
to fill the granaries and treasuries—
this is their duty.
The farmers go out early and return late,
plowing, sowing, and cultivating,
gathering abundant beans and grains—
this is their duty.
The women rise early and retire late,
spinning and weaving,
producing much hemp, silk, and kudzu fibers,
weaving cloth and silk—
this is their duty.
Now if the kings, dukes, and great men indulge in music and listen to it,
they will surely be unable to rise early and retire late,
to hear lawsuits and govern affairs,
thus the state becomes chaotic and the altars of land and grain endangered.
If the scholars and gentlemen indulge in music and listen to it,
they will surely be unable to exhaust the strength of their limbs,
or devote the wisdom of their thoughts,
internally managing the government offices,
externally collecting the profits from passes, markets, mountains, forests, marshes, and weirs,
to fill the granaries and treasuries,
thus the granaries and treasuries remain unfilled.
If the farmers indulge in music and listen to it,
they will surely be unable to go out early and return late,
to plow, sow, and cultivate,
gathering abundant beans and grains,
thus beans and grains become insufficient.
If the women indulge in music and listen to it,
they will surely be unable to rise early and retire late,
to spin and weave,
producing much hemp, silk, and kudzu fibers,
weaving cloth and silk,
thus cloth and silk are not produced.
It is said:
What causes the great men to neglect governance and abandon the state's affairs?
It is said: music.
Therefore, Mòzǐ says:
Engaging in music is wrong.
How do we know this is so?
It is said:
In the book of the former kings, the "Official Punishments" of Tāng has it.
It says:
"Those who constantly dance in the palace—
this is called the shamanic wind.
Their punishment:
gentlemen contribute two bundles of silk,
commoners are dealt with similarly, two hundred yellow coins."
And it further states:
"Alas!
Dancing extravagantly,
the yellow words are very evident,
but the Lord on High does not favor it,
and the nine regions are thereby lost.
The Lord on High is displeased,
sending down a hundred calamities;
their families are sure to suffer ruin."
Examining why the nine regions were lost,
it was merely due to the indulgence in decorative music.
In the "Wǔguān" it is said:
"Qǐ then indulged excessively in pleasure,
feasting in the wilds,
with resounding chimes,
and stone chimes forcefully played,
drowning in wine,
eating recklessly in the fields,
the myriad dances majestic,
their splendor heard in heaven,
yet Heaven did not approve."
Thus, above, the heavenly spirits do not bless it,
and below, the myriad people do not benefit from it.
Therefore, Mòzǐ says:
For the scholars and gentlemen of today,
if they truly wish to promote the benefits of the world
and eliminate the harms of the world,
they must recognize that regarding music as a thing,
it must be prohibited and stopped.
9.1 "Against Music, Part Two, Chapter Thirty-Three"
Missing.
9.2 "Against Music, Part Three, Chapter Thirty-Four"

9.3 "Against Fate, Part One, Chapter Thirty-Five"
Mòzǐ says:
In ancient times, the kings, dukes, and great men who governed the state
all desired the state's wealth,
the multitude of the people,
and order in punishments and administration.
Yet instead of gaining wealth, they obtained poverty;
instead of gaining multitude, they obtained few;
instead of gaining order, they obtained chaos.
Thus, they fundamentally lost what they desired
and obtained what they hated.
Why is this so?
Mòzǐ says:
Those who uphold fate are numerous among the people.
The words of those who uphold fate say:
"If fate decrees wealth, then wealth;
if fate decrees poverty, then poverty;
if fate decrees multitude, then multitude;
if fate decrees few, then few;
if fate decrees order, then order;
if fate decrees chaos, then chaos;
if fate decrees longevity, then longevity;
if fate decrees premature death, then premature death.
Fate—
even with vigorous effort,
what benefit is there?"
Above, they use this to persuade the kings, dukes, and great men;
below, they obstruct the people from their work.
Thus, those who uphold fate are unrighteous.
Therefore, regarding the words of those who uphold fate,
they must be clearly refuted.
Then how shall we clearly refute this argument?
What should be done?
Mòzǐ says:
Statements must have standards.
Statements without standards
are like trying to determine the direction of sunrise and sunset on a revolving potter's wheel—
the distinction between right and wrong, benefit and harm
cannot be clearly known.
Therefore, statements must have three tests.
What are the three tests?
Mòzǐ says:
There is rooting it in source,
verifying it in evidence,
and applying it in practice.
How to root it in source?
Above, root it in the affairs of the sage kings of old.
How to verify it in evidence?
Below, examine the evidence from the senses of the common people.
How to apply it in practice?
Implement it in punishments and administration,
and observe whether it matches the benefits of the state and the people.
This is what is meant by statements having three tests.
Yet the scholars and gentlemen of today
some believe fate exists.
Let us then examine the affairs of the sage kings.
In ancient times, the chaos under Jié
was received and ordered by Tāng;
the chaos under Zhòu
was received and ordered by King Wǔ.
The world did not change,
the people did not alter,
yet under Jié and Zhòu, the world was in chaos;
under Tāng and Wǔ, the world was in order.
How can it be said that fate exists?
Yet among the gentlemen of the world today,
some believe fate exists,
having supposedly examined the books of the ancient kings.
The books of the ancient kings,
which governed the state and administered to the people,
were the statutes.
In the statutes of the ancient kings,
has there ever been a statement such as "Blessings cannot be sought,
and calamities cannot be avoided;
reverence is of no benefit,
violence does no harm"?
What was used to hear cases and determine punishments
were the penal codes.
In the penal codes of the ancient kings,
has there ever been a statement such as "Blessings cannot be sought,
calamities cannot be avoided,
reverence is of no benefit,
violence does no harm"?
What was used to organize the army and direct its movements
were the oaths.
In the oaths of the ancient kings,
has there ever been a statement such as "Blessings cannot be sought,
calamities cannot be avoided,
reverence is of no benefit,
violence does no harm"?
Therefore, Mòzǐ says:
I have not yet fully enumerated them,
for the excellent books of the world cannot all be counted.
Speaking broadly about their main points,
these three categories suffice.
Now, even if one seeks the words of those who hold to fate,
they cannot necessarily be found.
Is it not appropriate, then, to reject them?
To adopt the words of those who hold to fate
is to overthrow righteousness in the world.
Those who overthrow righteousness in the world
are the ones who establish fate,
and this distresses the people.
To advocate what distresses the people
is to destroy the people of the world.
If so, then why do we desire the righteous to be in positions above?
What is the reason?
The answer is:
When the righteous are in positions above,
the world is necessarily well-ordered,
the Lord on High, mountains, rivers, and spirits and gods will have a firm master,
and the myriad people will receive great benefits from them.
How do we know this?
Mòzǐ says:
In ancient times, when Tāng was enfeoffed at Bó,
taking the long and short boundaries together,
his territory was a hundred lǐ square.
He loved all his people equally,
benefited one another,
and shared with them in times of scarcity.
Leading his people,
he honored Heaven and served the spirits.
Thus, Heaven and the spirits enriched him,
the feudal lords supported him,
the people were close to him,
the worthy scholars came to him,
and before the end of his life,
he became king over the world,
ruling the feudal lords.
In the past, King Wén was enfeoffed at Qízhōu,
taking the long and short boundaries together,
his territory was a hundred lǐ square.
He loved all his people equally,
benefited one another,
so that those nearby were content with his governance,
and those afar were drawn by his virtue.
Those who heard of King Wén all rose and hastened to him.
The weary, the unworthy, and those with weak limbs,
staying where they were, longed for him,
saying:
"If only King Wén's territory could reach us,
then would we not benefit just like King Wén's people?"
Thus, Heaven and the spirits enriched him,
the feudal lords supported him,
the people were close to him,
the worthy scholars came to him,
and before the end of his life,
he became king over the world,
ruling the feudal lords.
Earlier it was said:
When the righteous are in positions above,
the world is necessarily well-ordered,
the Lord on High, mountains, rivers, and spirits and gods will have a firm master,
and the myriad people will receive great benefits from them.
It is from this that I know it.
Therefore, the sage kings of old promulgated statutes and issued orders,
establishing rewards and punishments
to encourage the worthy.
Thus, at home they were filial and kind to their parents,
abroad they were respectful and deferential in the village,
in sitting and resting they had measure,
in going out and coming in they had rules,
and men and women were distinguished.
Therefore, when assigned to govern offices, they did not steal;
when defending the city, they did not revolt;
when the ruler was in difficulty, they would die for him;
when he went into exile, they would accompany him.
These were whom the superiors rewarded
and the people praised.
Those who hold to fate say:
"Those whom the superiors reward
are fated to be rewarded anyway;
it is not because of their worthiness that they are rewarded.
Therefore, at home they are not kind and filial to their parents,
abroad they are not respectful and deferential in the village,
in sitting and resting they have no measure,
in going out and coming in they have no rules,
and men and women are not distinguished.
Therefore, when assigned to govern offices, they steal;
when defending the city, they revolt;
when the ruler is in difficulty, they do not die for him;
when he goes into exile, they do not accompany him.
These are whom the superiors punish
and the people condemn.
Those who hold to fate say:
"Those whom the superiors punish
are fated to be punished anyway;
it is not because of their violence that they are punished.
(It is not because of their worthiness that they are rewarded)."
To act thus as a ruler is to be unrighteous,
as a minister is to be disloyal,
as a father is to be unkind,
as a son is to be unfilial,
as an elder brother is to be unworthy,
as a younger brother is to be disrespectful.
To stubbornly hold to this
is precisely the source of pernicious doctrines
and the way of violent men.
How, then, do we know that fate is the way of violent men?
In former times, the impoverished people of antiquity,
greedy for food and drink,
lazy in their work,
thus had insufficient wealth for clothing and food,
and the worries of hunger, cold, and starvation came upon them.
They did not say:
"I am weary and unworthy,
and not diligent in my work."
They invariably said:
"My fate is simply to be poor."
The violent kings of antiquity,
unable to restrain the excesses of their ears and eyes,
the perversity of their minds,
disobeyed their parents,
and consequently lost their states,
and overturned their altars of grain.
They did not say:
"I am weary and unworthy,
and govern poorly."
They invariably said:
"My fate simply destined me to lose it."
In the "Announcement of Zhònghuī" it is said:
"I have heard that the man of Xià
forged the Mandate of Heaven,
and proclaimed it to the people below.
Heaven punished him for his wickedness,
and thus he lost his army."
This speaks of how Tāng condemned Jié for holding to fate.
In the "Great Oath" it is said:
"Zhòu being of Yí nature,
refused to serve the Lord on High and the spirits and gods,
abandoning the sacrifices to his ancestors and the spirits of the land.
Instead, he said:
'My people have their fate;
there is no need to labor or repair.'
Heaven therefore abandoned him and did not protect him."
This speaks of how King Wǔ condemned Zhòu for holding to fate.
Now, to adopt the words of those who hold to fate
would mean that those above do not attend to governance,
and those below do not engage in work.
If those above do not attend to governance,
then penal administration becomes chaotic;
if those below do not engage in work,
then wealth and resources become insufficient.
Above, there would be nothing to offer as millet and wine
in sacrifice to the Lord on High and the spirits and gods;
to calm and attract the worthy and capable scholars of the world;
externally, there would be no means to receive the guests of the feudal lords;
internally, there would be no means to feed the hungry and clothe the cold,
and to care for the aged and weak.
Thus, fate is not beneficial to Heaven above,
not beneficial to the spirits in the middle,
nor beneficial to the people below.
To stubbornly hold to this
is precisely the source of pernicious doctrines
and the way of violent men.
Therefore, Mòzǐ stated:
Now, the scholars and gentlemen of the world,
sincerely desire the world to be wealthy and detest its poverty,
desire the world to be orderly and detest its chaos.
The words of those who uphold fate must be condemned,
for they are a great harm to the world.
9.4 "Against Fate, Part Three"
Mòzǐ stated:
In all speech, writing, and literary expression as a way,
one must first establish a standard of righteousness.
If words lack righteousness,
it is like setting a sundial on a spinning potter's wheel:
even with skilled craftsmen,
it will never be correctly aligned.
Yet now, the true and false in the world
cannot be easily discerned,
so speech is given three standards.
What are these three standards?
There is examining its basis,
investigating its origins,
and applying it in practice.
In examining its basis,
one verifies it against the will of Heaven and spirits,
and the deeds of the sage kings.
In investigating its origins,
one corroborates it with the writings of the former kings.
How is it applied?
It is put into effect through governance and punishments.
These are the three standards for speech.
Now, the scholars and gentlemen of the world
may say fate does not exist.
The way I know whether fate exists or not
is through the sensory experiences of the masses to determine existence or non-existence.
If it is heard,
or seen,
it is said to exist.
If it is not heard,
not seen,
it is said not to exist.
Then why not examine the experiences of the common people?
From ancient times to the present,
since the beginning of human life,
has anyone ever seen the form of fate,
or heard the sound of fate?
There has never been such a thing.
If one considers the common people foolish and unworthy,
and their sensory experiences insufficient to serve as a standard,
then why not examine the transmitted sayings and流传的话语 of the feudal lords?
From ancient times to the present,
since the beginning of human life,
has anyone ever heard the sound of fate,
or seen the body of fate?
There has never been such a thing.
Then why not examine the deeds of the sage kings?
The sage kings of old
promoted filial sons to encourage serving one's parents,
honored the worthy and virtuous to encourage doing good,
issued statutes and promulgated orders to educate,
and clarified rewards and punishments to encourage and deter.
In this way,
chaos could be turned into order,
and danger into safety.
If someone disagrees,
consider how the chaos under Jié
was ordered by Tāng;
the chaos under Zhòu
was ordered by King Wǔ.
The world did not change, nor did the people alter,
yet when the rulers changed their governance, the people were easily taught.
Under Tāng and Wǔ, there was order;
under Jié and Zhòu, there was chaos.
Safety, danger, order, and chaos
depend on the governance enacted by the rulers above;
how can it be said that there is fate?
Those who speak of fate
are also incorrect.
Now, those who uphold fate say:
"I did not invent this in later ages;
since the Three Dynasties of old, such words have been流传下来.
Why do you, sir, oppose them?"
The reply is:
Those who uphold fate,
do they not recall the sage and good men of the Three Dynasties?
Or rather the violent and unworthy men of the Three Dynasties?
How do we know?
Initially, the eminent scholars and valiant ministers
were cautious in speech and diligent in action,
thereby able to admonish their rulers above,
and teach and guide their people below,
Thus, above, they received rewards from their rulers,
and below, they earned the praise of their people.
The reputations of these eminent scholars and valiant ministers have not faded,
but have been passed down to the present,
and the world all says it was due to their efforts,
one.
" (I) have seen fate."
Therefore, the violent kings of the Three Dynasties of old,
indulged their senses in excess,
failed to guard against the perversions of their minds,
externally沉迷于 hunting and chasing with nets and arrows,
internally immersed in wine and pleasure,
and neglected the governance of their states and people.
They engaged in numerous useless activities,
oppressed and rebelled against the people,
causing those below not to be loyal to those above.
Thus, their states became empty ruins,
and they themselves faced punishment and execution.
They would certainly not say:
"I am incompetent and unworthy,
I have governed poorly."
They would必定 say:
"My fate was destined to perish."
Even the impoverished people of the Three Dynasties of old
were also like this.
Internally, they could not properly serve their parents,
externally, they could not properly serve their rulers,
despised respect and frugality but favored laziness and ease,
were greedy for food and drink but lazy in their work,
so that resources for clothing and food were insufficient,
leading to the worries of hunger, cold, and starvation.
They would certainly not say:
"I am incompetent and unworthy,
I have not worked diligently."
They would必定 say:
"My fate was destined to be poor."
Even the deceitful people of the Three Dynasties of old
were also like this.
They elaborately adorned the doctrine of fate,
to teach the masses of foolish and simple people.
The sage kings, concerned about this,
thus recorded it on bamboo and silk,
carved it on plates and vessels,
and engraved it on metal and stone.
In the book of the former kings, "The Announcement of Zhònghuǐ," it is said:
"I heard that the people of Xià falsified the Mandate of Heaven,
proclaiming fate to the people below,
and God despised this,
causing the destruction of their army."
This refers to King Jié of Xià upholding fate,
whom Tāng and Zhònghuǐ together condemned.
The words in the former kings' book "The Great Oath" also state,
saying:
"Zhòu, residing in his arrogance,
refused to serve God on High,
abandoned and neglected his ancestral spirits, not sacrificing to them.
Saying:
'My people have fate,
no need to labor diligently.'
Heaven also abandoned and did not protect him."
This refers to Zhòu upholding fate,
whom King Wǔ condemned in "The Great Oath."
It is also found in "The Three Dynasties" and "Bù Guó,"
saying:
"Do not uphold that Heaven has fate."
Now, "The Three Dynasties" and "Bù Guó" also say that fate does not exist.
In Shào Gōng's "Holding the Mandate," it is similarly stated,
moreover:
"Revere it!
There is no Mandate of Heaven;
only we two
should not create false words,
not claiming it descends from Heaven,
but attain it through effort."
In the poetry and documents of Shāng and Xià, it is said:
"Fate
was invented by the violent kings."
Now, the scholars and gentlemen of the world,
wishing to distinguish the causes of right and wrong, benefit and harm,
should vigorously condemn those who say there is fate.
They must vigorously oppose it.
Those who uphold fate
are a profound harm to the world,
and therefore Mòzǐ condemns them.
9.5 "Against Fate, Part Four"
Master Mòzǐ said:
Whenever engaging in speech and discourse,
one must first establish standards before speaking.
If one speaks without first establishing standards,
it is like trying to determine east and west while standing on a spinning potter's wheel—
I believe even if there were debates about directions,
one would ultimately be unable to reach a definitive conclusion.
Therefore, speech has three models.
What are the three models?
They are:
examining its basis,
investigating its origins,
and applying it practically.
How does one examine its basis?
By studying the deeds of the ancient sage kings.
How does one investigate its origins?
By observing the evidence of people's ears and eyes.
How does one apply it practically?
By implementing it in governance and observing its effects on the state and the myriad people.
These are called the three models.
Thus, when the sage kings of the three ancient dynasties—Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ—governed the world,
they said:
"We must promote filial sons to encourage service to parents,
and honor virtuous and worthy individuals to teach them to do good."
Therefore, in administering governance and education,
they rewarded the good and punished the violent.
They believed that by doing so,
the chaos under heaven
would become manageable and orderly;
the perils of the state
would become stabilizable.
If anyone doubts this,
consider how the disorder under Jié
was rectified by Tāng;
the chaos under Zhòu
was governed by King Wǔ.
During those times,
the world did not change, nor did the people alter,
yet when the rulers changed their governance, the people transformed their customs.
Under Jié and Zhòu, the world was in chaos;
under Tāng and Wǔ, the world was well-governed.
The order of the world
was due to the efforts of Tāng and Wǔ;
the chaos of the world
was the fault of Jié and Zhòu.
From this perspective,
safety and danger, order and chaos,
depend on how the rulers govern—
how can it be said that there is fate?
Thus, when Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ governed the world,
they said:
"We must ensure the hungry are fed,
the cold are clothed,
the weary can rest,
and the chaotic are brought to order."
Thereby, they gained glorious reputations and fine renown throughout the world.
How could this be attributed to fate?
It was due to their efforts.
Today, virtuous and worthy individuals,
who honor worthiness and delight in the Way and its arts,
thus receive rewards from kings, dukes, and great men above,
and earn the praise of the myriad people below.
They too gain glorious reputations and fine renown throughout the world.
How could this be considered a matter of fate?
It is also due to their efforts.
Yet those who now claim fate exists—
were they the sage and good people of the three ancient dynasties?
Or were they the violent and unworthy of the three ancient dynasties?
Judging by their arguments,
they certainly were not the sage and good people of the three ancient dynasties,
but must have been the violent and unworthy.
Now, those who assert the existence of fate
are like the violent kings of the three ancient dynasties—Jié, Zhòu, Yōu, and Lì—
who, noble as Sons of Heaven,
possessed the wealth of the world.
Yet they did not correct the desires of their ears and eyes,
but followed the inclinations of their hearts.
Externally, they indulged in hunting and archery,
internally, they drowned in wine and pleasure,
disregarding the governance of their state and people.
They engaged extensively in useless activities,
oppressed and rebelled against the people,
and thus lost their ancestral temples.
They did not say:
"I am incompetent and unworthy,
I have not governed diligently."
Instead, they insisted:
"It was my fate to lose it."
Similarly, the incompetent and unworthy people of the three ancient dynasties
acted this way.
They failed to serve their parents and rulers well,
despised respect and frugality,
preferred ease and simplicity,
were greedy for food and drink but lazy in work,
so their resources for clothing and food were insufficient,
and they suffered from hunger, cold, and starvation.
They did not say:
"I am incompetent and unworthy,
I have not worked hard."
Instead, they insisted:
"It is my fate to be poor."
The deceitful people of the three ancient dynasties
were just like this.
In the past, violent kings initiated this,
and the poor propagated it—
all of which confuses the masses and hinders simplicity.
The ancient sage kings were deeply concerned about this,
and long ago took action.
Therefore, they recorded it on bamboo and silk,
engraved it on metal and stone,
carved it on plates and vessels,
to pass down to future generations.
It is said:
What texts preserve this?
Yǔ's "Zǒng Dé" contains it.
It says:
"If sincerity does not shine forth to Heaven,
the people will not be protected.
Once a malevolent heart is guarded against,
Heaven inflicts calamity.
If one does not cultivate virtue carefully,
how can fate protect them?"
The "Gào of Zhònghuǐ" says:
"I heard that the people of Xià falsely proclaimed fate to the world,
and God increased their excess,
causing them to lose their army."
They treated what did not exist as existing,
hence it is called false.
If something exists and one says it exists,
how can that be called false?
In the past, Jié upheld fate in his actions,
and Tāng composed the "Gào of Zhònghuǐ" to oppose it.
The words of the "Tài Shì"
in the "Qù Fā" section say:
"Alas, you gentlemen!
Heaven possesses clear virtue,
its actions are very evident.
The mirror is not far—
it lies in the King of Yīn.
He claimed people have fate,
said reverence cannot be practiced,
claimed sacrifices are useless,
said violence is harmless.
God did not favor him,
so the nine regions were lost;
God did not comply,
and sent down his ruin.
Only we of Zhōu
received it from the Great God."
In the past, Zhòu upheld fate in his actions,
and King Wǔ composed the "Tài Shì" and "Qù Fā" to oppose it.
I say:
Why not examine the records of Shāng, Zhōu, Yú, and Xià—
how can it be that none of the ten bamboo strips' texts contain this?
Therefore, Mòzǐ said:
The gentlemen of today, in their practice of literature and articulation of speech,
do not merely labor their throats and tongues,
nor benefit their lips and mouths alone,
but truly intend to serve the penal administration of their states, cities, and the myriad people.
Now, the reason why kings, dukes, and great men rise early and retire late,
adjudicating lawsuits and governing,
distributing duties evenly throughout the day without daring to be idle or weary—
why is this?
The answer is:
They believe that diligence ensures order,
while negligence brings chaos;
diligence ensures peace,
while negligence leads to peril,
hence they dare not be idle or weary.
Now, the reason why ministers and officials exhaust the strength of their limbs,
drain the knowledge of their thoughts,
internally managing the government offices,
externally collecting profits from passes, markets, mountains, forests, marshes, and weirs,
to fill the government stores,
without daring to be idle or weary—
why is this?
The answer is:
They believe that diligence ensures nobility,
while negligence brings baseness;
diligence ensures honor,
while negligence leads to disgrace,
hence they dare not be idle or weary.
Now, the reason why farmers go out early and return late,
diligently plowing, sowing, planting, and cultivating,
gathering abundant beans and grains,
without daring to be idle or weary—
why is this?
The answer is:
They believe that diligence ensures wealth,
while negligence brings poverty;
diligence ensures satiety,
while negligence leads to hunger,
hence they dare not be idle or weary.
Now, the reason why women rise early and retire late,
diligently spinning, weaving, and sewing,
producing much hemp, silk, and grass-cloth thread,
weaving cloth and silk,
without daring to be idle or weary—
why is this?
The answer is:
They believe that diligence ensures wealth,
while negligence brings poverty;
diligence ensures warmth,
while negligence leads to cold,
hence they dare not be idle or weary.
Now, if kings, dukes, and great men,
truly believing in fate, were to practice it,
they would surely neglect adjudicating lawsuits and governing.
Ministers and officials would neglect managing government offices.
Farmers would neglect plowing, sowing, planting, and cultivating.
Women would neglect spinning, weaving, and sewing.
If kings, dukes, and great men neglect adjudicating lawsuits and governing,
and ministers and officials neglect managing government offices,
then I believe the world would surely fall into chaos.
If farmers neglect plowing, sowing, planting, and cultivating,
and women neglect spinning, weaving, and sewing,
then I believe the resources for food and clothing in the world would surely become insufficient.
If one governs the world in this manner,
above, serving heaven and ghosts,
heaven and ghosts would not accept it;
below, nurturing and supporting the common people,
the common people would not benefit,
and would surely scatter, becoming unusable.
Thus, defending internally would not be secure,
and attacking externally would not be victorious.
Therefore, the reason why the tyrannical kings of the Three Dynasties—Jié, Zhòu, Yōu, and Lì—lost their states,
and overturned their altars of soil and grain,
was this.
Hence, Mòzǐ said:
The scholar-gentlemen of today,
who truly desire to promote the benefits of the world,
and eliminate the harms of the world,
must strongly oppose the words of those who uphold fate.
It is imperative to vigorously reject it.
He said:
The doctrine of fate
was created by tyrannical kings,
and propagated by the desperate,
it is not the words of the benevolent.
Those who practice benevolence and righteousness today,
must examine and strongly oppose this.
9.6 "Against the Rú: Part One, Thirty-Eighth"
Missing.
9.7 "Against the Rú: Part Two, Thirty-Ninth"
The Rú say:
"Loving one's kin has its gradations,
honoring the worthy has its ranks."
This speaks to the differences in closeness and distance, honor and humility.
Their rites say:
"Mourning parents for three years,
wife and eldest son for three years,
uncles, brothers, and other sons for a period,
and distant clansmen for five months."
If the length of mourning is based on closeness and distance,
then the closer should have longer mourning and the more distant shorter,
yet here the wife and eldest son are treated the same as the father.
If it is based on honor and humility,
then honoring one's wife and son equally with parents,
while treating uncles and elder clansmen as inferior to one's son,
what inversion could be greater?
When their parent dies,
they lay out the corpse without encoffining,
climb the roof, peer into the well,
poke into rat holes,
and search among washing utensils,
seeking the deceased.
If they truly believe the deceased is there,
then they are utterly foolish.
If they believe the deceased is gone,
yet still search,
then their pretense is great indeed.
When taking a wife, they personally greet her,
dressed as a servant,
holding the reins and handing the mounting cord,
as if revering a stern parent.
The solemnity of the wedding ceremony
is like conducting a sacrifice.
They overturn the proper order of high and low,
disobey their parents,
lowering themselves to their wife and son,
who then encroach upon their superiors.
Serving parents in this way—
can this be called filial?
The Rú say:
"The wife serves in sacrifices,
the son will maintain the ancestral temple,
hence they are emphasized."
In response, it is said:
This is false speech.
Their elder clansmen maintained the ancestral temple for decades,
yet when they die,
they mourn them for a period;
the wives of their brothers serve in the sacrifices to the ancestors,
yet they do not mourn them.
But they mourn their wife and son for three years—
surely it is not because of maintaining sacrifices.
To prioritize wife and son,
creating heavy burdens,
and say:
"It is to emphasize closeness."
This is to thicken what is most private,
and slight what is most important—
is this not great deceit?
Some stubbornly uphold fate to argue, saying:
"Longevity, premature death, wealth, and poverty,
safety, danger, order, and chaos,
are inherently decreed by heaven,
and cannot be increased or decreased.
Failure, success, reward, and punishment,
fortune and misfortune have their limits—
human knowledge and strength
cannot alter them."
If officials believe this,
they will neglect their duties.
If commoners believe this,
they will neglect their work.
If officials do not govern, there will be chaos;
if farming is slack, there will be poverty.
Poverty and chaos are the roots of misgovernment.
Yet the Rú take this as their doctrine and teaching—
this is to harm the people of the world.
Moreover, they elaborate on rituals and music to corrupt people,
prolong mourning with feigned grief to deceive their kin,
establish fatalism to alleviate poverty while appearing lofty and aloof,
betray fundamentals and neglect duties while indulging in idleness and sloth.
They covet food and drink,
are lazy in performing tasks,
fall into hunger and cold,
endanger themselves to freezing and starvation,
with no means to escape it.
This torments people's vitality,
like hidden mice,
gazing like rams,
and rising like running boars.
Gentlemen laugh at them,
and they angrily say:
"You aimless people,
how can you understand good Ruists!"
In summer, they beg for wheat and millet;
after the five grains are harvested,
great funerals follow,
with all the descendants accompanying.
They get to eat and drink their fill;
managing several funerals fully
is enough to sustain them.
They rely on others' households for their prosperity,
depend on others' fields for their dignity.
When wealthy families have funerals,
they are greatly pleased,
saying:
"This is the source of our clothing and food."
The Ruists say:
"A gentleman must use ancient speech and attire to be benevolent."
In response, it is said:
The so-called ancient speech and attire
were all once new,
and if the ancients spoke and wore them,
then they were not gentlemen either.
So must one wear non-gentlemen's clothes,
speak non-gentlemen's words,
to then be benevolent?
They also say:
"Gentlemen follow traditions but do not create."
In response, it is said:
In ancient times, Yì made the bow,
Yǔ made armor,
Xīzhòng made carts,
Qiǎochuí made boats.
So are today's tanners, armorers, cartwrights, and craftsmen all gentlemen,
while Yì, Yǔ, Xīzhòng, and Qiǎochuí all petty men?
Moreover, what they follow,
someone must have created it,
so then what they follow are all ways of petty men.
They also say:
"A gentleman, when victorious, does not chase the fleeing,
does not shoot those covering in boxes,
and if they are strong, helps them with their chariots."
In response, it is said:
If all are benevolent people,
then there is no reason for conflict.
Benevolent people inform each other with principles of choice and judgment,
the without-cause yield to the with-cause,
the ignorant follow the knowledgeable,
those without argument must submit,
upon seeing goodness, they must change,
why would they conflict?
If two violent parties contend,
and the victor wishes not to chase the fleeing,
not shoot those covering in boxes,
and if exhausted, helps them with chariots,
even if fully capable, still cannot be considered a gentleman.
Intending for a violent and cruel state,
a sage would rid the world of harm,
raise an army to punish,
but if the victorious then use Ruist methods to order soldiers:
"Do not chase the fleeing,
do not shoot those covering in boxes,
if exhausted, help them with chariots,"
the violent and disorderly survive,
the world's harms are not removed,
this is to collectively harm parents and deeply injure the world,
no unrighteousness is greater.
They also say:
"A gentleman is like a bell,
struck, it rings;
unstruck, it does not ring."
In response, it is said:
A benevolent person serves superiors with utmost loyalty,
serves parents with filial piety,
strives for goodness and praises it,
when there are faults, advises against them,
this is the way of a minister.
Now, struck, it rings;
unstruck, it does not ring,
hiding knowledge and reserving strength,
calmly waiting to be asked before responding,
even if there are great benefits for the ruler or parents,
if not asked, does not speak.
If a great rebellion is about to occur,
thieves and robbers are about to act,
like a trap about to spring,
others do not know,
but one alone knows,
even if the ruler and parents are present,
if not asked, does not speak,
this is the agent of great chaos.
With this, as a minister, one is not loyal,
as a child, not filial,
serving elders, not respectful,
interacting with others, not sincere and good.
Holding back and not speaking at court,
seeing profit, one acts,
though oneself fears to speak late,
if the ruler speaks and there is no profit,
then one folds hands high and looks down,
deep as if choking,
saying:
"I have not learned that."
When urgently needed,
one's conduct is far lost.
The one way of doctrine and learning
is benevolence and righteousness.
It is greatly used to govern people,
slightly to appoint officials,
broadly applied everywhere,
closely to cultivate oneself,
not dwelling in unrighteousness,
not acting against reason,
striving to promote the benefits of the world,
whether direct or circuitous,
stopping when beneficial,
this is the way of a gentleman.
Based on what is heard of Kǒng Qiū's conduct,
it is fundamentally contrary and erroneous to this.
Duke Jǐng of Qí asked Yàn Zǐ:
"What kind of person is Confucius?"
Yàn Zǐ did not answer,
the duke asked again,
still no answer.
Duke Jǐng said:
"Many have spoken to me about Kǒng Qiū,
all considering him a worthy man.
Now I ask you,
and you do not answer,
why?"
Yàn Zǐ replied:
"Yīng is unworthy,
insufficient to know a worthy man.
Nevertheless,
Yīng hears that a so-called worthy man,
upon entering another's state,
must strive to harmonize the closeness between ruler and minister,
and quell resentments between high and low.
When Kǒng Qiū went to Jīng,
knowing Bái Gōng's plot,
yet presented Shí Qǐ to him,
nearly causing the ruler's demise,
and Bái Gōng was executed.
Yīng hears that a worthy man, gaining the top, is not wasteful;
gaining the bottom, is not dangerous;
his words, heard by the ruler, must benefit people;
his teachings, followed below, must reach above;
thus his words are clear and easily understood,
his actions clear and easily followed,
his righteous conduct can be made clear to the people,
his plans and thoughts can communicate between ruler and minister.
Now Kǒng Qiū deeply schemes and conspires to serve rebels,
laboriously thinks and exhausts knowledge to act evilly,
encourages subordinates to rebel against superiors,
teaches ministers to kill rulers,
this is not the conduct of a worthy man.
Entering another's state,
and associating with its rebels,
is not of the righteous kind.
Knowing someone is disloyal,
urging them to cause chaos,
is not benevolent or righteous.
Avoiding people and then plotting,
evading others and then speaking,
his righteous conduct cannot be made clear to the people,
his plans and thoughts cannot communicate with the ruler,
Minister Yīng does not see how Kǒng Qiū differs from Bái Gōng,
hence did not answer."
Duke Jǐng said:
"Alas!
Many have bestowed advice upon me,
but without you, sir,
I would never have known Kǒng Qiū is the same as Bái Gōng."
Kǒng Qiū went to Qí
and had an audience with Duke Jǐng.
Duke Jǐng was pleased
and wished to enfeoff him with Níxī.
He informed Yànzǐ of this.
Yànzǐ said:
"It cannot be.
Now, the Rú
are grandiose and self-indulgent,
and cannot be employed to instruct the common people.
They delight in music and lead others into excess,
and cannot be entrusted with governance.
They establish fate and neglect affairs,
and cannot be made to uphold their duties.
They emphasize mourning and follow sorrow,
and cannot be made to show kindness to the people.
They wear unusual garments and force their countenances,
and cannot be made to guide the masses.
Kǒng Qiū adorns himself with elaborate attire to bewitch the world,
strums strings, sings, drums, and dances to gather followers,
multiplies the rituals of ascending and descending to display ceremony,
and strives for the etiquette of hurrying and gliding to impress the crowd.
His broad learning cannot be used to deliberate on worldly matters,
his laborious thoughts cannot benefit the people,
a long life would not suffice to exhaust his learning,
the prime of one's years cannot fully practice his rituals,
accumulated wealth cannot cover the expenses of his music,
he amasses ornate and heterodox arts to win over the rulers of the age,
and promotes lavish music and sounds to corrupt the people.
His way cannot be relied upon for the age,
his learning cannot guide the masses.
Now if you, my lord, enfeeff him
to conform to the customs of Qí,
it is not the way to lead the state and set an example for the people."
The duke said:
"Well said."
Thereupon, he treated him with generous courtesy,
withheld the enfeeffment,
received him with respect but did not inquire about his way.
Kǒng Qiū then became resentful towards Duke Jǐng and Yànzǐ,
and placed Chīyí Zǐpí at the gate of Tián Cháng,
informed Nánguō Huìzǐ of what he intended to do,
and returned to Lǔ.
After a while,
he learned that Qí was about to attack Lǔ,
and told Zǐgòng:
"Cì!
Now is the time to undertake great deeds."
He then sent Zǐgòng to Qí,
and through Nánguō Huìzǐ, had an audience with Tián Cháng,
urging him to attack Wú,
in order to instruct the Gāo, Guó, Bào, and Yàn families,
preventing them from hindering Tián Cháng's rebellion,
and urged Yuè to attack Wú.
Within three years,
Qí and Wú suffered the calamity of states being destroyed,
corpses lay scattered beyond count,
all due to Kǒng Qiū's machinations.
Kǒng Qiū served as Minister of Crime in Lǔ,
yet abandoned the ducal house to side with Jìsūn.
When Jìsūn served as prime minister to the ruler of Lǔ and then fled,
Jìsūn and the city's people struggled at the gate bar,
breaking the bolt.
Kǒng Qiū was in dire straits between Cài and Chén,
with only wild vegetable soup without even grain,
for ten days.
When Zǐlù prepared a sacrificial pig,
Kǒng Qiū ate it without asking where the meat came from.
When someone else removed his garment
to buy wine,
Kǒng Qiū drank it without asking where the wine came from.
When Duke Āi welcomed Kǒng Qiū,
if the mat was not straight, he would not sit,
if the meat was not properly cut, he would not eat.
Zǐlù came forward
and asked:
"Why is this contrary to your behavior in Cài and Chén?"
Kǒng Qiū said:
"Come,
I will tell you.
Formerly, I acted with you for mere survival,
now I act with you for mere righteousness."
When starved and in want, one does not refuse to take recklessly to preserve life;
when full and satisfied, one feigns conduct to adorn oneself.
Filthy, wicked, deceitful, and false—
what could be greater than this?
Kǒng Qiū was sitting leisurely with his disciples,
and said:
"When Shùn saw Gǔsǒu, he became uneasy;
at that time, the world was in peril!
Was not Zhōu Gōng Dàn a true man?
Why did he abandon his own family and dwell elsewhere?"
Kǒng Qiū's actions
stem from the inclinations of his mind.
His followers and disciples all emulated Kǒng Qiū:
Zǐgòng and Jìlù assisted Kōng Kuāng to bring chaos in Wèi,
Yánghǔ caused chaos in Qí,
Bìxī rebelled with Zhōngmóu,
Qīdiāo inflicted punishments and mutilations—
nothing is greater than these.
As for being a disciple,
the later generation takes him as teacher,
must cultivate his words,
model his actions,
and only stop when their strength is insufficient and wisdom falls short.
Now that Kǒng Qiū's conduct is such,
the Rú scholars can be doubted.
10.1 "Canon I" (Chapter 40)
10.1.1 Cause: that which, when obtained, leads to accomplishment.
10.1.2 Stopping: that which persists for a duration.
10.1.3 Part: that which is divided from the whole.
10.1.4 Necessity: that which does not cease.
10.1.5 Knowing: the faculty.
10.1.6 Level: being of the same height.
10.1.7 Considering: seeking.
10.1.8 Same length: that which fully corresponds with the standard.
10.1.9 Knowing: making contact.
10.1.10 Center: having the same length.
10.1.11 Wisdom: clarity.
10.1.12 Thickness: that which has magnitude.
10.1.13 Benevolence: love expressed through the body.
10.1.14 Midday: due south.
10.1.15 Righteousness: that which is beneficial.
10.1.16 Straight: aligned.

cannot be.

10.1.53 Harm: that which, when obtained, brings dislike.

10.1.55 Governance: seeking and obtaining.

10.1.59 Criticism: clarifying badness.

10.3 "Explanations of the Canons, Part One, Forty-Two"
10.3.1 Cause.
A minor cause: having it does not necessarily lead to the effect, lacking it necessarily does not lead to the effect; it is a part,
like having a point.
A major cause: having it necessarily leads to the effect without condition,
like the completion of seeing in sight.
Like one of two,
or the point of a line.
10.3.3 Knowing faculty.
The knowing faculty is that by which one knows,
and necessarily knows,
like clarity.
10.3.4 Deliberation.
Deliberation is using one's knowing to seek something,
but not necessarily obtaining it,
like squinting.
10.3.5 Knowledge.
Knowledge is using one's knowing to encounter things,
and being able to depict them,
like seeing.
10.3.6 Wisdom.
Wisdom is using one's knowing to discuss things,
and that knowing becomes evident,
like clarity.
10.3.7 Benevolence.
Loving the people is not for using the people,
unlike loving horses,
like clarity.
10.3.8 Righteousness.
The will takes the world as its duty,
and is able to benefit it,
without necessarily being employed.
10.3.9 Ritual.
The noble are addressed as "Lord",
the lowly by name,
yet both have respect and neglect,
distinguishing different statuses.
10.3.10 Action.
Actions not done for fame are true conduct.
Actions done for fame are cunning,
like being a thief.
10.3.11 Substance.
The manifestation of one's will and spirit,
makes others like oneself,
unlike golden sounds and jade garments.
10.3.12 Loyalty.
Not benefiting the weak child, Hài, enough to stop the entering countenance.
10.3.13 Filial piety.
Taking parents as one's duty,
and being able to benefit them,
without necessarily gaining [recognition].
10.3.14 Trustworthiness.
Not because one's words are appropriate,
but making someone check the city wall,
and obtaining gold.
10.3.15 Assistance.
Being with people, encountering people,
many are troubled.
To do this for that's sake,
is not to do it.
10.3.17 Integrity.
Even if one does it oneself,
knowing it is also hearing.
10.3.18 What is ordered, if not by oneself, is not carried out.
10.3.19 Responsibility.
Doing what one dislikes for oneself,
to fulfill what others urgently need.
10.3.20 Courage.
Because one dares in this,
it is called so.
Not because one does not dare in that,
harms it.
10.3.21 Strength.
Heaviness is called downward,
and heaviness is old.
The life of a pillar,
cannot necessarily be calculated.
10.3.23 Resting.
10.3.24 Dreaming.
Calmly.
10.3.26 Benefit.
Gaining this and being happy,
then this is benefit.
Its harm,
is not this.
To obtain this and yet detest it,
then it is harm.
Its benefit,
is not this.
10.3.28 Governance.
My affairs are well-governed,
while others govern north and south.
10.3.29 To praise must be based on their conduct; their words delight people.
10.3.30 To criticize must be based on their conduct; their words delight.
10.3.31 Recommendation.
Inform with the formal name,
and present its reality.
10.3.32 Reason.
Speech,
is what emerges from the mouths of the people.
The people are like drawings.
Speech is called speech,
as names convey meaning.
10.3.33 Moreover.
From the front it is called 'moreover',
from the back it is called 'already',
and what is about to happen is also 'moreover'.
10.3.34 Like a stone.
The ruler uses such names.
10.3.35 Achievement does not wait for the season,

is the superior repaying the achievements of the inferior.
if the offense is not prohibited,
only harm, no crime, perhaps then...

Two people both see this pillar,

10.3.40 Duration,
past and present, morning and evening.
east, west, home, south, north.
If it cannot contain even a foot,

If nothing cannot contain a foot,

10.3.43 Exhaustion,
merely cessation of movement.
10.3.44 Beginning.
Time may have duration,

10.3.45 Transformation.
Like a frog turning into a quail.
10.3.46 Diminution.
What is partially removed,

Some parts are removed, some remain,

10.3.47 Circular,

10.3.48 Storehouse.
The area and cavity like this,

Partial, collective displacement,

Non-lasting non-stop,

Lasting non-stop,

refers to what is firmly held,

From this going,

Two feet and one foot,

This is without sameness.

10.3.60 Interval,
refers to the sandwiching.

Both have points,

What is so,

All oxen,
a pivot is not an ox,

Some call it an ox,

this is disputing that.

Not both correct,

Incorrect like a dog.

Wishing to cut off a finger,

If knowing it, being cautious of it,

This is like eating dried meat.

The benefit or harm outside the wall is unknown,
running and obtaining a coin,

Observe the principle of exhausted knowledge and suspended on desires,
cutting meat is not wise,
cutting a finger is not foolish,
what is done and what is not,

Making clothes,
is completion.
Curing illness,
is elimination.

Reason,

this name,

Dog and canine,
