shallow what is shallow,
increase what is increasing,
respect what is respected.
Next, examine the basis,
compare the causes,
to reach the optimal meaning.
Further, examine the sounds and names,
based on requests for repetition.
Correcting desires and aversions,
people can thereby attain their true feelings.
All who encounter constraints and generate desires or aversions,
people may not necessarily attain their true feelings.
This is the sage's method of nurturing.
Benevolence without beneficial love,
beneficial love arises from calculation.
Past calculations,
are not today's calculations;
past love for people,
is not today's love for people.
Loving Huò is loving people,
arising from calculating Huò's benefit,
not calculating Zāng's benefit.
Yet loving Zāng is loving people,
just as loving Huò is loving people.
If abandoning one's love benefits the world,
can it not be abandoned?
Past knowledge of walls,
is not today's knowledge of walls.
Honored as the Son of Heaven,
his benefiting others is not greater than that of a commoner,
it is not increased.
Two sons serving their parents,
one encounters plenty,
one encounters scarcity,
their care for their parents is similar,
not because one's actions are more beneficial,
External circumstances cannot deepen our benefits.
Suppose Zāng were to die,
and the world harmed,
I would support and nurture Zāng ten thousand times more,
but my love for Zāng would not deepen.
The similarity between tall and short people,
lies in their shared human form,
hence they are similar.
A person's finger,
differs from a person's head,
as parts of the human body,
are not of one form,
hence they differ.
Drawing a sword differs from wielding a sword,
a sword is named by its form,
its forms vary,
hence they differ.
The wood of a poplar tree,
and the wood of a peach tree are similar.
All not named by quantity or number,
if broken,
all remain so.
Thus, one person's finger,
is not the person.
But this one person's finger,
belongs to this one person.
One face of a square,
is not the square.
The face of a square wood,
is part of the square wood.
A human ghost,
is not a human.
An elder brother's ghost,
is the elder brother.
Arguments arise from reasons,
grow through principles,
and proceed by categories.
To set up an argument without clarity on its origin,
is negligence.
Today, without the Dào, one cannot act;
even with strong limbs,
if unclear about the Dào,
one's困境,
can be expected immediately.
Arguments proceed by categories,
to set up an argument without clarity on its category,
will surely lead to困境.
Thus, persuasive arguments,
their category lies in鼓栗.
The sage,
acting for the world,
their category lies in追迷.
Some long-lived, some short-lived,
their benefit to the world is similar,
their category lies in誉石.
A day with a million births,
love does not deepen,
its category lies in恶害.
Love for two generations may vary in depth,
yet loving both generations is similar,
its category lies in蛇文.
Loving equally,
yet choosing to kill one of them,
its category lies in阬下之鼠.
Small benevolence and great benevolence,
their conduct in depth is similar,
their category lies in申凡.
Promoting benefits and eliminating harms,
its category lies in漏雍.
Deep love for parents not matching one's conduct,
yet acting by category,
its category lies in江上井.
Not acting for oneself can be learned,
its category lies in猎走.
Loving people not for praise,
its category lies in逆旅.
Loving others' parents,
as one loves one's own,
its category lies in官苟.
Universal love is similar,
singular love is similar.
its category lies in death.
11.2 "Xiǎo Qǔ Dì Sì Shí Wǔ"
The purpose of debate
is to clarify the distinction between right and wrong,
examine the principles of order and chaos,
illuminate the points of similarity and difference,
investigate the logic of names and realities,
handle benefits and harms,
and resolve doubts.
It traces the nature of all things,
and discusses the comparisons among various statements.
It uses names to represent realities,
employs propositions to express ideas,
and relies on arguments to present reasons.
It selects by category,
and gives by category.
What one possesses oneself, one does not condemn in others;
what one lacks oneself, one does not demand from others.
"Huò" (partial affirmation)
means not exhaustive.
"Jiǎ" (hypothetical)
means currently not so.
"Xiào" (standard)
serves as a model.
What is taken as standard
is that by which the model is established.
Therefore, if it matches the standard,
then it is correct.
If it does not match the standard,
then it is wrong.
This is what "xiào" means.
"Pì" (analogy)
is citing another thing to clarify this one.
"Móu" (parallel inference)
is comparing propositions and proceeding accordingly.
"Yuán" (citation)
says:
You approve this,
why should I alone not approve it?
"Tuī" (extension)
is taking what they do not accept
as similar to what they do accept,
and presenting it to them.
This is like saying they are the same;
how could I say they are different?
Things may have similarities but are not completely identical.
In parallel inference of propositions,
there is a limit to its validity.
That something is so
has a reason for being so;
though the fact of being so may be the same,
the reasons for being so may not necessarily be the same.
In accepting something,
there is a reason for accepting it;
though the acceptance may be the same,
the reasons for acceptance may not necessarily be the same.
Therefore, the methods of analogy, parallel inference, citation, and extension
may lead to differences when applied,
become precarious when extended,
err when taken too far,
and drift away from the root when flowing unchecked.
Thus they must be carefully examined
and cannot be used indiscriminately.
Hence, statements are multifaceted,
with different categories and diverse reasons,
so they cannot be viewed one-sidedly.
Things may be "affirming the premise leads to affirming the conclusion",
or "affirming the premise does not lead to affirming the conclusion",
or "not affirming the premise leads to affirming the conclusion",
or "one term applies universally while another does not",
or "one is right and the other...
is wrong".
A white horse
is a horse.
Riding a white horse
is riding a horse.
A black horse
is a horse.
Riding a black horse
is riding a horse.
Huò
is a person.
Loving Huò
is loving a person.
Zāng
is a person.
Loving Zāng
is loving a person.
These are cases of "affirming the premise leads to affirming the conclusion".
Huò's parent
is a person.
Huò serving his parent
is not serving a person.
His younger brother
is a beautiful person.
Loving his younger brother
is not loving a beautiful person.
A carriage
is made of wood.
Riding a carriage
is not riding wood.
A boat
is made of wood.
Riding a boat
is not riding wood.
is a person.
Having many robbers
is not having many people.
Having no robbers
is not having no people.
How to clarify this?
Hating many robbers
is not hating many people;
desiring no robbers
is not desiring no people;
the world universally agrees with this.
If this is so,
then although a robber is a person,
loving a robber is not loving a person,
not loving a robber is not not loving a person,
killing a robber is not killing a person.
There is no difficulty here;
this and that are of the same category.
The world accepts that but does not condemn itself,
yet the Mòists have this and condemn it,
for no reason at all—
is this what is called "internally glued and externally closed"?
The mind lacks openness within,
stuck and unable to resolve—
this is a case of "affirming the premise does not lead to affirming the conclusion".
Moreover, studying books
is not the books themselves.
Liking to study books
is liking books.
Moreover, fighting cocks
is not the cocks themselves.
Liking to fight cocks
is liking cocks.
Moreover, about to enter a well
is not entering the well.
Stopping someone about to enter a well
is stopping them from entering the well.
Moreover, about to go out the door
is not going out the door.
Stopping someone about to go out the door
is stopping them from going out the door.
The world universally agrees with this.
If this is so,
then "about to die young"
is not dying young,
preventing about to die young
is preventing dying young.
Upholding fatalism
is not fate itself.
Opposing upholding fatalism
is opposing fate.
There is no difficulty here;
this and that are of the same category.
The world accepts that but does not condemn itself,
yet the Mòists have this and condemn it,
for no reason at all—
is this what is called "internally glued and externally closed"?
The mind lacks openness within,
stuck and unable to resolve—
this is a case of "not affirming the premise leads to affirming the conclusion".
Loving people
requires universally loving people
before it can be called loving people.
Not loving people
does not require universally not loving people;
failing to love universally
constitutes not loving people.
Riding a horse
does not require universally riding horses
before it can be called riding a horse.
Having ridden a horse
constitutes riding a horse.
As for not riding a horse,
it requires universally not riding horses
before it can be called not riding a horse.
This is a case of "one term applies universally while another does not".
Residing in a state,
then it is called residing in the state.
Having a house in a state,
does not mean having the state.
The fruit of a peach tree,
is a peach.
The fruit of a jujube tree,
is not a jujube.
Inquiring about someone's illness,
is inquiring about the person.
Detesting someone's illness,
is not detesting the person.
A person's ghost,
is not the person.
An elder brother's ghost,
is the elder brother.
Offering sacrifices to a person's ghost,
is not offering sacrifices to the person.
Offering sacrifices to an elder brother's ghost,
is offering sacrifices to the elder brother.
If a horse's eye is blind,
then it is called "the horse is blind."
If a horse's eye is large,
it is not called "the horse is large."
If an ox's hair is yellow,
then it is called "the ox is yellow."
If an ox's hair is abundant,
it is not called "the ox is abundant."
One horse,
is a horse,
two horses,
are horses.
A horse having four legs,
means one horse has four legs,
not two horses having four legs.
One horse,
is a horse.
Some horses being white,
means among two horses, some are white,
not one horse being partially white.
This is a case where one is right and one is wrong.
11.3 "Gēng Zhù Dì Sìshíliù"
Master Mòzǐ was angry with Gēng Zhùzǐ,
Gēng Zhùzǐ said:
"Am I not better than others?"
Master Mòzǐ said:
"I am going to ascend the Tàiháng Mountains,
driving a steed and a sheep,
which one should I whip?"
Gēng Zhùzǐ said:
"Whip the steed."
Master Mòzǐ said:
"Why whip the steed?"
Gēng Zhùzǐ said:
"The steed is worthy of being driven hard."
Master Mòzǐ said:
"I also consider you worthy of being driven hard."
Wū Mǎzǐ said to Master Mòzǐ:
"Who is wiser, ghosts and spirits or sages?"
Master Mòzǐ said:
"The wisdom of ghosts and spirits compared to sages,
is like sharp ears and clear eyes compared to the deaf and blind.
In the past, Xiàhòu Kāi sent Fēi Lián to mine metal from mountains and rivers,
and had it cast at Kūnwú,
then had Wēng Nán divine with the white-ruò turtle,
saying:
'When the tripod is completed with three legs and square,
it will cook without fire,
store itself without being moved,
move on its own without being transported,
used for sacrifices at the ruins of Kūnwú,
go upwards!'
The diviner interpreted the cracks and said:
'It will be enjoyed!
Billowing white clouds,
one south, one north,
one west, one east,
the nine tripods once completed,
will be moved to three states.'
The Xiàhòu clan lost them,
the Yīn people received them.
The Yīn people lost them,
the Zhōu people received them.
The passing of the tripods from Xiàhòu to Yīn and Zhōu,
spanned several hundred years.
Even if sages gathered their best ministers and outstanding chancellors to plan,
could they know what would happen hundreds of years later?
Yet ghosts and spirits knew it.
Therefore it is said:
The wisdom of ghosts and spirits compared to sages,
is like sharp ears and clear eyes compared to the deaf and blind."
Zhìtú Yú and Xiàn Zǐshuò asked Master Mòzǐ:
"In practicing righteousness, what is the most important task?"
Master Mòzǐ said:
"It is like building a wall,
those who can build, build,
those who can fill earth, fill earth,
those who can measure, measure,
then the wall is completed.
Practicing righteousness is like this,
those who can debate, debate,
those who can explain texts, explain texts,
those who can handle affairs, handle affairs,
then righteous deeds are accomplished."
Wū Mǎzǐ said to Master Mòzǐ:
"You love all under heaven equally,
but no benefit has been seen.
I do not love all under heaven,
yet no harm has been seen.
Neither has achieved results,
why do you alone consider yourself right and me wrong?"
Master Mòzǐ said:
"Suppose there is a fire here,
one person carries water to extinguish it,
another adds fire to fuel it,
neither has achieved results yet,
which of the two would you value?"
Wū Mǎzǐ said:
"I approve of the intention of the one carrying water,
and disapprove of the intention of the one adding fire."
Master Mòzǐ said:
"I also approve of my intention,
and disapprove of your intention."
Master Mòzǐ recommended Gēng Zhùzǐ for a position in Chǔ,
several disciples visited him,
he fed them only three shēng of grain,
treating them not generously.
The disciples reported back to Master Mòzǐ:
"Gēng Zhùzǐ's stay in Chǔ is useless,
when we visited him,
he fed us only three shēng,
treating us not generously."
Master Mòzǐ said:
"It cannot be known yet."
Not long after,
Gēng Zhùzǐ sent ten jīn to Master Mòzǐ,
saying:
"Your disciple dares not die,
here are ten jīn,
hoping for your use, Master."
Master Mòzǐ said:
"Indeed, it could not be known."
Wū Mǎzǐ said to Master Mòzǐ:
"In your practice of righteousness,
people do not see and help you,
ghosts do not see and enrich you,
yet you still do it.
You have a madness!"
Master Mòzǐ said:
"Suppose you have two servants here,
one works only when he sees you,
and does not work when he does not see you.
The other works whether he sees you or not.
Which of the two would you value?"
Wū Mǎzǐ said:
"I value the one who works whether he sees me or not."
Master Mòzǐ said:
"Then you also value someone with a madness."
Disciples of Zǐxià asked Master Mòzǐ:
"Do gentlemen fight?"
Master Mòzǐ said:
"Gentlemen do not fight."
Zǐxià's disciples said:
"Even dogs and pigs fight,
how can there be gentlemen who do not fight?"
Master Mòzǐ said:
How lamentable!
In speech, you cite Tāng and Wén,
in action, you compare to dogs and pigs,
how lamentable!"
Wū Mǎzǐ said to Master Mòzǐ:
"Abandoning present people to praise ancient kings,
is like praising dried bones.
It is like a carpenter
who knows dried wood,
but does not know living wood."
Master Mòzǐ said:
"The reason the world survives,
is due to the teachings of the ancient kings' way.
Now to praise the ancient kings,
is to praise what enables the world to survive.
To be praiseworthy and not praise,
is not benevolent."
Mòzǐ said:
"The jade of Hé Shì,
the pearl of Suí Hóu,
and the tripod vessels with nine legs,
these are what the feudal lords call fine treasures.
But can they enrich the state,
multiply the people,
bring order to punishments and governance,
and secure the altars of soil and grain?
The answer is:
They cannot.
What is valued as a fine treasure
is that which can benefit the people.
Yet the jade of Hé Shì,
the pearl of Suí Hóu,
and the tripod vessels with nine legs
cannot benefit people,
thus they are not the fine treasures of the world.
Now if righteousness is used to govern the state,
the state will surely be enriched,
the people will surely multiply,
punishments and governance will surely be orderly,
and the altars of soil and grain will surely be secure.
What is valued as a fine treasure
is that which can benefit the people,
and righteousness can benefit people,
therefore it is said:
Righteousness
is the fine treasure of the world."
Lord Yè Gōngzǐgāo asked Zhòngní about governance,
saying:
"What is the way of one who excels in governance?"
Zhòngní replied:
"One who excels in governance
makes the distant feel close,
and renews the old."
Mòzǐ heard this and
said:
"Lord Yè Gōngzǐgāo did not get to the heart of his question,
and Zhòngní did not get to the heart of his answer either.
How could Lord Yè Gōngzǐgāo not know
that one who excels in governance makes the distant feel close and renews the old?
He was asking about the means to achieve this.
Not to tell people what they do not know,
but to tell them what they need to know,
hence Lord Yè Gōngzǐgāo did not get to the heart of his question,
and Zhòngní did not get to the heart of his answer either."
Mòzǐ said to Lord Lǔyáng Wénjūn:
"A large state attacking a small state
is like a child playing horse.
When a child plays horse,
he uses his own legs and gets tired.
Now when a large state attacks a small state,
the defenders—farmers cannot plow,
women cannot weave,
as they focus on defense.
The attackers—farmers also cannot plow,
women cannot weave,
as they focus on attack.
Thus, a large state attacking a small state
is indeed like a child playing horse."
Mòzǐ said:
"Words that can be put into action
should be often spoken.
Those that cannot be acted upon
should not be often spoken.
To often speak what cannot be acted upon
is to engage in idle talk."
Mòzǐ sent Guǎn Qiáoyóu to recommend Gāo Shízǐ in Wèi,
where the ruler of Wèi offered him a generous salary
and appointed him to a high position.
Gāo Shízǐ spoke his mind fully at every court audience,
but his words were never implemented.
He left and went to Qí,
where he met Mòzǐ
and said:
"Because of your recommendation, the ruler of Wèi
granted me a generous salary
and appointed me to a high position.
I spoke my mind fully at every court audience,
yet my words were not implemented,
so I left.
Would the ruler of Wèi not consider me mad?"
Mòzǐ said:
"If your departure was in accordance with the Way,
what harm is there in being called mad?
In ancient times, Zhōu Gōngdàn opposed Guǎn Shū,
resigned from the position of one of the three highest ministers,
and went east to live in Shānggài,
where everyone called him mad.
Later generations praised his virtue,
spread his fame,
and it continues to this day.
Moreover, I have heard
that practicing righteousness is not about avoiding slander and seeking praise;
if your departure was in accordance with the Way,
what harm is there in being called mad?"
Gāo Shízǐ said:
"In leaving,
how dare I not follow the Way?
Formerly, you once said:
'When the world lacks the Way,
a benevolent person does not remain in a position of high emolument.'
Now the ruler of Wèi is without the Way,
and if I greedily cling to his salary and rank,
then I would be indulging in deceit and harming others."
Mòzǐ was pleased
and called Zǐ Qínzǐ
to say:
"Listen to this!
Those who turn their backs on righteousness and face salary—
I have often heard of them;
those who turn their backs on salary and face righteousness—
in Gāo Shízǐ I have seen it!"
Mòzǐ said:
"The gentlemen of the world,
if poor and called rich, become angry;
if without righteousness and called righteous, become pleased—
is this not perverse?"
Gōng Mèngzǐ said:
"The ancients had models,
and we follow them threefold."
Mòzǐ said:
"Which ancients are you referring to, saying we follow their models threefold?
You do not understand that those who came before also had predecessors."
Someone who had turned against Mòzǐ and then returned said,
"Have I done anything wrong?
I returned after all."
Mòzǐ said:
"This is like an army in retreat,
where the one who lags behind seeks a reward."
Gōng Mèngzǐ said:
"A gentleman does not create,
but only transmits."
Mòzǐ said:
"Not so.
Among those who are not gentlemen,
some do not follow the good of antiquity nor create in the present.
Among the next level of non-gentlemen,
some do not follow the good of antiquity,
but when they themselves have something good, they create it,
wanting the good to come from themselves.
Now, to transmit without creating
is no different from not liking to follow yet creating.
I believe we should transmit the good of antiquity
and create the good of the present,
so that goodness may increase."
Wū Mǎzǐ said to Mòzǐ:
"I differ from you;
I cannot practice impartial love.
I love the people of Zōu more than those of Yuè,
the people of Lǔ more than those of Zōu,
my villagers more than the people of Lǔ,
my family more than my villagers,
my parents more than my family,
and myself more than my parents,
because they are closer to me.
To strike me causes pain,
to strike others does not cause me pain;
why should I not relieve what pains me
rather than what does not pain me?
Therefore, for my sake,
I would kill others to benefit myself,
but not kill myself to benefit others."
Mòzǐ said:
"Will you conceal your principle,
or will you proclaim it to others?"
Wū Mǎzǐ said:
"Why should I conceal my principle?
I will proclaim it to others."
Mòzǐ said:
"Then if one person approves of you,
one will want to kill you to benefit themselves;
if ten approve of you,
ten will want to kill you to benefit themselves;
if the whole world approves of you,
the whole world will want to kill you to benefit themselves.
If one person disapproves of you,
one will want to kill you,
considering you a spreader of inauspicious words;
if ten disapprove,
ten will want to kill you,
considering you a spreader of inauspicious words;
if the whole world disapproves,
the whole world will want to kill you,
considering you a spreader of inauspicious words.
Whether they approve or disapprove of you,
they will want to kill you—
this is what is called letting one's words bring
constant danger to one's life."
Mòzǐ said:
"Do you dislike speaking of benefit?
If one refrains from speaking of what is beneficial,
that is merely wagging the tongue."
Mòzǐ said to Lord Wén of Lǔyáng:
"Suppose there is a man here
who has plenty of sheep and cattle,
and his cook cuts and prepares them,
so much that he cannot eat them all.
Yet upon seeing another's pancake,
he still stealthily steals it,
saying:
'Give me something to eat.'
Is it that he does not know he has more than enough food,
or that he has a stealing sickness?"
Lord Wén of Lǔyáng said:
"He has a stealing sickness."
Mòzǐ said:
"The fields within the four borders of Chǔ
are vast and wild, more than can be cultivated,
with countless empty spaces,
more than can be occupied.
Yet when you see the border towns of Sòng and Zhèng,
you still stealthily seize them.
How is this different from that?"
Lord Wén of Lǔyáng said:
"This is just like that,
indeed I have a stealing sickness."
Mòzǐ said:
"Jìsūn Shào and Mèng Bócháng governed the state of Lǔ,
but could not trust each other,
so they prayed at the village shrine,
saying:
'Please make us harmonious.'
This is like covering their eyes
and praying at the village shrine,
'Please make us all see.'
Is that not absurd?"
Mòzǐ said to Luò Gǔlí:
"I hear you are fond of courage."
Luò Gǔlí said:
"Indeed,
when I hear there is a brave man in my village,
I must go and kill him."
Mòzǐ said:
"All under heaven wish to associate with what they admire,
and avoid what they dislike.
Now when you hear there is a brave man in your village,
you must go and kill him,
this is not being fond of courage,
this is disliking courage."
12.1 "Valuing Righteousness, Chapter Forty-Seven"
Mòzǐ said:
Nothing in the world is more valuable than righteousness.
Suppose we say to a man:
"I will give you a hat and shoes,
but cut off your hands and feet,
would you do it?"
He certainly would not.
Why?
Because hats and shoes are not as valuable as hands and feet.
Again, suppose we say:
"I will give you the whole world,
but kill you,
would you do it?"
He certainly would not.
Why?
Because the world is not as valuable as one's own life.
Yet people will fight over a single word and kill each other,
this is valuing righteousness above their own lives.
Therefore it is said:
Nothing in the world is more valuable than righteousness.
When Mòzǐ went from Lǔ to Qí,
he visited an old friend,
who said to Mòzǐ:
"Nowadays no one in the world practices righteousness,
yet you alone torment yourself to do so.
You should stop."
Mòzǐ said:
"Suppose there is a man here
who has ten sons,
only one of whom farms while the other nine remain idle.
Then the one who farms must work even harder.
Why?
Because there are many eaters and few farmers.
Now that no one in the world practices righteousness,
you should be encouraging me,
why do you stop me?"
When Mòzǐ traveled south to Chǔ,
he presented a book to King Huì,
but King Huì excused himself due to old age,
and sent Mù Hè to meet Mòzǐ.
Mòzǐ persuaded Mù Hè,
and Mù Hè was greatly pleased,
saying to Mòzǐ:
"Your words are indeed excellent,
but our king is the great king of all under heaven.
Is it not likely he would say these are 'the doings of lowly people'
and not use them?"
Mòzǐ said:
"Only if they are practicable.
It is like medicine -
if it is a herbal root,
the Son of Heaven will eat it to cure his illness.
Would he say 'it's just a herbal root'
and not eat it?
Now farmers pay their taxes to the nobles,
who use them to make wine and millet offerings
to sacrifice to God and the spirits.
Would they say 'these are the doings of lowly people'
and not enjoy them?
Therefore, even if I am a lowly person,
compared above to farmers,
and below to medicine,
am I really inferior to a herbal root?
Moreover, has my lord heard the story of Tāng?
Once when Tāng was going to see Yī Yǐn,
he ordered the son of the Péng family to drive his carriage.
On the way, the son of the Péng family asked:
'Where is Your Majesty going?'
Tāng said:
'I am going to see Yī Yǐn.'
The son of the Péng family said:
'Yī Yǐn
is a lowly person in the world.
If Your Majesty wishes to see him,
you could simply summon him for questioning -
that would be a great honor for him.'
Tāng said:
'This is beyond your understanding.
Suppose there is medicine here
that when eaten makes the ears hear better
and the eyes see clearer -
then I would certainly be eager to take it.
Now Yī Yǐn is to our state
like a good physician and effective medicine.
For you to not want me to see Yī Yǐn
is to not want what is good for me.'
Thereupon he made the son of the Péng family get down,
and did not let him drive.
If one can act like this,
then it is acceptable."
Mòzǐ said:
In all speech and action,
what benefits Heaven, spirits and the people should be done;
in all speech and action,
what harms Heaven, spirits and the people should be abandoned.
In all speech and action,
what accords with the sage kings Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén and Wǔ should be done;
in all speech and action,
what accords with the tyrants Jié, Zhòu, Yōu and Lì should be abandoned.
Mòzǐ said:
Words that can improve conduct should be constantly spoken;
words that cannot improve conduct should not be constantly spoken.
To constantly speak words that cannot improve conduct
is merely wagging the tongue.
Mòzǐ said:
In silence, think;
when speaking, instruct;
when acting, serve.
If these three are practiced in turn,
one will surely become a sage.
One must eliminate the six biases -
eliminate joy,
eliminate anger,
eliminate pleasure,
eliminate sorrow,
eliminate love,
and practice benevolence and righteousness.
When hands, feet, mouth, nose, ears all engage in righteousness,
one will surely become a sage.
Mòzǐ said to his disciples:
If you cannot practice righteousness,
do not reject its principles.
It is like a carpenter who cannot carve well -
he should not blame his marking line.
Mòzǐ said:
The gentlemen of today -
if asked to be the butcher of a single pig,
will decline if they cannot do it;
but if asked to be prime minister of a state,
will accept even if they cannot do it.
Is this not absurd?
Mòzǐ said:
"Suppose a blind man declares:
'Brightness
is white;
darkness
is black.'
Even those with clear sight cannot dispute this.
But if you mix white and black together
and ask the blind man to choose between them,
he cannot tell.
Thus I say the blind man doesn't know white from black
not because he cannot name them,
but because he cannot choose.
Now when the gentlemen of today speak of benevolence,
even Yǔ and Tāng could not dispute their definitions.
But if you mix benevolent and non-benevolent acts together
and ask these gentlemen to choose,
they cannot tell.
Thus I say the gentlemen of today don't know benevolence
not because they cannot name it,
but because they cannot choose."
Mòzǐ said:
"People today are less careful in conducting themselves
than merchants are in spending a single coin.
When a merchant spends a coin,
he dares not do so recklessly for trade,
but must choose good value.
Yet scholars today in conducting themselves are not like this -
whatever their whims desire, they do.
In serious cases they incur punishments,
in minor cases they suffer disgrace.
Thus scholars are less careful in conducting themselves
than merchants are in spending a single coin."
Mòzǐ said:
"The gentlemen of today
wish to accomplish righteousness,
yet become angry when helped to cultivate themselves.
This is like wanting a wall built
yet becoming angry when people help construct it.
Is this not absurd?"
Mòzǐ said:
"The sage kings of antiquity,
wishing to transmit their Way to later ages,
therefore wrote it on bamboo and silk,
engraved it on metal and stone,
and passed it down to later generations,
wanting posterity to emulate it.
Now hearing the legacy of former kings yet not practicing it
is to abandon the transmission of former kings."
When Mòzǐ traveled south to Wèi,
his carriage was loaded with many books.
Xián Tángzǐ saw this and found it strange,
saying:
"Our master taught Gōngshàng Guò:
'Just measure what is straight and crooked.'
Now you carry many books -
what need is there?"
Mòzǐ said:
"Formerly, Duke Zhōu Dàn read a hundred documents each morning
and received seventy scholars each evening.
Thus Duke Zhōu Dàn assisted the Son of Heaven,
and his achievements endure to this day.
I, Dí, have no duties to a sovereign above,
nor the difficulties of farming below -
how dare I neglect this?
I have heard that
things reaching the same conclusion
may indeed contain errors,
yet people's understanding varies,
hence the many books.
Now regarding Guò's mind,
it repeatedly penetrates subtle principles,
and having already grasped the essentials of things reaching the same conclusion,
therefore I don't teach him with books.
Why do you find this strange?"
Mòzǐ said to Gōngliáng Huánzǐ:
"Wèi is a small state
situated between Qí and Jìn,
like a poor family living between rich families.
If a poor family imitates the rich in food, clothing, and expenditure,
it will surely perish quickly.
Now examining your household,
you have hundreds of decorated carriages,
hundreds of horses fed on beans and grain,
and hundreds of women dressed in embroidered silks.
If I took the expenses for decorated carriages and horse feed and the wealth for embroidered clothes to maintain scholars,
I could certainly support over a thousand.
If trouble arose,
you could deploy hundreds before you
and hundreds behind you.
Which is safer - having hundreds of women before and behind you,
or maintaining scholars? I believe the latter is safer."
Mòzǐ secured an official position in Wèi for someone,
but the appointee went there and returned.
Mòzǐ asked:
"Why did you return?"
He replied:
"What they told me didn't match reality.
They said 'we'll treat you with a thousand measures,'
but gave me only five hundred,
so I left."
Mòzǐ said:
"If they had given you over a thousand measures,
would you have left?"
He replied:
"No."
Mòzǐ said:
"Then it wasn't because they were untrustworthy,
but because the amount was too small."
Mòzǐ said:
"The gentlemen of common custom
regard righteous men less highly than they regard grain-carriers.
Suppose there is someone here
resting by the roadside with carried grain,
wanting to rise but unable to.
When a gentleman sees this,
regardless of age or status,
he will certainly help him rise.
Why?
He says:
'It is right.'
Yet when a gentleman practicing righteousness
offers them the way of former kings,
not only do they refuse to practice it,
they further slander and reject it.
Thus these gentlemen of common custom regard righteous men
less highly than they regard grain-carriers."
Mòzǐ said:
"Merchants travel to the four directions
when prices differ severalfold.
Even with difficulties at passes and bridges,
and dangers from bandits and thieves,
they certainly go.
Now scholars sitting and discussing righteousness
face no difficulties at passes and bridges,
no dangers from bandits and thieves,
and the benefits are incalculably greater,
yet they don't act.
Thus scholars' calculation of profit
is less perceptive than merchants'."
When Mòzǐ went north to Qí,
he met a fortune-teller
who said:
"The Emperor will kill the black dragon in the north today,
and since your complexion is dark,
you cannot go north."
Mòzǐ didn't listen
and proceeded north to the Zī River,
but failed to cross and returned.
The fortune-teller said:
"I told you, sir, you couldn't go north."
Mòzǐ said:
"Southerners cannot go north,
northerners cannot go south.
Some have dark complexions,
some have light complexions.
Why do all fail to cross?
Moreover, if the Emperor kills the green dragon in the east on jiǎ-yǐ days,
the red dragon in the south on bǐng-dīng days,
the white dragon in the west on gēng-xīn days,
and the black dragon in the north on rén-guǐ days,
if we follow your words,
this would prohibit all travel under heaven.
This would confine hearts and empty the world.
Your words cannot be followed."
Mòzǐ said:
"My words are sufficient for application.
To abandon my words and change one's thinking
is like abandoning the harvest to glean scattered grains.
To use others' words to attack mine
is like throwing eggs at stone.
Even if all the eggs in the world were thrown,
the stone would remain as it is,
indestructible."
12.2 "Gōng Mèng - Chapter Forty-Eight"
Gōng Mèngzǐ said to Mòzǐ:
"The gentleman holds himself in readiness and waits.
When asked, he speaks;
when not asked, he remains silent.
He is like a bell:
struck, it rings;
unstruck, it does not ring."
Mòzǐ replied:
"This statement involves three scenarios,
and you, sir, now know only one of them,
and do not yet understand what it truly means.
If a ruler commits licentious and violent acts in the state,
and one remonstrates directly, it is called disrespect;
if one remonstrates through his attendants, it is called meddling.
This is what perplexes the gentleman.
If a ruler governs in such a way
that he is about to bring calamity upon the state,
as if a crossbow mechanism is about to be triggered,
the gentleman must remonstrate,
for it benefits the ruler.
In such cases,
even unstruck, the bell must ring.
If a ruler engages in unrighteous and aberrant conduct,
even if he has obtained ingenious strategies
applicable to military affairs,
and desires to attack and invade innocent states,
the ruler, upon acquiring them, will surely use them
to expand his territory
and accumulate excessive taxes and resources.
Such actions will inevitably lead to disgrace;
the attacked will suffer harm,
and the attackers will also suffer harm,
resulting in mutual detriment.
In such cases,
even unstruck, the bell must ring.
Moreover, you said:
'The gentleman holds himself in readiness,
waits to be asked before speaking,
and remains silent when not asked.
He is like a bell:
struck, it rings;
unstruck, it does not ring.'
Now, no one has struck you, yet you speak.
Is this what you call 'unstruck yet ringing'?
Or do you mean that this is not the way of a gentleman?"
Gōng Mèngzǐ said to Mòzǐ:
"If one is truly a good person,
who would not know it?
It is like a fine jade:
left in its place, unseen,
it still possesses surplus essence.
It is like a beautiful woman:
staying indoors, unseen,
people will contend to seek her.
But if she parades herself about,
no one would want her.
Now, you go around persuading everyone;
how toilsome it is!"
Mòzǐ replied:
"In this chaotic age,
those seeking beautiful women are many;
even if a beautiful woman remains unseen,
many will seek her.
But today, those seeking goodness are few.
If one does not vigorously persuade others,
no one will come to know it.
Moreover, suppose there are two men here:
one skilled in astrology,
who goes about practicing divination for people,
and another who stays at home without going out.
Which of them would earn more offerings?"
Gōng Mèngzǐ said:
"The one who goes about practicing divination for people
would earn more offerings."
Mòzǐ said:
"Benevolence and righteousness are equally important.
He who goes about persuading others
also achieves more good deeds.
Why then should one not go about persuading others?"
Gōng Mèngzǐ, wearing a ceremonial cap and a formal sash,
in Confucian attire,
went to see Mòzǐ and said:
"Does a gentleman act only after donning the proper attire?
Or does he wear the attire after his actions?"
Mòzǐ replied:
"Action does not lie in attire."
Gōng Mèngzǐ asked:
"How do you know this is so?"
Mòzǐ said:
"In the past, Duke Huán of Qí wore a high crown and broad belt,
carried a golden sword and wooden shield,
and governed his state,
which became well-ordered.
In the past, Duke Wén of Jìn wore clothes of coarse cloth,
a sheepskin robe,
and a leather sword belt,
and governed his state,
which became well-ordered.
In the past, King Zhuāng of Chǔ wore a bright cap with silk tassels,
a deep red robe and broad sleeves,
and governed his state,
which became well-ordered.
In the past, King Gōujiàn of Yuè cut his hair and tattooed his body,
and governed his state,
which became well-ordered.
These four rulers
wore different attire,
yet their actions were the same.
From this, I, Dí, know that action does not lie in attire."
Gōng Mèngzǐ said:
"Well said.
I have heard that 'to delay in doing good is inauspicious.'
May I discard my sash and cap,
and see you again, Master?"
Mòzǐ replied:
"Please meet with me as you are.
If you must discard your sash and cap before meeting,
then indeed action does lie in attire."
Gōng Mèngzǐ said:
"A gentleman must use ancient speech and attire
to be benevolent."
Mòzǐ replied:
"In the past, Fèi Zhòng, a minister of King Zhòu of Shāng, was a villain of the world,
while Jīzǐ and Wēizǐ were sages of the world.
They used the same speech, yet one was benevolent, the others were not.
The Duke of Zhōu, Dàn, was a sage of the world,
while Guān Shū was a villain of the world.
They wore the same attire, yet one was benevolent, the other was not.
Thus, it does not lie in ancient attire or ancient speech.
Moreover, you emulate the Zhōu dynasty
but not the Xià dynasty;
your antiquity is not true antiquity."
Gōng Mèngzǐ said to Mòzǐ:
"In the ranking of the sage kings of old,
the highest sages were established as sons of Heaven,
the next as high ministers and officials.
Now, Confucius was versed in the *Book of Songs* and *Book of Documents*,
discerning in rites and music,
and knowledgeable about all things.
If Confucius had lived under a sage king,
would he not have been made son of Heaven?"
Mòzǐ replied:
"The wise
must honor Heaven, serve ghosts,
love people, and practice frugality;
only then are they wise.
Now, you say Confucius was versed in the *Book of Songs* and *Book of Documents*,
discerning in rites and music,
and knowledgeable about all things,
and claim he could have been son of Heaven.
This is like counting the notches on a tally and considering oneself wealthy."
Gōng Mèngzǐ said:
"Poverty, wealth, longevity, and premature death
are determined by Heaven
and cannot be increased or decreased."
He also said:
"A gentleman must study."
Mòzǐ replied:
"To teach people to study while holding that fate is predetermined
is like telling someone to bind their hair but removing their cap."
Gōng Mèngzǐ said to Mòzǐ:
"There is righteousness and unrighteousness,
but no such thing as auspiciousness or inauspiciousness."
Mòzǐ replied:
"The sage kings of old all considered ghosts and spirits to be divine and intelligent,
capable of bringing fortune or misfortune,
and held that there is auspiciousness and inauspiciousness.
Thus, their governance was orderly, and the state was secure.
From Jié and Zhòu onward,
all considered ghosts and spirits not divine and intelligent,
incapable of bringing fortune or misfortune,
and held that there is no auspiciousness or inauspiciousness.
Thus, their governance was chaotic, and the state was endangered.
Therefore, the book *Zǐ Yì* of the former kings says:
'Your arrogance
comes from you,
and is inauspicious.'
This means that wrongdoing brings punishment,
and doing good brings reward."
Master Mòzǐ said to Gōng Mèngzǐ:
"In funeral rites,
when the ruler, parents, wife, or eldest son dies,
one observes three years of mourning.
For uncles and brothers, one year;
for close relatives, five months;
for aunts, sisters, maternal uncles, and nephews, several months of mourning.
Some, during intervals without mourning, recite the three hundred Poems,
play the three hundred Poems on strings,
sing the three hundred Poems,
dance the three hundred Poems.
If we follow your advice,
when would gentlemen have time to attend to governance?
When would common people have time for their work?"
Gōng Mèngzǐ said:
"When the state is in chaos, govern it;
when the state is well-governed, practice rites and music.
When the state is poor, work;
when the state is wealthy, practice rites and music."
Master Mòzǐ said:
"A state's order comes from governing it,
hence it is orderly.
If governing is neglected,
then the state's order is also lost.
A state's wealth comes from work,
hence it is wealthy.
If work is neglected,
then the state's wealth is also lost.
Therefore, even a well-governed state,
must be urged without satiety,
only then is it acceptable.
Now you say, 'When the state is well-governed, practice rites and music;
when in chaos, govern it,'
this is like digging a well when thirsty,
or seeking a doctor when dead.
In ancient times, the three dynasties' tyrants Jié, Zhòu, Yōu, and Lì
indulged in music,
disregarding their people,
thus they met with punishments and executions,
and their states became desolate and ruined,
all because they followed this way."
Gōng Mèngzǐ said:
"There are no ghosts or spirits."
And also said:
"Gentlemen must learn sacrificial rites."
Master Mòzǐ said:
"To hold that there are no ghosts yet learn sacrificial rites,
is like learning guest rites without having guests,
or making a fish net without having fish."
Gōng Mèngzǐ said to Master Mòzǐ:
"You consider the three-year mourning wrong,
but your three-day mourning is also wrong."
Master Mòzǐ said:
"You criticize the three-day mourning for not being three years,
is like a naked person accusing one who lifts his clothes of being disrespectful."
Gōng Mèngzǐ said to Master Mòzǐ:
"If one's knowledge surpasses others,
can they be called wise?"
Master Mòzǐ said:
"A fool's knowledge may surpass others in some ways,
but can the fool therefore be called wise?"
Gōng Mèngzǐ said:
"The three-year mourning
learns from children's longing for parents."
Master Mòzǐ said:
"The knowledge of an infant
is solely to long for parents.
When parents are not found,
they cry without ceasing;
what is the reason for this?
It is the height of foolishness.
Then, can the knowledge of Confucians
be said to surpass that of an infant?"
Master Mòzǐ asked a Confucian:
"Why make music?"
The reply was:
"Music is for pleasure."
Master Mòzǐ said:
"You have not answered me.
If I ask why build a house,
and you say to avoid cold in winter,
avoid heat in summer,
and for the separation of men and women,
then you have told me the reason for building a house.
Now I ask why make music,
and you say music is for pleasure,
that is like asking why build a house,
and saying a house is for a house."
Master Mòzǐ said to Chéngzǐ:
"The Confucian way is sufficient to ruin the world
in four policies.
Confucians regard Heaven as not clear,
ghosts as not divine,
displeasing Heaven and ghosts;
this is enough to ruin the world.
Also, elaborate funerals and prolonged mourning,
heavy coffins,
many burial clothes and quilts,
seeing off the dead as if moving,
three years of weeping,
supporting to rise later,
walking with a cane later,
ears hearing nothing,
eyes seeing nothing;
this is enough to ruin the world.
Also, playing strings, singing, drumming, and dancing,
practicing music;
this is enough to ruin the world.
Also, believing in fate,
that poverty and wealth, longevity and premature death, order and chaos, safety and danger have fixed limits,
cannot be increased or decreased.
If those above practice this,
they will not attend to governance;
if those below practice this,
they will not work;
this is enough to ruin the world."
Chéngzǐ said:
"How severe,
sir, your slander of Confucians is."
Master Mòzǐ said:
"If Confucians originally did not have these four policies,
and I spoke of them,
then it would be slander.
But now Confucians do have these four policies,
and I speak of them,
then it is not slander,
but reporting what I have heard."
Chéngzǐ had no reply and left.
Master Mòzǐ said:
"He is lost!"
He returned,
sat down again.
Coming forward, he said again:
"Earlier, sir, in your words,
there was something worth hearing.
If according to your words,
then you neither praise Yǔ nor slander Jié and Zhòu."
Master Mòzǐ said:
"Not so.
To respond to familiar words with appropriate discussion
is agility.
Attack heavily, and I respond heavily;
attack lightly, and I respond lightly.
To respond to familiar words with discussion,
is like carrying a cart shaft to hit moths."
Master Mòzǐ debated with Chéngzǐ,
and praised Confucius.
Chéngzǐ said:
"You oppose Confucians,
why do you praise Confucius?"
Master Mòzǐ said:
"This is also right and cannot be changed.
When birds hear of heat and drought, they fly high;
when fish hear of heat and drought, they dive deep.
Facing this,
even if Yǔ or Tāng were to plan for them,
they certainly could not change it.
Birds and fish may be called foolish,
yet Yǔ and Tāng would still follow along.
How could I, Dí, not have praise for Confucius?"
There was a person wandering at Master Mòzǐ's gate,
who said to Master Mòzǐ:
"You, sir, consider ghosts and spirits to be intelligent and perceptive,
capable of bringing fortune and misfortune,
enriching those who do good,
and bringing disaster to the violent.
Now I have served you for a long time,
yet fortune has not come.
Could it be that
your words are not entirely good?
Or that the ghosts and spirits are not intelligent?
Why is it that I have not obtained fortune?"
Master Mòzǐ said:
"Even though you have not obtained fortune,
how can you say my words are not good?
And how can you say the ghosts and spirits are not intelligent?
Have you also heard about the punishment for hiding fugitives?"
He replied:
"I have not heard of it."
Master Mòzǐ said:
"Suppose there is a person here
who is ten times better than you,
can you praise him ten times
and not praise yourself once?"
He replied:
"I cannot."
"Suppose there is a person here
who is a hundred times better than you,
can you praise his goodness throughout your life,
and not praise yourself once?"
He replied:
"I cannot."
Master Mòzǐ said:
"Hiding one person
still constitutes a crime.
Now the things you have hidden are so numerous,
you are bound to have heavy guilt,
so how can you seek fortune?"
When Master Mòzǐ was ill,
Diébí came forward and asked:
"You, sir, consider ghosts and spirits to be intelligent,
capable of bringing fortune and misfortune,
rewarding the good,
and punishing the evil.
Now you, sir,
are a sage,
why do you have illness?
Could it be that
your words are not entirely good?
Or that the ghosts and spirits are not intelligent and perceptive?"
Master Mòzǐ said:
"Even though I am ill,
how can you say they are not intelligent?
There are many ways people can fall ill:
some get ill from cold and heat,
some from toil and hardship.
If there are a hundred doors and one is left open,
how can you say thieves have no way to enter?"
There was a person wandering at Master Mòzǐ's gate,
physically strong and healthy,
with quick and thorough thinking,
whom Master Mòzǐ wanted to have follow him and learn.
Master Mòzǐ said:
"For now, study,
and I will appoint you to office."
Encouraged by these good words, he studied,
and that same year,
he requested an official position from Master Mòzǐ.
Master Mòzǐ said:
"I will not appoint you to office.
Have you heard the story from Lǔ?
In Lǔ, there were five brothers.
Their father died,
and the eldest son loved drinking and would not bury him.
The four younger brothers said:
'If you bury our father,
we will buy you wine.'
Encouraged by these good words, he buried him.
After the burial, he demanded wine from his four brothers.
The four brothers said:
'We cannot give you wine.
You buried your father,
we buried our father -
is he our father alone?
If you did not bury him,
people would laugh at you,
so we encouraged you to bury him.'
Now you practice righteousness,
and I also practice righteousness -
is righteousness mine alone?
If you do not study,
people will laugh at you,
so I encouraged you to study."
There was a person wandering at Master Mòzǐ's gate,
Master Mòzǐ said:
"Why not study?"
He replied:
"None of my clansmen study."
Master Mòzǐ said:
"Not so.
Those who love beauty,
would they say 'since none of my clansmen love it,
therefore I will not love it'?
Those who desire wealth and honor,
would they say 'since none of my clansmen desire it,
therefore I will not desire it'?
Those who love beauty and desire wealth and honor,
do not look to others but still strive for them.
Righteousness
is the great vessel of the world;
why look to others?
You must strive for it!"
Some disciples reported to Master Mòzǐ about learning archery,
Master Mòzǐ said:
"It cannot be done.
The wise must assess what their capabilities allow and then engage in it.
A warrior of the state, while fighting and helping others,
still cannot manage both.
Now you are not warriors of the state,
how can you accomplish both learning and archery?"
Some disciples reported to Master Mòzǐ:
"Gàozǐ speaks of righteousness but acts very badly;
we request to abandon him."
Master Mòzǐ said:
"It cannot be done.
To praise my words while criticizing my actions
is better than nothing.
Suppose there is a person here
named Dí who is very unkind,
yet respects heaven, serves ghosts, and loves people - though very unkind,
it is still better than nothing.
Now Gàozǐ's speech is very eloquent,
he speaks of benevolence and righteousness and does not criticize me;
even if Gàozǐ criticizes,
it is still better than nothing."
Several disciples reported to Master Mòzǐ, saying:
"Gàozǐ prevails in practicing benevolence."
Master Mòzǐ said:
"Not necessarily so.
When Gàozǐ practices benevolence,
it is like standing on tiptoe to appear tall,
or leaning to appear broad—
it cannot last long."
Gàozǐ said to Master Mòzǐ:
"I govern the state and handle administration."
Master Mòzǐ said:
"In administration,
what one says with the mouth
must be carried out by the body.
Now you speak with your mouth
but do not act with your body—
this is disorder in your own person.
If you cannot govern your own person,
how can you govern the state's administration?
You should stop;
your own person is in disorder."
13.1 "The Questions of Lǔ - Chapter Forty-Nine"
The ruler of Lǔ said to Master Mòzǐ:
"I fear Qí will attack us.
Can we be saved?"
Master Mòzǐ said:
"Yes.
In the past, the sage kings of the Three Dynasties—Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ—
were lords of only a hundred lǐ,
yet they advocated loyalty and practiced righteousness,
and thus took the world.
The tyrannical kings of the Three Dynasties—Jié, Zhòu, Yōu, and Lì—
practiced enmity and violence,
and thus lost the world.
I wish that you, my lord, would above revere Heaven and serve the spirits,
and below love and benefit the common people,
generously prepare hides and silks,
humble your speech,
urgently and universally court the neighboring lords,
and drive the state to serve Qí.
Then the crisis can be averted.
Unless you are willing, there is nothing to be done."
When Qí was about to attack Lǔ,
Master Mòzǐ said to Xiàng Zǐniú:
"Attacking Lǔ
is a great mistake for Qí.
In the past, the king of Wú campaigned east against Yuè,
driving them to Mount Kuàijī;
west against Chǔ,
forcing King Zhāo to take refuge in Suí;
north against Qí,
capturing the crown prince and bringing him back to Wú.
The lords avenged their grievances,
the people suffered from the toil and refused to serve,
thus the state became desolate,
and he himself was executed.
In the past, Zhì Bó attacked the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans,
annexing the lands of the three Jìn.
The lords avenged their grievances,
the people suffered from the toil and refused to serve,
thus the state became desolate,
and he himself was executed.
Therefore, when a great state attacks a small one,
it is mutual harm,
and the fault will rebound upon the state."
Master Mòzǐ went to see the great king of Qí,
and said:
"Suppose there is a knife here,
and it is tested on a human head,
cutting it off instantly.
Can it be called sharp?"
The great king said:
"Sharp."
Master Mòzǐ said:
"If it is tested on many human heads,
cutting them off instantly,
can it be called sharp?"
The great king said:
"Sharp."
Master Mòzǐ said:
"The knife is indeed sharp,
but who will suffer the inauspiciousness?"
The great king said:
"The knife gains its sharpness,
the tester suffers the inauspiciousness."
Master Mòzǐ said:
"In annihilating states and overthrowing armies,
harming and killing the common people,
who will suffer the inauspiciousness?"
The great king bowed and thought,
then said:
"I will suffer the inauspiciousness."
Lǔyáng Wénjūn was about to attack Zhèng.
Master Mòzǐ heard of it and went to stop him,
saying to Wénjūn:
"If now within the four borders of Lǔ, the great cities attack the small ones,
the great families attack the small ones,
kill their people,
and seize their oxen, horses, dogs, pigs, cloth, silk, grain, goods, and wealth,
what would you think?"
Lǔyáng Wénjūn said:
"Within the four borders of Lǔ,
all are my subjects.
If the great cities attack the small ones,
the great families attack the small ones,
and seize their goods and wealth,
then I would certainly punish them severely."
Master Mòzǐ said:
"Heaven encompasses the whole world
just as you encompass the four borders.
Now you raise an army to attack Zhèng—
will Heaven's punishment not come?"
Lǔyáng Wénjūn said:
"Why do you stop me from attacking Zhèng?
I attack Zhèng in accordance with Heaven's will.
The people of Zhèng have for three generations killed their fathers,
so Heaven has punished them,
causing three years of poor harvests.
I am going to assist Heaven in punishing them."
Master Mòzǐ said:
"The people of Zhèng have for three generations killed their fathers,
and Heaven has punished them,
causing three years of poor harvests—
Heaven's punishment is sufficient.
Now you again raise an army to attack Zhèng,
saying:
'I attack Zhèng
in accordance with Heaven's will.'
Suppose there is a man here
whose son is violent and useless,
so the father whips him.
If the father of the neighboring family takes a stick and beats him,
saying:
'I beat him
in accordance with his father's will,'
would that not be absurd?
Master Mòzǐ said to Lǔyáng Wénjūn:
"Attacking a neighboring state,
killing its people,
seizing its oxen, horses, grain, goods, and wealth,
then recording it on bamboo and silk,
engraving it on metal and stone,
inscribing it on bells and tripods,
to pass down to later generations,
saying:
'None have as much as I.'
Now if a lowly person
also attacks his neighbor,
kills their people,
seizes their dogs, pigs, food, grain, and clothing,
and also records it on bamboo and silk,
inscribing it on mats and vessels,
to pass down to later generations,
saying:
'None have as much as I,'
would that be acceptable?"
Lǔyáng Wénjūn said:
"Indeed.
From your words, I see that
what the world deems acceptable
is not necessarily so."
Master Mòzǐ said to Lǔyáng Wénjūn:
"The gentlemen of the world
all know small matters but not great ones.
Suppose there is a man here
who steals a dog or a pig—
he is called unrighteous.
But if he steals a state or a city,
he is considered righteous.
This is like calling a small white thing white,
but a large white thing black.
Thus, when gentlemen of the world know small matters but not great ones,
this saying refers to them."
Lǔyáng Wénjūn said to Master Mòzǐ:
"South of Chǔ,
there is a state of cannibals.
When the firstborn son is born there,
they dismember and eat him,
calling it 'beneficial for younger brothers.'
If it is delicious,
they present it to their ruler.
The ruler is pleased
and rewards the father.
Is this not a vile custom?"
Master Mòzǐ said:
"Even the customs of the central states
are like this.
Killing the father and rewarding the son—
how is that different from eating the son and rewarding the father?
If they do not practice benevolence and righteousness,
why criticize the barbarians for eating their sons?"
The favorite concubine of the Lord of Lǔ died,
and the Lord composed a eulogy for her,
which the people of Lǔ praised and adopted.
Mòzǐ heard of this
and said:
"A eulogy
is meant to convey the will of the deceased.
Now it is praised and adopted,
this is like using a badger to pull a carriage."
Lǔyáng Wénjūn said to Mòzǐ:
"Someone described a loyal minister to me
who stoops when ordered to stoop,
looks up when ordered to look up,
remains quiet when at rest,
and responds when called.
Can he be called a loyal minister?"
Mòzǐ replied:
"Stooping when ordered to stoop,
and looking up when ordered to look up,
this resembles a shadow.
Remaining quiet when at rest,
and responding when called,
this resembles an echo.
What would you gain from a shadow or an echo?
According to Dí's definition of a loyal minister,
when the ruler has faults, he subtly remonstrates;
when he himself has good ideas, he consults with the ruler,
daring not to disclose them to outsiders;
he corrects the ruler's errors and guides him toward goodness,
promoting unity with superiors without forming cliques below,
so that praise and goodness belong to the ruler while resentment and enmity fall upon the ministers,
with joy and comfort above and worry and sorrow among the officials.
This is what Dí calls a loyal minister."
The Lord of Lǔ said to Mòzǐ:
"I have two sons:
one loves learning,
the other enjoys sharing wealth with others.
Which one should be made crown prince?"
Mòzǐ said:
"It cannot be determined yet,
for their actions might be motivated by rewards or other purposes.
The angler's deference
is not a gift to the fish;
using insects as bait for mice
is not out of love for them.
I hope you will observe them by combining their intentions with their achievements."
A man from Lǔ had his son study under Mòzǐ,
and the son died in battle.
The father blamed Mòzǐ.
Mòzǐ said:
"You wanted your son to learn from my son,
and now he has completed his studies.
He died in battle,
yet you are angry,
as if wanting to trade grain
but resenting the transaction.
Is this not wasteful?"
In the southern borderlands of Lǔ, there was a man named Wú Lǜ
who made pottery in winter and farmed in summer,
comparing himself to Shùn.
Mòzǐ heard of him and went to see him.
Wú Lǜ said to Mòzǐ:
"Righteousness is just righteousness,
why must it be spoken of?"
Mòzǐ said:
"Does what you call righteousness
involve using strength to benefit others
or using wealth to share with others?"
Wú Lǜ said:
"Yes."
Mòzǐ said:
"Dí has considered this.
If Dí were to farm to feed all under heaven,
at best,
he could only equal one farmer's yield.
Distributed throughout the world,
each person would not get even one shēng of grain.
Even if each received one shēng,
it would not fill the hungry of the world,
as is evident.
If Dí were to weave to clothe all under heaven,
at best,
he could only equal one woman's weaving.
Distributed throughout the world,
each person would not get even a foot of cloth.
Even if each received a foot,
it would not warm the cold of the world,
as is evident.
If Dí were to don armor and take up arms to save the feudal lords from calamity,
at best,
he could only equal one soldier in battle.
One soldier's fight
cannot resist three armies,
as is evident.
Dí believes it is better to study the way of the ancient kings and seek their teachings,
understand the words of the sages and examine their meanings,
persuade kings and dukes above,
and commoners and pedestrians below.
If kings and dukes follow my words,
their states will surely be well-governed;
if commoners follow my words,
their conduct will surely be cultivated.
Thus, Dí believes that even without farming to feed the hungry
or weaving to clothe the cold,
the merit is greater than farming to feed or weaving to clothe.
Therefore, Dí holds that even without farming or weaving,
the merit surpasses that of farming and weaving."
Wú Lǜ said to Mòzǐ:
"Righteousness is just righteousness,
why must it be spoken of?"
Mòzǐ said:
"Suppose the world did not know farming:
who has greater merit, one who teaches farming or one who farms alone without teaching?"
Wú Lǜ said:
"One who teaches farming has greater merit."
Mòzǐ said:
"Suppose attacking an unjust state:
who has greater merit, one who drums and urges the masses to advance or one who advances alone without drumming?"
Wú Lǜ said:
"One who drums and urges the masses has greater merit."
Mòzǐ said:
"Few commoners in the world know righteousness,
so teaching righteousness to the world has great merit.
Why not speak of it?
If we can drum and advance toward righteousness,
then would my righteousness not progress even further?"
Mòzǐ sent Gōngshàng Guò to Yuè,
and Gōngshàng Guò persuaded the King of Yuè,
who was greatly pleased
and said to Gōngshàng Guò:
"If you, sir, can bring Mòzǐ to Yuè to teach me,
I will grant him five hundred lǐ of land from the former state of Wú."
Gōngshàng Guò agreed.
The king then prepared fifty chariots for Gōngshàng Guò
to welcome Mòzǐ from Lǔ,
saying:
"I used your teachings to persuade the King of Yuè,
and he was greatly pleased,
saying to me:
'If you can bring Mòzǐ to Yuè to teach me,
I will grant you five hundred lǐ of land from the former state of Wú.'"
Mòzǐ said to Gōngshàng Guò:
"What do you think of the King of Yuè's intentions?
If the King of Yuè will heed my words
and adopt my way,
then Dí will go,
eating only to fill my belly,
clothing only to cover my body,
and comparing myself to the other ministers,
not seeking enfeoffment.
But if the King of Yuè does not heed my words
or adopt my way,
and I go there,
then I would be selling righteousness.
Selling it equally,
I might as well do so in the central states;
why must it be in Yuè?"
While Mòzǐ was traveling,
Wèi Yuè said:
"When you meet the rulers of the four regions,
what will you speak of first?"
Mòzǐ said:
"Upon entering any state,
one must choose what is urgent and act accordingly.
If the state is chaotic,
speak of exalting the worthy and promoting unity;
if the state is poor,
speak of frugality in use and moderation in funerals;
if the state indulges in music and drunkenness,
speak of condemning music and fatalism;
if the state is licentious and devoid of ritual,
speak of revering heaven and serving ghosts;
if the state is bent on aggression and invasion,
then speak of universal love and condemning aggression.
Thus it is said:
choose what is urgent and act accordingly."
Master Mozi sent his disciple Cáo Gōngzǐ to Sòng,
and after three years he returned.
He saw Master Mozi and said:
"When I first studied under your guidance,
I wore coarse short robes,
ate soup of wild herbs,
if I got some in the morning, by evening I might have none,
and thus could not make offerings to the spirits and gods.
But now, thanks to your teachings,
my family has become wealthier than before,
and with ample means, I carefully sacrifice to the spirits and gods.
Yet many of my followers have died,
my livestock do not thrive,
and I myself am deeply afflicted by illness.
I doubt that your Way can be of any use."
Master Mozi said:
"Not so.
What the spirits and gods desire from humans is much:
they want those in high positions with ample salaries to yield them to the worthy,
and those with abundant wealth to share it with the poor.
How could the spirits and gods only crave the grabbing of millet and grasping of lungs?
Now, you hold high rank and salary but do not yield them to the worthy—
this is the first inauspicious act.
You have much wealth but do not share it with the poor—
this is the second inauspicious act.
Now, in serving the spirits and gods,
you only perform sacrifices and that's all,
yet you say:
'How did illness come upon me?'
This is like having a hundred doors and closing only one,
then saying:
'How could thieves get in?'
To seek blessings in this manner—
from the existence
of such strange spirits—
how could it be possible?"
A Lǔ priest sacrificed one piglet
and sought a hundred blessings from the spirits and gods.
Master Mozi heard of this
and said:
"This won't do.
If you give others little but expect much from them,
then others would only fear that you might bestow anything upon them.
Now, sacrificing one piglet to seek a hundred blessings from the spirits and gods,
the spirits and gods would only fear that you might sacrifice oxen and sheep.
In ancient times, the sage kings served the spirits and gods,
offering sacrifices and that was all.
Now, to sacrifice a piglet and seek a hundred blessings,
then one's wealth is worse than poverty."
Péng Qīngshēngzǐ said:
"The past can be known,
but the future cannot be known."
Master Mozi said:
"Suppose your parent were a hundred lǐ away,
and encountered danger,
with a deadline of one day:
if you reach them, they live;
if not, they die.
Now, here is a sturdy carriage with fine horses,
and there a nag with wheels square at the corners.
If you were to choose,
which would you ride?"
He replied:
"Ride the fine horses and sturdy carriage,
to arrive quickly."
Master Mozi said:
"Then how can you say the future cannot be known?"
Mèng Shān praised Prince Lǘ, saying:
"During the disaster caused by Báigōng,
he seized Prince Lǘ,
pressed an axe to his waist,
and held a spear to his heart,
saying to him:
'Become king and live,
refuse and die.'
Prince Lǘ said:
'How you insult me!
You killed my relatives,
and offer me the state of Chǔ as a favor.
If I gained the whole world unjustly,
I would not do it,
let alone the state of Chǔ!'
So he refused and did not become king.
Was Prince Lǘ not benevolent?"
Master Mozi said:
"Difficult it was, indeed,
but not benevolent.
If he considered the king unrighteous,
why did he not accept the throne and govern?
If he considered Báigōng unjust,
why did he not accept the kingship,
execute Báigōng, and then restore the king?
Therefore, I say:
difficult it was,
but not benevolent."
Master Mozi sent Shèng Chuò to serve Xiàng Zǐniú.
Xiàng Zǐniú invaded the territory of Lǔ three times,
and Shèng Chuò followed him each time.
Master Mozi heard of this
and sent Gāo Sūnzǐ to request his dismissal,
saying:
"I sent Chuò
to curb arrogance and correct favoritism.
Now Chuò,
with a generous salary, deceives his master.
His master invaded Lǔ three times,
and Chuò followed each time—
this is like whipping a horse on the breastplate.
I, Dí, have heard that
to speak of righteousness but not practice it
is to violate clarity.
It's not that Chuò does not know this,
but his salary overcomes righteousness."
Once, the people of Chǔ and Yuè fought a naval battle on the river.
The Chǔ people advanced with the current
and retreated against it;
seeing advantage, they advanced,
seeing disadvantage, they found retreat difficult.
The Yuè people advanced against the current
and retreated with it;
seeing advantage, they advanced,
seeing disadvantage, they retreated quickly.
The Yuè people used this tactic
and repeatedly defeated the Chǔ people.
Gōngshūzǐ traveled south from Lǔ to Chǔ,
and there began to make devices for naval warfare,
creating the hook-and-push equipment:
hooking those who retreated,
pushing those who advanced.
Measuring the length of the hooks and pushes,
he made weapons accordingly.
The weapons of Chǔ became effective,
while those of Yuè were not,
and the Chǔ people used this tactic
to repeatedly defeat the Yuè people.
Gōngshūzǐ prided himself on his skill
and said to Master Mozi:
"In naval warfare, I have the hook and push.
I wonder if your righteousness also has a hook and push?"
Master Mozi said:
"The hook and push of my righteousness
is superior to your naval hook and push.
My hook and push—
I hook with love,
and push with respect.
Without hooking with love, there is no closeness;
without pushing with respect, there is quick familiarity,
and familiarity without closeness
leads to quick separation.
Thus, mutual love and mutual respect
are like mutual benefit.
Now, you hook to stop others,
others also hook to stop you;
you push to keep others away,
others also push to keep you away.
Mutual hooking and mutual pushing
are like mutual harm.
Therefore, the hook and push of my righteousness
is superior to your naval hook and push."
Gōngshūzǐ carved bamboo and wood to make a magpie,
which, when completed, flew
and did not come down for three days.
Gōngshūzǐ considered this the pinnacle of skill.
Master Mozi said to Gōngshūzǐ:
"Your making of a magpie
is not as good as my making of a linchpin.
In a moment, I carve a three-inch piece of wood,
and it bears a weight of fifty shi.
Therefore, what is considered skillful
is what benefits people—that is called skill;
what does not benefit people is called clumsiness."
Gōngshūzǐ said to Master Mozi:
"Before I met you,
I wished to obtain Sòng.
But after meeting you,
if given Sòng unjustly,
I would not take it."
Master Mozi said:
"Before I met you,
you wished to obtain Sòng.
After I met you,
if given Sòng unjustly, you would not take it—
that means I have given you Sòng.
You devote yourself to righteousness,
and I will further give you the world."
13.2 "Gōngshū Fiftieth"
Gōngshū Bān had finished constructing the cloud-ladder devices for Chǔ,
and was about to use them to attack Sòng.
Master Mòzǐ heard of this,
set out from Qí and traveled ten days and ten nights,
until he reached Yǐng,
where he met Gōngshū Bān.
Gōngshū Bān said:
"What instructions does the Master have for me?"
Master Mòzǐ said:
"There is someone in the north who has insulted me,
I wish to borrow your help to kill him."
Gōngshū Bān was displeased.
Master Mòzǐ said:
"I beg to offer ten pieces of gold."
Gōngshū Bān said:
"I uphold righteousness and firmly do not kill people."
Master Mòzǐ rose,
bowed twice and said:
"Let me explain.
I heard in the north that you were making ladders,
to be used to attack Sòng.
What crime has Sòng committed?
The state of Jīng has more than enough land,
but not enough people.
To kill what you lack and contend for what you have in excess,
cannot be called wise.
To attack Sòng when it has committed no crime,
cannot be called benevolent.
To know this and not oppose it,
cannot be called loyal.
To oppose it but not succeed,
cannot be called strong.
To uphold righteousness by not killing a few but killing many,
cannot be called understanding categories."
Gōngshū Bān was convinced.
Master Mòzǐ said:
"Then why not stop?"
Gōngshū Bān said:
"I cannot,
I have already spoken about it to the king."
Master Mòzǐ said:
"Why not introduce me to the king?"
Gōngshū Bān said:
"Agreed."
Master Mòzǐ saw the king,
and said:
"Suppose there is a man here,
who abandons his ornate carriage,
but desires to steal his neighbor's broken cart;
abandons his embroidered silks,
but desires to steal his neighbor's coarse short robe;
abandons his fine grain and meat,
but desires to steal his neighbor's husks and dregs.
What kind of person is this?"
The king said:
"He must have a stealing sickness."
Master Mòzǐ said:
"The land of Jīng,
is five thousand li square,
while the land of Sòng,
is five hundred li square.
This is like the ornate carriage compared to the broken cart.
Jīng has Yúnmèng,
filled with rhinoceroses, sì, deer, and elk,
and the fish, turtles, yuán, and tuó of the Jiāng and Hàn rivers are the richest in the world;
Sòng is said to have no pheasants, rabbits, foxes, or badgers.
This is like the fine grain and meat compared to the husks and dregs.
Jīng has tall pines, patterned zǐ, catalpas, nán, and camphor trees,
while Sòng has no tall trees.
This is like the embroidered silks compared to the coarse short robe.
I consider your officials' attack on Sòng in these three matters
to be of the same category."
The king said:
"Well said.
However,
Gōngshū Bān has made the cloud-ladders for me,
so I must take Sòng."
Thereupon, he summoned Gōngshū Bān.
Master Mòzǐ loosened his belt to form a city wall,
and used small tablets as devices.
Gōngshū Bān set up nine variations of攻城 tactics,
but Master Mòzǐ repelled them nine times.
Gōngshū Bān's offensive devices were exhausted,
while Master Mòzǐ's defensive measures remained ample.
Gōngshū Bān was defeated,
and said:
"I know how to defeat you,
but I will not say."
Master Mòzǐ also said:
"I know how you would defeat me,
but I will not say."
The king of Chǔ asked the reason,
Master Mòzǐ said:
"Gōngshū Zǐ's intention
is nothing more than to have me killed.
If I am killed,
Sòng will be unable to defend itself,
and can be attacked.
However, my disciples Qíngǔlí and three hundred others
are already holding my defensive devices,
waiting on Sòng's city walls for the Chǔ invaders.
Even if I am killed,
they cannot be stopped."
The king of Chǔ said:
"Well said.
I will not attack Sòng."
Master Mòzǐ returned,
passed through Sòng,
it was raining,
he sought shelter under a gate tower,
but the gatekeeper would not let him in.
Therefore it is said:
Those who work in spirit,
the masses do not know their achievements.
Those who contend in the open,
the masses know of them.
14.1 "Preparation of the City Gate Fifty-two"
Qíngǔlí asked Master Mòzǐ:
"According to the words of the sage,
the phoenix does not appear,
the feudal lords betray the states of Yīn and Zhōu,
and armed conflicts are arising throughout the world,
the great attack the small,
the strong seize the weak.
I wish to defend a small state,
how should I proceed?"
Master Mòzǐ said:
"Against what kinds of attacks are you defending?"
Qíngǔlí replied:
"In the present age, the common methods of attack are:
overlooking, hooking, ramming, laddering, filling, flooding, tunneling, hollowing out, ant-style assault, fényūn chariots, and xuān chariots.
May I ask how to defend against these twelve methods?"
Master Mòzǐ said:
"If our city moats and walls are repaired,
defensive equipment is prepared,
provisions are sufficient,
superiors and inferiors are harmonious,
and we have the aid of neighboring feudal lords,
this is how we can hold.
Moreover, even if the defenders are skilled,
it may still be impossible to defend.
If the ruler employs them,
must the defenders also be capable?
If the defenders are incapable,
and the ruler employs them,
then it may still be impossible to defend.
Therefore, the defenders must be skilled,
and the ruler respects and employs them,
then it is possible to defend."
Thus, the general method of defending a city:
prepare the city gates,
install hanging gates with sinking mechanisms,
two zhàng long,
eight chǐ wide,
make them symmetrical.
The number of door leaves,
should overlap by three cùn,
apply earth on the leaves,
not exceeding two cùn.
The trench should be one zhàng five deep,
width matching the leaves,
the trench length according to capacity,
at the end of the trench install a suspension,
able to accommodate one person.
When the enemy arrives,
all doors and windows should be chiseled and covered with孜 holes,
each with two covers,
one chiseled and tied with rope,
four chǐ long.
To rescue against fire arrows from chariots,
shot at the city gate,
chisel the leaves to make栈,
coat them,
use water hemp buckets and leather basins to extinguish.
Door leaves and thin supports should be chiseled half a cùn,
one cùn one涿 peg,
pegs two cùn long,
exposed one cùn,
spaced seven cùn apart,
thickly coated to prepare against fire.
On the city gate, chisel to rescue against gate fire,
each with a hanging water container,
holding three dàn or more,
large and small mixed.
Gate posts and bolts must be firmly secured,
secured with metal or iron plates.
Gate bolts double-layered,
plated with iron,
must be sturdy.
Shūguān bolts two chǐ,
shūguān one xiàn,
sealed with the guard's seal,
periodically have someone inspect the seal,
and check how deep the bolt enters the huán.
Gatekeepers must not carry axes, jǐn, chisels, saws, or hammers.
On the city wall, every two paces there is a trench,
the trench's standard depth is one zhang three chi,
with a crown length of ten chi,
and a side length of six chi.
Every two paces, a bamboo screen,
nine chi wide,
twelve chi long.
Every two paces, set up connected clubs,
one each of long axes and long hammers,
twenty spears,
arranged around within two paces.
Every two paces, a wooden crossbow,
must shoot over fifty paces.
And produce many arrows,
preferably not using bamboo shafts,
but oak, Zhào, yú, or elm,
are acceptable.
Seek Qí iron arrows,
to shoot at enemy troops and watchtowers.
Every two paces, pile stones,
five hundred stones each weighing over half a jūn.
Not less than a hundred to resist,
sharp plows and walls can all be well arranged.
Every two paces, pile brushwood,
one arm-span thick,
one zhang long,
twenty bundles.
Every five paces, an earthen jar,
filled with water.
There is a ladle,
the ladle can hold one dǒu.
Every five paces, pile five hundred dog corpses,
the dog corpses three chi long,
wrapped in reeds,
with a jar at the end,
firmly tied with rope.
Every ten paces, pile logs,
over two arm-spans thick,
twenty pieces eight chi long.
Every twenty-five paces, a stove,
the stove has an iron pot holding one dàn or more,
prepared for boiling water.
And hold sand,
no less than a thousand dàn.
Every thirty paces, set up a watchtower,
the tower extends four chi beyond the parapet,
three chi wide,
four chi broad,
boarded on three sides closely fitted,
in summer, also cover the top.

14.2 Preparation Against Elevated Attacks - Chapter 53
Qínzǐ bowed repeatedly and said:

Mòzǐ said:
Are you asking about defending against yángqián?
Yángqián

enough to tire their troops,
but not enough to harm the city.
Defend by building tower walls,
overlooking the yángqián,
extending twenty chǐ out on each side,

using strong crossbows,
assisted by mechanical devices,
and unusual instruments,
then the attack via yángqián will fail.
Prepare against elevated attacks with repeating crossbow carts,
made from large square timber one chǐ square,

They have two axles and three wheels,

There are two posts on the left and right sides,

The crossbow arms align with the frame front and back,

The repeating crossbow mechanism and housing are bronze, weighing one shí thirty jīn,
with a deer[-shape] winch to draw the string.
The frame is three and a half units in circumference,

three cùn square,

The hook and spike arms are one chǐ four cùn wide,
seven cùn thick,

The horizontal arms are flush with the outside of the frame,

six cùn wide,
three cùn thick,

There is a sighting device,
and a flexible winch,

The base
weighs one shí,
made from timber five cùn in circumference.
The bolts are ten chǐ long,

The bolts are three chǐ higher than the crossbow arm,

Ten men operate this cart,

nor establish order externally,

the weak to belittle the strong,

lest you bring harm upon yourself.

Sparrow holes

Outside the pillars,

Close to the ground,

At the inner mouth of the tunnel, make a stove,
shaped like a kiln,
The tunnel should accommodate seven or eight bundles of mugwort,

When the tunnel is nearly completed,

If the tunnel encounters the enemy,
